title: Ratbert's Garbage Christmas Gift

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The best things in life are free, so I got you this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This looks like trash from my garbage can.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I only chewed on the delicious parts!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Spank you very much.

situation: Ratbert presents Dilbert with a small wrapped gift, explaining that the best things in life are free. Dilbert opens it and recognizes the contents as trash from his own garbage can. Ratbert cheerfully admits he only chewed the tasty bits, and Dilbert responds with a pointed, sarcastic thank-you.
punchline: Ratbert's 'free' gift is literally Dilbert's own garbage, partly eaten, and Dilbert's 'Spank you very much' is a sarcastic stand-in for a thank-you.
summary: A cheap-minded pet hands over a present that turns out to be his owner's own half-eaten rubbish, earning a sour, sarcastic thanks.

title: Department Mole Announces Himself Openly

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm the official department mole. I'll be reporting your every misstep to your Pointy-Haired Boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Won't this have a chilling effect on our creativity and honesty?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That didn't take long.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting, Ratbert introduces himself as the official department mole who will report every mistake to the boss. Dilbert objects that this will chill creativity and honesty among the team. Ratbert, noting the immediate reaction, jots down Dilbert's complaint.
punchline: Dilbert's open objection to the surveillance is itself treated as the first reportable offense, showing that the mole's presence instantly stifles honest speech.
summary: A self-declared office informant wastes no time proving that his mere presence makes candid talk risky.

file: 2008/2008-08-20_company sent_local community_authorized_million dollars_fight for it_hobos_alley way.gif
title: Corporate Charity Hobo Fight Contest

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company sent me to give money to a hobo. It's our way of helping the local community.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm authorized to give a million dollars to one of you.

transcript.speaker: Hobo
transcript.text: How do you decide which one?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could fight for it.

transcript.speaker: Hobo
transcript.text: Say "go."

setting: Alley with a burning trash barrel
situation: Dilbert approaches two hobos standing around a burning barrel and explains that his company wants to give a million dollars to one of them as community outreach. When asked how he will choose which one gets the money, he suggests they fight for it. One hobo, holding a bottle, eagerly tells him to say 'go.'
punchline: Dilbert turns corporate charity into a brawl by making the needy compete violently for the money, and the hobo is all too ready to start.
summary: A company's charitable gift to the homeless turns into a gladiator match when its messenger decides the winner should be whoever wins a fistfight.

file: 2008/2008-10-18_philanthropist_eat for one day_opulent life_super models_stop giving_inspire_try harder.gif
title: Dogbert's Self-Serving Philanthropy Philosophy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Philanthropist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If I give a man a fish, he will eat for one day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if I inspire him by my opulent lifestyle and my squiring of supermodels, he might try harder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't stop giving.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's like a curse.

setting: Outdoor countryside path and wooden fence with hills behind
situation: Dogbert, billed as a philanthropist, walks with Dilbert and reworks the give-a-man-a-fish proverb. He claims the best way to help people is to inspire them with his luxurious lifestyle and supermodel companions. Dilbert observes that Dogbert can't stop giving, and Dogbert sarcastically agrees that it's like a curse.
punchline: Dogbert presents flaunting his wealth and glamorous life as charity, then smugly laments his generosity as a burden.
summary: A self-satisfied dog recasts a famous proverb about charity so that showing off his riches becomes his gift to humanity.

title: Acting Boss Practices Lying

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm in charge while our Pointy-Haired Boss is on vacation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I expect each of you to be professional and productive during this time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nice lying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I practiced in front of a mirror.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Dilbert announces to his coworkers at a meeting table that he is in charge while the boss is away and tells them to be professional and productive. Wally sarcastically compliments his lying, and Dilbert admits he rehearsed the speech in a mirror.
punchline: Dilbert's demand for professionalism and productivity is so unbelievable that even he admits it was a rehearsed lie, showing neither he nor his team has any intention of working while the boss is gone.
summary: A temporarily promoted engineer delivers an unconvincing demand for hard work, and a coworker praises the performance as a well-practiced fib.

title: Emotional Investment Means Dysfunctional Families

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to have the same emotional investment in this company as you have with your families.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm divorced.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm single.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have never been kissed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mission accomplished.

situation: The Boss tells his employees at a conference table that he wants them to be as emotionally invested in the company as they are in their families. Wally says he is divorced, Dilbert says he is single, and Asok says he has never been kissed. The Boss smugly declares success.
punchline: The employees have no healthy family relationships, so the Boss's wish for equal emotional investment in the company is already achieved, which is bleakly funny and shows how little life they have outside work.
summary: A manager asks his team to care about the company like family, and their sad personal lives prove they already do.

file: 2008/2008-03-27_date_stories of woe_no tv or internet_carving canoe_woman runs out.gif
title: Dilbert's Boring Date Story

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My cable system wasn't working last night. I didn't have TV or Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I stared at the wall until it was time for bed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I considered carving a canoe out of a tree trunk, but it seemed like a lot of work.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Check!

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date and tells the woman across from him about his night without cable TV or Internet. He explains that he just stared at a wall until bedtime and mentions considering carving a canoe from a tree trunk. His date, visibly horrified, waves frantically to call for the check.
punchline: Dilbert's dull, rambling anecdote about having nothing to do without TV or Internet is so boring and pathetic that his date desperately wants to end the evening immediately.
summary: A man's tedious tale of an entertainment-free evening drives his dinner companion to flag down the waiter in a panic.

file: 2008/2008-05-02_alternative fuel divison_oil into watwer_uninhabitable wasteland_water into fuel.gif
title: Turning Water Into Fuel, Fixed Later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our alternative fuel division has found a way to turn fresh water into fuel!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that turn the world into an uninhabitable wasteland in the long run?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not if someone finds a way to turn oil into water.

situation: The Boss presents a slide showing water turning into fuel, boasting about the alternative fuel division's breakthrough. Dilbert objects that using up fresh water would eventually make the planet uninhabitable. The Boss dismisses the concern by assuming someone will invent the reverse process.
punchline: The Boss waves away a serious flaw by relying on an imaginary future invention that undoes the damage, which is a flimsy plan that merely reverses the original problem.
summary: A manager brushes off an environmental objection to a new fuel idea by assuming a future miracle will fix it.

title: Maintaining the Illusion of Value

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's obvious what I need to do next.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I'll let you tell me so you can maintain the illusion of value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop being this way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saw that coming a mile away.

setting: Conference room with a glass wall
situation: The Boss meets with Dilbert and announces that the next step is obvious, but says he will let Dilbert suggest it so Dilbert can feel useful. Dilbert objects to this condescension, and the Boss replies that he saw the objection coming.
punchline: The Boss condescendingly pretends to humor Dilbert's input, then smugly claims he predicted Dilbert's objection, making himself unbeatable in the exchange.
summary: A manager patronizes his employee by pretending to need his advice, then brags that he anticipated the complaint.

file: 2008/2008-10-19_idea squirrel_steals your ideas_treats you like a nut_tackle him_boss office_squirrel_great ideas.gif
title: Idea Squirrel Steals Your Ideas

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Anyway, that's what I think should be done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Idea Squirrel!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What? What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Idea Squirrel steals your ideas and treats you like a nut for saying they were yours!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do I do now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your only hope is to tackle him before he gets to our boss's office.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Squirrel
transcript.text: Grrr...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is the squirrel that always has great ideas fighting with that nut?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

setting: Office cubicles and the boss's office
situation: After a coworker shares his idea with Dilbert, Dilbert spots the Idea Squirrel and warns that it steals ideas and makes the real owner look like a nut when they claim credit. Dilbert tells the coworker to tackle the squirrel before it reaches the boss's office. The coworker tackles it and gets mauled, and the boss watches the fight.
punchline: The boss sees the credit-stealing squirrel as the source of great ideas and the coworker who tackled it as a nut, proving the warning true.
summary: A furry thief of workplace brainstorms gets confronted by its victim, only to have management side with the thief.

title: Doctor's Note for Sick Days

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a doctor's note for the two days of work I missed.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You look healthy to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got better.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: How do I know you were sick?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The note just needs to say I was sick.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: So you want me to lie?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not a lie. I really was sick.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: If your company doesn't trust you, why should I?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good point.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I let the people in your waiting room cough on me? Then you can write a note saying I have what they have.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: As long as I didn't recommend it, I think that passes ethical muster.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You have nine diseases?

transcript.speaker: Green-skinned patient
transcript.text: That have names.

setting: A doctor's examination room and waiting room
situation: Dilbert asks his doctor for a note excusing two days of missed work, even though he has already recovered. The doctor refuses to vouch for an illness he cannot see, so Dilbert proposes deliberately catching something from the sick people in the waiting room. The doctor approves as long as it wasn't his idea, and Dilbert sits next to a sickly green patient.
punchline: The doctor's ethics only extend to not recommending the scheme himself, so deliberately infecting yourself to get a legitimate sick note is deemed acceptable.
summary: A man who wants proof of a past illness is told the best solution is to catch something contagious from the waiting room so the doctor can honestly write it up.

title: Begging for a Corporate Bailout

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our plan is to beg for a government bailout.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's good for everyone because otherwise our bloated carcass will blot out the sun.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have cookies and lemonade in the back.

setting: A podium at a press conference, with an exterior view of a corporate office building
situation: A company executive stands at a podium and announces that the company's plan is to ask the government for a bailout. He justifies it by admitting the company is so bloated that its collapse would be a disaster for everyone. He then wraps up the announcement by offering refreshments to the audience.
punchline: The executive openly admits his company is a bloated mess that deserves to fail, yet pitches the taxpayer-funded rescue as a favor to everyone, then casually offers cookies and lemonade as if it were a bake sale.
summary: A boss cheerfully pitches a taxpayer rescue for his oversized company as a public service and finishes with snacks.

title: Witness Confesses To Attempted Murder

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Where were you on the day that Dilbert was pushed out of your office window?

transcript.speaker: Witness
transcript.text: I was directly behind him, in this position, yelling "Die, die, die!"

transcript.speaker: Witness
transcript.text: The first question is just practice, right?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a lawyer, questions a bald witness on the stand about where he was when Dilbert was pushed out of his office window. The witness cheerfully demonstrates how he stood behind Dilbert shouting "Die, die, die!", openly confessing. He then asks whether the first question is just practice, showing he never understood the testimony was real.
punchline: The witness incriminates himself by enthusiastically re-enacting the murder attempt, then naively assumes the questioning hasn't really begun.
summary: A clueless witness gleefully admits on the stand to shoving Dilbert out a window, believing the opening question was only a warm-up.

title: Elbonian Inflation Potato Money Exchange

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: The inflation rate in Elbonia climbed to a billion percent.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 1
transcript.text: Quickly hand me the potato and I'll tell my cousin in Phlimsk to let go of the other end of my money.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 2
transcript.text: Make it snappy.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 1
transcript.text: Bradley! I have the potato!

setting: Dilbert's living room, and a muddy Elbonian village
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert watch a TV news report saying Elbonia's inflation rate has hit a billion percent. The scene cuts to two mud-covered Elbonians who exchange a potato for money, with a cousin far away literally holding the other end of a long measuring-tape-like strip of cash.
punchline: With inflation so extreme, money is worth so little that people barter in potatoes, and even a cash transaction must be hurriedly completed before the money loses its value.
summary: A news report about runaway inflation in a fictional backwater is followed by villagers frantically swapping a potato for currency that is rapidly becoming worthless.

file: 2008/2008-06-27_attend a meeting_bully you_making decions_bad for dept_no respect.gif
title: Bullied Into Covering for Absent Boss

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need you to attend a meeting for your boss while he's on vacation.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I plan to bully you into making decisions that are bad for your department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's almost as if you have no respect for me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yeah, almost.

setting: Office hallway near a cubicle wall
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to attend a meeting on behalf of his vacationing boss. He then openly admits he intends to bully Dilbert into making decisions that will harm Dilbert's own department. Dilbert remarks that this suggests a lack of respect, and the coworker agrees, but only 'almost'.
punchline: The coworker admits his lack of respect for Dilbert is only 'almost' total, which is a backhanded way of confirming that he has essentially no respect for him at all.
summary: A manipulative colleague cheerfully announces plans to push Dilbert around in a stand-in meeting and barely bothers to deny holding him in contempt.

title: Putrid Ideas Come With Warnings

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I'll tell you my idea if you promise not to reject it before thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already rejected it because only putrid ideas come with warnings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My time management is getting better.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't pretend to care.

situation: An intern asks Dilbert to promise he won't reject an idea before thinking about it. Dilbert says he has already rejected it, because only bad ideas need a warning attached. In the last panel, at home, Dilbert announces his time management is improving and Dogbert, sitting on the couch, says he can't even pretend to care.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses the intern's idea in advance, reasoning that anything needing a disclaimer must be bad, and then Dogbert coldly dismisses Dilbert's own small boast.
summary: A hopeful intern asks for an open mind but gets pre-emptively shot down, and Dilbert then receives the same brush-off from his dog.

title: Mordac Zaps Unauthorized Computer User

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Do you know how the system distinguishes between authorized and illegal access?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: ZAP!

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: It doesn't.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ha ha!!!

setting: Office cubicle with a computer desk
situation: Mordac, the head of IT security, asks an employee seated at a computer whether he knows how the system tells authorized users from illegal ones. The computer then electrocutes the employee, leaving him a smoking skeleton. Mordac deadpans that the system doesn't distinguish at all.
punchline: The security system punishes every user with electric shocks, authorized or not, showing Mordac's indifference to legitimate users and his hostility toward anyone using computers.
summary: An IT security chief's question about access control is answered by a shocking demonstration that the system treats everyone as an intruder.

title: Anti-Dilbert Needs Matterscreen

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I created an anti-Dilbert, but I don't know how to prevent him from being annihilated by matter when he leaves the vacuum.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: If you don't know how to do it, and he's the anti-you, that means he knows how.

transcript.speaker: Anti-Dilbert
transcript.text: Matterscreen, SPF 50.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Duh.

setting: Outdoors by a curb and garbage truck, then a lab with a large vacuum chamber
situation: Dilbert tells a garbage man that he has created an anti-Dilbert but cannot figure out how to keep him from being annihilated by matter when he leaves the vacuum chamber. The garbage man reasons that since the anti-Dilbert is the opposite of Dilbert, he must know the solution. The anti-Dilbert, visible in the chamber window, says the answer is matterscreen, SPF 50.
punchline: The garbage man's backwards logic that the anti-Dilbert must know what Dilbert doesn't turns out to work, with the solution being a sunscreen-style joke: matterscreen, SPF 50.
summary: A scientist's antimatter duplicate turns out to hold the answer to his own survival problem, and it is a silly sunscreen pun.

file: 2008/2008-12-14_agree_disagree_idea_plan_terrible idea_worst ever idea_bordering irresponsible_disagrees with everyone_idea is awful_manipulate me_terrible tidea_dance puppet dance.gif
title: Reverse Psychology Pitch Backfires Brilliantly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute to look at my terrible idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the worst idea ever. Totally impractical, and bordering on irresponsible.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why are you saying that about your own idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you're one of those jerks who automatically disagrees with everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm telling you my idea is awful so you will feel compelled to say it is great.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now that I know how you plan to manipulate me, it won't work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm so surprised to hear that you disagree.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now look at my terrible, terrible idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dance, puppet, dance.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This is a great idea!

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker to review his idea, deliberately calling it terrible because he knows the coworker reflexively disagrees with everyone. The coworker announces he has seen through the trick and will not be manipulated. Dilbert feigns surprise at the disagreement and presents the idea again, and the coworker ends up calling it great.
punchline: By announcing he won't be manipulated, the coworker disagrees with Dilbert's own reverse psychology, which is exactly the contrarian reaction Dilbert was counting on, so the coworker ends up praising the idea after all.
summary: A man tricks a habitual naysayer into endorsing his proposal by insisting it is dreadful, then exploits the man's attempt to resist the trick.

title: Reclaiming Stolen Conference Room Chairs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I want you to take any conference room chairs that are in cubicles and put them back where they belong.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: People are going to steal the chairs back as soon as I leave.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe, but do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: So... we agree that there's no way to tell if I really did it?

situation: The Boss orders Carol to collect conference room chairs that employees have taken into their cubicles and return them. Carol points out that people will simply steal the chairs back once she leaves. The Boss tells her to do it anyway, and Carol concludes that her work can never be verified.
punchline: Because the task is futile and unverifiable, Carol realizes she can safely do nothing and the boss would never be able to tell.
summary: Asked to repeatedly restore chairs that coworkers will just snatch again, an employee notes that nobody could ever check whether she actually did the job.

title: Literal Poison Pill Takeover Defense

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You can thwart this unfriendly takeover by using something called a poison pill.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I keep one in my watch. I'll take it immediately.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That's not. . .

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I suppose I could feed your tainted CEO carcass to the executives of the other company.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Gurgle

situation: Ratbert, acting as an advisor, tells the CEO he can fend off an unfriendly takeover with a 'poison pill.' The CEO misunderstands it as a literal pill, pulls one from his watch and swallows it. He dies, and Ratbert coolly notes that the poisoned corpse can at least be fed to the rival company's executives.
punchline: The CEO takes the financial term 'poison pill' literally and kills himself, and Ratbert shrugs it off by finding a darkly practical use for the body.
summary: A clueless chief executive swallows an actual poison tablet when told about a corporate takeover defense, leaving his adviser to improvise a grim new plan.

title: Engineers Unimpressed By Percentage Increase

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks to Marketing, sales have increased 100%!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Are you asking a room full of engineers to be excited about a big percentage increase over a trivial base?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You leave me no choice but to give you the stink eye.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Make it stop!

setting: Conference room during a sales presentation
situation: The Boss presents a chart at a meeting, boasting that marketing doubled sales. Dilbert points out that engineers won't be impressed by a large percentage gain from a tiny starting figure. The Boss responds by glaring at him with the 'stink eye', and Dilbert reacts as if in real pain.
punchline: The Boss's feeble threat of a disapproving glare is treated as a painful weapon, mocking both his weak authority and his misleading use of a 100% statistic on a trivial base.
summary: A manager touts doubled sales from a minuscule starting point, and when an engineer calls out the weak statistic, the manager's only retaliation is an unintimidating glare.

title: Canary Warns of Boring Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I got a canary to warn us when our meetings are too boring.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Canaries die of boredom before humans, so. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess he knew that.

situation: The Boss explains that he brought a canary to the meeting to act as an early warning system for when meetings become too boring, since canaries die of boredom before humans do. The second panel shows the office building exterior while he trails off. In the last panel the canary is lying dead or collapsed on the table, and Dilbert remarks that the canary must have known that.
punchline: The canary has already died of boredom during the meeting, proving the Boss's meetings are unbearably dull, and the Boss didn't notice until Dilbert pointed it out.
summary: A manager brings a canary to meetings as a boredom detector, and the bird promptly keels over mid-meeting.

file: 2008/2008-05-13_make copies_mental task_bloated cadaver_staple or no_asks secretary.gif
title: Insulting a Coworker Into Making Copies

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Our boss asked me to make some copies. But I fear doing such a menial task will brand me as unimportant.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I was hoping you could make the copies for me since your career is already a bloated cadaver.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: If I am reading your body language correctly, you are wondering "Staple or no staple?"

situation: Asok explains that he has been asked to make copies but fears the menial task will make him look unimportant. He asks a coworker in the next cubicle to do it for him, insulting her career in the process. The coworker, seething with anger, crumples paper in her fist while Asok cheerfully guesses she is only wondering whether to staple the copies.
punchline: Asok is so oblivious that he mistakes his coworker's furious reaction to his insult for a polite question about stapling, and assumes she has agreed to do his work.
summary: A status-conscious young employee dumps his photocopying on a colleague after insulting her, then misreads her steaming rage as willingness to help.

file: 2008/2008-07-24_sympathy_in need of sympathy_so sorry_face injured_being thorough.gif
title: Dogbert's Overly Thorough Sympathy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need some sympathy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm so sorry your face looks like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My face isn't injured.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, excuse me for being thorough.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert on the back of the couch
situation: Dilbert, wearing head bandages and an arm cast, asks Dogbert for some sympathy. Dogbert offers condolences for how Dilbert's face looks, and Dilbert points out that his face isn't injured. Dogbert claims he was just covering every base.
punchline: Dogbert's 'sympathy' is really a backhanded insult about Dilbert's normal-looking face, which he passes off as being thorough.
summary: A bandaged Dilbert seeks comfort from Dogbert, who instead delivers a sly insult disguised as exhaustive sympathy.

title: Legacy Systems: Biggest Rind in Compost

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How would you like to be in charge of the legacy systems?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's like being the biggest rind in the compost heap.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I surrender to the bacteria.

situation: The Boss stands beside Dilbert's desk and offers him the job of managing the company's legacy systems. Dilbert compares the role to being the biggest rind in a compost heap, meaning he'd be the largest piece of garbage waiting to decay. The Boss tells him to do it anyway, and Dilbert slumps back in his chair in defeat.
punchline: Dilbert's compost metaphor shows that maintaining legacy systems is a thankless dead-end job, and the Boss's 'do it anyway' reveals the assignment isn't actually a choice.
summary: Offered the unglamorous job of looking after the company's ancient software, Dilbert likens himself to rotting kitchen scraps and then gives in when his boss insists.

file: 2008/2008-04-03_project_customer calls_can't deliver on time_features needed_getting waterboarded_birthday_price went up.gif
title: Dilbert Offers Help, Gets Awful Tasks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project is on hold. Do you need any help on yours?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sure. Call these customers and tell them we can't deliver on time or with the features they need.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any tasks that DON'T feel like getting waterboarded on your birthday?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And tell them the price went up.

situation: Dilbert, whose own project is on hold, offers to help Alice with hers. Alice hands him the unpleasant job of phoning customers to say the product will be late and lacking features. When Dilbert asks for a less awful task, she adds that he must also tell them the price went up.
punchline: Dilbert's offer of help backfires as Alice piles on ever worse customer news, making the job go from unpleasant to unbearable.
summary: A idle engineer volunteers to help a coworker and is stuck delivering a trio of terrible messages to angry customers.

file: 2008/2008-04-20_appear to be concerned_decision making_frequently thwarted_impractical advice_no one decides_perpetual problems_rarely disappointed_unwarranted optimism.gif
title: Dilbert Seeks Useless Boss Advice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have an issue.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Lordy lord.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one in the department wants to be left out of the decision making.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But no one is willing to make a decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As a result, all of my problems are perpetual.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you do something about that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can appear to be concerned.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's this expression?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you combine that with some impractical advice and unwarranted optimism?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm frequently thwarted, but rarely disappointed.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert brings the Boss a problem: everyone wants a say in decisions but nobody will actually make one, so his problems never get resolved. The Boss offers only to look concerned and strikes a pose. Dilbert, resigned, asks him to add impractical advice and false optimism, then goes home to Dogbert.
punchline: Dilbert has such low expectations of management that he knows the best he'll get is fake concern and bad advice, so he is never truly disappointed.
summary: A worker stuck in a decision-free department asks his manager for help and settles for a show of sympathy and empty encouragement.

title: Dogbert Diversifies Into Diseased Livestock

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Financial Advisor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should invest all of your money in diseased livestock.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It would be unwise to invest in just one sick cow, but if you aggregate a bunch of them together, the risk goes away.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's called math.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Suddenly I feel all savvy.

setting: Dogbert's financial advisor office, at a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a financial advisor, tells the Boss to put all his money into diseased livestock. He justifies it by claiming that pooling many sick cows together eliminates the risk of any single one. The Boss, impressed by the pseudo-mathematical reasoning, says he feels savvy.
punchline: Dogbert misuses the idea of diversification and aggregation to claim that bundling lots of bad assets makes them safe, and the gullible Boss is flattered into believing it, which mirrors how toxic mortgage securities were rationalized.
summary: A scheming dog advisor convinces his client that a heap of sick cows is a safe investment as long as there are enough of them.

file: 2008/2008-07-15_brain_part of brain_controls morality_the natural_glows from within.gif
title: Missing Morality Makes Perfect Manager

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My doctor says everything is fine except for the part of my brain that controls morality.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gasp! The management prophesies are true. You must be the one they call. . .

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The Natural?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He glows from within.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his doctor found nothing wrong with him except for the part of his brain that controls morality. The Boss gasps, believing an ancient management prophecy is being fulfilled, and Catbert and the Boss marvel that Dilbert must be 'The Natural' who glows from within.
punchline: The joke implies that lacking a sense of morality is the ideal qualification for a manager, so Dilbert's defect marks him as the prophesied perfect leader.
summary: A moral deficiency that worries a doctor thrills the company's leaders, who see it as the sign of a born manager.

file: 2008/2008-02-29_300 iq_computer_convincing people_desk_evil director_human resources_nobel prize_track record_unix_technology_business.gif
title: Catbert's Impossible Job Posting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, the evil director of Human Resources, posts a job opening.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Requirements:

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Candidate must have an I.Q. of 300, two centuries of Unix experience and a track record of winning Nobel Prizes.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: 90% of my job is convincing people they don't deserve theirs.

setting: Catbert's office in the Human Resources department
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, types up a job posting at his computer. The listed requirements are absurdly impossible, including a 300 IQ, two centuries of Unix experience and Nobel Prizes. In the last panel his thought bubble reveals that the impossible requirements are deliberate.
punchline: Catbert writes impossible job requirements on purpose so that nobody qualifies, because his real job is making people feel unworthy of the jobs they already hold.
summary: An HR villain drafts a ridiculous wish list for a vacancy, then privately admits his main duty is making employees feel they don't deserve their positions.

file: 2008/2008-01-07_mole hired_boss_sneak_mole as mole_people think_gas bag_bad press_bad thoughts_worthless_self important.gif
title: Employee Mole Delivers Brutal Feedback

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What have you learned this week working as my employee mole?

transcript.speaker: Mole
transcript.text: Some of the people in this building think you're a worthless, self-important gas bag.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do the other people think?

transcript.speaker: Mole
transcript.text: They don't know you.

situation: The Boss asks his newly hired employee mole what intelligence he has gathered about what coworkers think of him. The mole reports that some people consider him a worthless, self-important gas bag. The Boss hopefully asks about everyone else's opinion and is told they simply don't know him.
punchline: Even the people who haven't formed a negative opinion of the Boss only lack one because they've never met him, implying everyone who knows him thinks he's awful.
summary: A boss fishing for reassurance from his spy gets a devastating verdict on his reputation.

file: 2008/2008-12-07_computer_defense_security_workstation_logged in_netowrk_teach someone a lesson_activating defensive wedgie system_violated perimeter_technology.gif
title: Network Security Wedgie Defense System

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This workstation is still logged in to the network.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time to teach someone a lesson about security.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll just go in here and . . .

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Warning! Warning! Idiot alert!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Activating defensive wedgie system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to go. Some idiot violated my perimeter.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Beep beep

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please make it stop.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then how would you learn?

situation: The Boss finds an unattended workstation still logged in and decides to snoop around to teach its owner a security lesson. The computer sounds an idiot alert and a mechanical arm gives him a wedgie. Dilbert, alerted by his phone, comes to see the intruder and refuses to stop the punishment.
punchline: Dilbert's security system physically punishes intruders with wedgies, and he sarcastically implies the punishment is educational for the Boss, who was the one violating security.
summary: A snooping manager triggers a booby-trapped computer that wedgies him, and its owner declines to end the lesson.

title: Internet Tempts Dilbert From Working

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want to be productive, but the Internet is calling to me.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Psst!

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Hey, buddy. I've got pictures of gadgets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cool ones?

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Sure, let's pretend that matters.

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk thinking that he wants to be productive, but the Internet is tempting him. His computer whispers to him like a shady dealer, offering pictures of gadgets. Dilbert asks whether they are cool ones, and the computer sarcastically replies that they will pretend it matters.
punchline: The computer sarcastically admits that browsing gadget pictures is meaningless, yet Dilbert is going to give in to the distraction anyway.
summary: A distracted office worker is lured away from his tasks by his own computer offering a stream of shiny gadget photos.

title: Made-Up Numbers Are Just As Useful

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't have any accurate numbers so I just made up this one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies have shown that accurate numbers aren't any more useful than the ones you make up.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: How many studies showed that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eighty-seven.

situation: Dilbert presents a slide showing a dollar figure and admits he invented it because he had no accurate data. He defends himself by claiming studies show accurate numbers are no more useful than invented ones. When an attendee asks how many studies, he answers with another made-up number.
punchline: Dilbert backs up his claim that made-up numbers are as good as real ones by citing a number of studies that he obviously just made up too.
summary: A presenter confesses to inventing his figures, then props up the excuse with a fabricated statistic about research that probably doesn't exist.

title: Speakerphone Complaint Solved Too Easily

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Loud Howard insists on using his speakerphone in his cubicle. You have to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll move him to a private office that just became available. Problem solved.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need to punch you until we both forget what happened here.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Spare the glasses.

situation: Alice, with Dilbert and Asok beside her, complains to the Boss that Loud Howard keeps using his speakerphone in his cubicle. The Boss calmly offers a sensible fix: moving Loud Howard into a newly available private office. Alice is so enraged that the problem was solved by something that simple, and so irritated at having to ask, that she wants to hit him, and Dilbert asks her to spare his glasses.
punchline: The Boss finally offers a competent, reasonable solution, which is so out of character that Alice feels she must violently erase the memory of it, and Dilbert's concern is only for his glasses.
summary: A noisy coworker's phone habit gets an unexpectedly easy fix from management, leaving an angry employee ready to throw punches.

title: Jury Verdict Based On Boredom

transcript.speaker: Jury Foreman
transcript.text: We find in favor of the plaintiff dude.

transcript.speaker: Jury Foreman
transcript.text: There was some discussion about which one is the plaintiff — the complainy guy or the weasel.

transcript.speaker: Jury Foreman
transcript.text: But we were unanimous in not wanting to be here any longer.

transcript.speaker: Jurors
transcript.text: Aye!

situation: A jury foreman stands and reads the verdict to the court. He admits the jurors weren't sure which party was the plaintiff, and that their only point of agreement was that they wanted to leave. The other jurors chime in with an enthusiastic 'Aye!'
punchline: The jury reached its verdict without understanding the case, driven only by their shared desire to go home, which mocks how arbitrary and careless jury decisions can be.
summary: A clueless jury announces a verdict while confessing they never worked out who was suing whom and just wanted out of there.

title: Aggressive Coffee Machine Grabs Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You must be the new coffee machine.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thoop!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's aggressive, but I like that in my coffee makers.

situation: Wally, holding an empty mug, greets a large metal coffee machine with tentacle-like arms. The machine shoots out a long tube and yanks Wally's necktie, pulling him toward it. Wally ends up with his tie stretched out in front of Dilbert and casually remarks on the machine's behavior.
punchline: Wally calmly accepts being physically attacked by the machine, treating its aggression as a desirable feature in a coffee maker.
summary: A menacing new office appliance snags a coworker by the necktie, and he shrugs it off as an acceptable trait in a source of caffeine.

title: Offsite Hotel Was Actually Hell

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That hotel you booked for the management offsite meeting wasn't actually a hotel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm fairly sure it was the foyer to hell.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What gave you that idea?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our concierge was a swarm of locusts!!!

situation: The Boss complains to a female employee, who had booked the hotel for the management offsite meeting, that it wasn't really a hotel. A building exterior is shown as he says it was the foyer to hell. When she asks what made him think that, he shouts that the concierge was a swarm of locusts.
punchline: The Boss's evidence for the hotel being the entrance to hell is an absurdly biblical plague of locusts working the front desk, which he treats as the employee's booking error.
summary: After a management retreat goes horribly wrong, the boss blames his subordinate for sending him to what he believes was the antechamber of the underworld.

title: New Guy's Towering Armpits Warning

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't get too friendly with the new guy. His armpits are 66 inches off the ground.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He seems nice. I fail to see how the height of his armpits is relevant.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll see.

transcript.speaker: Tall coworker
transcript.text: Hey, little buddy. Let me tell you about my weekend.

setting: Office lunch table, then a cubicle
situation: At lunch, Wally warns Asok not to befriend the new guy, citing the odd detail that his armpits are 66 inches off the ground. Asok doesn't see why that matters. Back at his cubicle, the very tall new coworker looms over the partition and calls Asok 'little buddy', ready to share his weekend story.
punchline: The new guy's height means his armpits are at Asok's face level, so friendly chats will involve an unpleasant close encounter with them.
summary: A coworker's cryptic warning about a tall newcomer's anatomy is explained when the giant leans over a cubicle wall to chat with a short colleague.

title: The Bullying Cow Supervisor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Cow Supervisor

transcript.speaker: Cow Supervisor
transcript.text: I overcame a lot of bias against cows to get this job.

transcript.speaker: Cow Supervisor
transcript.text: People think that a cow with strong leadership skills is just a jerk.

transcript.speaker: Cow Supervisor
transcript.text: Is that what YOU think, Baldy? Huh? Do you? Do you?

transcript.speaker: Baldy
transcript.text: Um... I'll say no.

situation: A cow in a necktie, newly promoted to supervisor, tells a bald employee that he overcame prejudice against cows to get the job. He complains that strong leadership in a cow gets mistaken for being a jerk, then aggressively jabs a finger at the employee and demands to know whether he thinks so too. The nervous employee, holding a coffee mug, quickly says no.
punchline: The cow proves the stereotype right by bullying his subordinate into agreeing that he is not a jerk, and the employee answers in fear.
summary: A cow boss insists he is misjudged as a jerk while intimidating a coworker into agreeing with him.

file: 2008/2008-03-12_pronouned hay-soos_fixed eye sight_hair regrow_40 shares_punch pilot light_ceo_team organizer.gif
title: Boss Plans to Punch Jesus

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pronounced Hay-soos

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The new team leader, Jesus, is gaining quite a following.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He fixed my eyesight and made my hair regrow. I think he wants your job as CEO.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For forty shares of stock, I could point him out at lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll punch his pilot light out!

situation: Wally, now sporting a huge head of regrown hair, visits the boss's office with his coffee mug. He warns the boss that a new team leader named Jesus (pronounced Hay-soos) is gaining a following by performing miracles like fixing eyesight and regrowing hair. Wally then offers to point the man out for forty shares of stock, and the boss angrily vows to punch him.
punchline: Wally, who is lazy and opportunistic, turns a miracle worker's popularity into a stock-for-information deal, while the paranoid boss immediately responds with violence rather than recognizing the benefit of the new hire.
summary: A coworker with newly sprouted hair tips off the paranoid CEO that a charismatic miracle-working new hire could steal his job, then tries to profit from the gossip.

file: 2008/2008-11-06_evil director_human reasources_resume_sense of desparation_janitor_clean toiltes_bury janitor.gif
title: Catbert Hires Someone to Bury Janitor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've seen your resume and I sense desperation.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our janitor recently passed away, so I have a job for you.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: You want me to clean toilets?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, I want you to bury the janitor.

setting: Catbert's human resources office; final panel shows the exterior of an office building
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, interviews a desperate job applicant and says he has an opening because the janitor recently died. The applicant assumes he'll be taking over the cleaning duties, but Catbert reveals the job is to bury the dead janitor.
punchline: The applicant's desperation is exploited for a job even worse than cleaning toilets: disposing of the previous employee's body.
summary: A cruel HR boss offers a desperate jobseeker a position that turns out to involve burying his predecessor.

title: Stupid Rule Requires Telling Someone

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Director of Green

transcript.speaker: Director of Green
transcript.text: Turn off your computer while you're thinking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's stupid.

transcript.speaker: Director of Green
transcript.text: If it weren't stupid, you wouldn't need me to tell you to do it.

situation: The Director of Green, a manager in charge of environmental initiatives, stands over Dilbert and tells him to turn off his computer whenever he is thinking. Dilbert objects that the instruction is stupid. The Director replies that this is exactly why he has to be told to do it.
punchline: The Director's circular logic implies that any policy people would not follow voluntarily is justified by the fact that it needs enforcing, so being stupid becomes proof that it is necessary.
summary: A green-minded manager defends a silly energy-saving order by arguing that its silliness is the very reason it must be mandated.

file: 2008/2008-06-19_rumor control_paid per rumor_terrorit training campo_exotic dancer_weekends.gif
title: Rumor Control Replaces One Rumor Worse

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm from the Dogbert Rumor Control Service.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People are saying Ted is an exotic male dancer on weekends. I know it isn't true because he spends all of his free time in a terrorist training camp.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Isn't that worse?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I get paid per rumor. It's not a perfect system.

situation: Dogbert arrives at Alice's desk offering a rumor control service. He claims to debunk a rumor that Ted moonlights as an exotic dancer by revealing that Ted actually spends his free time at a terrorist training camp. Alice points out this is worse, and Dogbert admits he is paid per rumor.
punchline: Dogbert's rumor control service is paid per rumor, so he has an incentive to create new, worse rumors while supposedly squashing old ones.
summary: A self-appointed rumor controller swaps one harmless office rumor for a far more alarming one because his pay depends on how many rumors he handles.

file: 2008/2008-04-11_advice to intern_don't finish on deadline_freedom_overworked_less time_nitpick.gif
title: Never Finish Before the Deadline

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Heed my advice, young Asok. Only an idiot finishes a project before the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The less time you give people to nitpick, the more time you have to pretend you are overworked.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Freedom is just another word for people finding out you're useless.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Wally sits across a table from Asok over lunch and dispenses cynical career advice. He tells the young intern never to finish a project early, because early delivery leaves reviewers time to find faults and leaves him no cover for looking busy. He ends by saying that free time just exposes how useless a person is.
punchline: Wally admits that his strategy of dragging work out to the deadline exists only to hide the fact that he has nothing useful to do.
summary: Over lunch, a lazy veteran coaches a naive young colleague to stretch out his work so nobody discovers he contributes nothing.

title: Already Used To Head Cameras

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We've installed surveillance cameras to monitor your work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It might seem like an unconscionable assault on your privacy, but you'll get used to it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm already a little bit used to it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Used to what?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells staff in a meeting that surveillance cameras now monitor their work and that they will get used to the privacy invasion. In the last panel a bald coworker wearing a camera rigged to a headband on his forehead says he is already used to it, and Dilbert, who has a similar camera on his own head, asks what he means.
punchline: The employees are already wearing monitoring cameras strapped to their heads without realizing it, so they are 'used to' surveillance before even noticing it.
summary: After HR announces workplace monitoring cameras, one employee reveals he has long been accustomed to the contraption on his head while Dilbert remains oblivious to his own.

title: Smartphone Versus Hammer Showdown

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can your phone do this?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let me see.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bam! Bam! Bam!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can your hammer do that?

situation: A coworker proudly shows off a feature on his phone and asks Alice if her phone can do the same. She takes it and angrily smashes it against the table repeatedly with a hammer, while Dilbert looks on. She then asks him whether his hammer could do that.
punchline: Alice turns the gadget one-upmanship around by destroying his phone with a hammer, implying that the tool he considers inferior is far better at violence than his phone is at anything.
summary: A man brags about his phone's abilities, and Alice answers by pulverizing it with a hammer.

file: 2008/2008-12-08_computer_hacking_illegal_support_technology_diagnose computer problem_remotely_spam server_snoop files_pilfer bank act..gif
title: Tech Support Hijacks Your Computer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: May I remotely take over your computer to diagnose the problem?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now hold while I snoop into your personal files, pilfer your bank accounts and turn your computer into a spam server.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's illegal!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So are 75% of your personal files, but you don't see me getting all huffy.

setting: Dogbert's Tech Support call, with Dogbert and a customer at their own computers
situation: Dogbert, working as a tech support agent, asks a customer for permission to remotely take over their computer. Once granted, he cheerfully announces he will snoop through files, steal from bank accounts and make the machine a spam server. When the customer objects that this is illegal, Dogbert retorts that most of the customer's own files are illegal too.
punchline: Dogbert deflects the customer's legitimate complaint by pointing out that the customer's own files (pirated media and the like) are mostly illegal, so he has no moral high ground.
summary: A pet-run help desk gains remote access to a caller's machine and cheerfully admits to planned crimes, then shrugs off the objection by calling out the caller's own dubious files.

title: Boss Won't Spend Political Capital

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I try to give you the raise you deserve, the people above me will just reduce it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe you could use some of your political capital to argue my case.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe not.

setting: The Boss's office, across his desk during a salary discussion
situation: The Boss tells Alice he can't give her the raise she deserves because his superiors would just cut it. Alice suggests he spend some of his political capital to argue for her. The Boss flatly refuses, and Alice is left glaring angrily.
punchline: The Boss values his own political standing far more than fairly rewarding his employee, so he simply won't advocate for her.
summary: A manager pleads helplessness about a pay increase and then declines to lift a finger when his employee proposes a way forward.

title: Drunken Lemurs Versus Managers Comic

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our surveillance cameras caught you posting this anti-management comic on the wall.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This comic compares managers to drunken lemurs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you think drunken lemurs are like managers?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: No. Some lemurs can hold their liquor.

situation: The Boss calls a bald employee into his office after surveillance cameras caught him posting an anti-management comic on the wall. The Boss reads the comic aloud, which likens managers to drunken lemurs, and asks the employee whether he really thinks the two are alike. The employee answers that they are not alike, because some lemurs can hold their liquor.
punchline: The employee's denial is actually a deeper insult: he says managers are worse than drunken lemurs, because at least some lemurs can handle their alcohol.
summary: Confronted over a comic mocking managers, a worker defends himself with a reply that is even more insulting than the comic itself.

file: 2008/2008-05-25_engineers_hauled away_human resources_questioning mental stability_sealed in concrete_wrapped in plastic_bodies hidden_business.gif
title: Engineer Fails Psychological Evaluation Spectacularly

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why???

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Catbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How'd it go?
