situation: The Boss sends Dilbert to Human Resources for a psychological evaluation, arguing that everything an engineer says is abnormal. Catbert, running the evaluation, asks Dilbert how many bodies are hidden under his house, and Dilbert's technically logical answers keep getting more incriminating. He ends up strapped to a hand truck and carted away by police officers.
punchline: Dilbert's literal, engineer-style reasoning about hidden bodies makes him sound like a murderer, so the evaluation confirms the Boss's claim that engineers are abnormal.
summary: A routine mental health screening goes badly wrong when an engineer answers a trick question with cold, overly precise logic and gets hauled off by police.

file: 2008/2008-11-16_imagination_experince_email_boss_hurts brain_think about it_team players_new projects_form of evil_people squander it.gif
title: Experience Means Never Doing Work

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or am I doing your job, plus mine?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's not your imagination, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's a little thing I call experience.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Once a week, I e-mail our Pointy-Haired Boss and ask him a question.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I make the question so complicated that it hurts his brain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He'll spend the rest of the week avoiding me so he doesn't need to think about it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Meanwhile he seeks out team players and hammers them with new projects.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So... experience is a form of evil?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Not always. Some people squander it.

situation: Asok complains that he is doing both his own work and his coworker's. The coworker explains that his experience lets him email the boss a deliberately complicated question each week, so the boss avoids him and instead dumps new projects on eager team players like Asok.
punchline: The coworker's 'experience' is really expertise in manipulating the boss to avoid work, so he admits it is evil but says other people just waste it.
summary: A slacking veteran reveals to an overworked young colleague how he confuses the boss into leaving him alone while others get buried in assignments.

title: Antimatter Dilbert Meets Coffee Splash

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm the Antimatter Dilbert. If my thin film of matterscreen washed off, I would come in contact with matter and be annihilated.

transcript.speaker: SFX
transcript.text: Kaboom!

transcript.speaker: SFX
transcript.text: Sploosh!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Once again, my first instinct wasn't the best.

situation: Dilbert announces to Alice that he is the Antimatter Dilbert and would be annihilated if his protective matterscreen washed off. Alice reacts instinctively by throwing her coffee at him, which causes an explosion. Afterward she is left standing in the aftermath, reflecting on her poor decision.
punchline: Alice's impulse to douse the annoying Dilbert with coffee backfires spectacularly because he really was made of antimatter, so her first instinct was a mistake.
summary: A colleague's bizarre physics claim gets tested the hard way when Alice reacts with a hot beverage and ends up with explosive consequences.

title: Security Clamps Strip-Search Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My only hope for productivity is to smuggle in my home laptop.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Clamp

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Clamp

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Clamp

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Now hand over the non-standard cell phone you keep in the elastic of your underpants.

situation: Dilbert thinks to himself that he must sneak his home laptop into work to get anything done. Mechanical clamps seize him, strip off his clothes and dangle him upside down, and his laptop falls to the floor. A grinning security guard then demands the unauthorized cell phone hidden in his underpants.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to bypass restrictive company technology rules is foiled by an absurdly invasive security system that knows even where he hides his contraband phone.
summary: A worker's scheme to sneak in his own laptop ends with robotic clamps stripping him down and a guard confiscating his hidden phone.

title: CEO Admits Company Is Insolvent Hologram

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO visits

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: We're going to change our focus...

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: From pretending to make good products, to pretending to be solvent.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Bzzzt

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: On a related note, I've always been a hologram.

setting: Conference room during a CEO visit
situation: The CEO addresses a meeting and announces a change of company focus. He reveals the new strategy is to pretend to be financially solvent instead of pretending to make good products. His image then flickers and he vanishes, leaving an empty chair, revealing he was only ever a hologram.
punchline: The company has been faking both quality and financial health, and the CEO himself turns out to be fake too, as a literal hologram.
summary: A visiting chief executive reveals the firm's new strategy is faking financial stability, then flickers out of existence as a projected image.

title: Imaginary Friends Ruin Dinner Date

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Do you have any hobbies?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to read obscure articles on the Internet and imagine having friends who are interested in the same things.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: But you do have friends, right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it too late to change the subject?

setting: Restaurant table on a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date at a table with a pink tablecloth, and his date asks about his hobbies. He admits he reads obscure internet articles and imagines having friends who share his interests. When she asks whether he actually has friends, he awkwardly tries to change the subject.
punchline: Dilbert's hobby is really a confession of loneliness, and his attempt to dodge the follow-up question confirms he has no real friends.
summary: A man on a date accidentally reveals his social isolation while describing his solitary online pastime.

file: 2008/2008-05-24_churn butter_needs_next budget cycle_not in budget_broken computer.gif
title: Churning Butter Until Budget Arrives

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My computer is broken. I need a new one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't have the budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do things that don't require a computer until the next budget cycle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like churning my own butter?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You make it sound creepy.

setting: The Boss's office, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss his computer is broken and he needs a replacement. The Boss refuses because there is no budget and tells him to find work that doesn't need a computer until the next budget cycle. Dilbert sarcastically suggests churning his own butter, and the Boss says it sounds creepy.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically offers an absurd non-computer task to show how unreasonable the Boss's order is, and the Boss misses the sarcasm entirely, only objecting that the phrasing sounds creepy.
summary: Denied a replacement for his dead computer, an employee mockingly proposes homemade dairy work as his new job, and his oblivious manager just finds the idea unsettling.

title: Boss's Bargain ERP Contract Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saved a fortune by personally negotiating the contract for our new ERP system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You bought outdated hardware and forgot several components that are required.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I like software with my hardware, but that's just me.

situation: The Boss brags to the group that he saved a fortune by personally negotiating the contract for the new ERP system. Dilbert, holding a document, points out that the Boss bought outdated hardware and left out required components. Dilbert adds sarcastically that he prefers his hardware to come with software.
punchline: The Boss's supposed savings came from buying obsolete, incomplete equipment, and Dilbert sarcastically notes that he expected the system to include software.
summary: A boss takes credit for a cheap purchasing deal until an engineer reveals the bargain was missing essential parts, including any software at all.

file: 2008/2008-04-13_brilliant ideas_carnage_honesty_ignorance_ludicrous ideas_mean spirited_mistaken self image_roll eyes_share project_verbally demolish.gif
title: Alice's Cooperation Means Demolishing Ideas

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Alice, I'm hoping we can work together on this project in the spirit of cooperation.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll have some ideas, and you'll have some ideas, and together we can pick the best ones.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sure, that's one approach.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But I prefer to exhale deeply and roll my eyes while you prattle.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then I will verbally demolish your ludicrous ideas, and dismantle your mistaken self-image as a competent man.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The carnage will create a striking contrast for the warm, clear glow of my brilliant ideas.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Later, I will round out the package by spreading amusing stories about how ignorant you are.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is there any chance of doing it my way?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now watch the eyes.

situation: A male coworker proposes a cooperative, idea-sharing approach to a joint project with Alice. Alice calmly lays out her actual method: sigh and roll her eyes at his ideas, tear them apart, make her own ideas look brilliant, and then mock him to others. When he asks if they can do it his way, she responds by rolling her eyes.
punchline: Alice answers the request to collaborate by openly describing her plan to humiliate him, then demonstrates the eye-roll as her rejection of any alternative.
summary: A hopeful colleague proposes teamwork, and Alice cheerfully explains her plan to belittle him step by step before proving it with a withering eye roll.

file: 2008/2008-07-12_masters degree_business_promoted to management_less useful_3 years_night classes_rock.gif
title: Dogbert Offers Faster Uselessness Training

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking about getting a master's degree in business so I can get promoted to management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How long does it take to learn how to be less useful?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Three years of night classes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hold still and I'll save you three years.

situation: Dilbert stands on a grassy hill and tells Dogbert he is considering a business master's degree to get promoted into management. He asks how long it takes to learn to be less useful, and Dogbert answers that it takes three years of night classes. Dogbert then picks up a rock and offers to speed things up by hitting Dilbert on the head.
punchline: Dogbert offers to knock Dilbert unconscious or brain-damage him with a rock, since being less useful is what management promotion really requires, and that is quicker than an MBA.
summary: A man planning to earn an MBA to reach management is told by his dog that a rock to the head would get him there three years sooner.

title: Dogbert Escalates Complaint to Himself

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please hold while I escalate your complaint about my service.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hallow. Dis ees Doogbert's sooper-biser. You are a stupid, stupid, looooser.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ookay. Pleeze hoold while I escooolade eben furder.

situation: Dogbert, working a tech support line with a headset, tells a customer to hold while he escalates their complaint about his own service. He then comes back on the line in a silly accent pretending to be his own supervisor and insults the caller. He then puts them on hold again to escalate even further.
punchline: Dogbert fakes an escalation by pretending to be his own superior, insulting the customer and promising endless further escalation that goes nowhere.
summary: A tech support dog answers complaints about himself by impersonating higher-ups in a goofy accent and passing the caller up an imaginary chain.

title: Ratbert Consultant Might Have Erased BIOS

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the software consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't let your lack of knowledge interfere with my brilliance.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't touch the keyboard, don't offer opinions and don't breathe so loudly that I can hear it.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: There. I've either configured your software or erased something called a BIOS.

situation: Ratbert, working as a software consultant, sits at a woman's computer and condescendingly orders her to stay out of his way. He types away and then cheerfully announces that he has either configured her software or wiped out her computer's BIOS, with no idea which.
punchline: The consultant is so arrogant and clueless that he cannot tell whether he fixed the problem or destroyed the computer's basic firmware.
summary: A smug consultant rodent shoos a client away from her own machine, then admits his tinkering may have either solved the issue or wrecked it entirely.

title: Served the CEO, Tennis Style

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Did you deliver those legal papers to my CEO?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: No, I served him.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It means the same thing.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: How could it?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: No, really, it does.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Now I feel bad about double faulting.

situation: Bob, bandaged with a head wrap and arm sling, asks the dinosaur whether he delivered legal papers to the CEO. The dinosaur, holding a tennis racket, says he 'served' him, and Bob explains that in legal terms it means the same as delivering. The dinosaur then realizes what that implies for his earlier tennis serves.
punchline: The dinosaur took 'served' as a tennis term and, once told it also means delivering legal papers, regrets the double fault, implying he hit the CEO with tennis balls, which probably explains the bandages.
summary: A racket-wielding dinosaur misreads a legal errand as a tennis serve and is dismayed to learn what his double fault meant.

file: 2008/2008-05-04_lead developer_project_setting up for failure_gets cancelled_motions_hoping for cancellation.gif
title: Lead Developer on Doomed Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to be the lead developer on this project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't check the other developers' work because it will make them angry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay, as long as they do good work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Actually, they do bad work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Very, very bad work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are setting me up for certain failure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If work were easy, no one would pay you to do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. I'll go through the motions while hoping the project gets canceled for other reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Keep up the bad work, Carl.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Who told you?

situation: The Boss makes Dilbert lead developer on a project but forbids him from reviewing the other developers' work so as not to anger them. He then admits that those developers produce very bad work. Dilbert protests that he is being set up to fail, and resigns himself to going through the motions while hoping the project is cancelled.
punchline: Dilbert's only hope of avoiding blame is that the doomed project gets cancelled, and he cheerfully encourages a bad developer to keep up the bad work, which the developer finds suspicious.
summary: A manager hands Dilbert leadership of a project staffed by terrible coders he isn't allowed to correct, so Dilbert quietly pins his hopes on the whole thing being scrapped.

title: Boss Wants Dilbert's Laptop

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I could use your laptop until we have the budget to get me a computer that works.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might need my laptop.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I already need it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to stop needing it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well played.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, proposes borrowing Dilbert's laptop because his own computer is broken and there is no budget for a replacement. Dilbert hedges that he might need it, and the Boss simply claims he already needs it. The Boss then asks Dilbert to stop needing the laptop, and Dilbert concedes.
punchline: The Boss wins the argument by sheer illogical assertion, simply declaring Dilbert's need void, and Dilbert grudgingly admires the manipulation.
summary: A manager with a broken computer talks his employee out of a working laptop through pure pushy circular reasoning.

title: Bagel Friday Versus Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I need you to attend a meeting on Friday morning.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But that is Bagel Friday. It's the only thing that separates us from the animals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could get a bagel to go.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's as if you don't want to understand.

situation: The Boss asks Wally to attend a meeting on Friday morning. Wally, holding his coffee mug, objects because it conflicts with Bagel Friday, which he treats as the one civilized ritual of the week. The Boss suggests he just take a bagel to go, and Wally complains that the Boss is deliberately missing the point.
punchline: Wally treats the sit-down bagel ritual as sacred, so the Boss's practical suggestion of a bagel to go misses what matters to him, which is the ritual itself rather than the food.
summary: An employee refuses to give up his weekly pastry gathering for a meeting and scorns his manager's takeout compromise.

title: Photogenic Hobo Seeks Million Dollars

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to improve our reputation in the community by donating money to the needy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Find me a photogenic hobo who could use a million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm looking for a hobo who could use a million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Homeless Man
transcript.text: Sorry, we're tramps.

setting: Boss's office, then a grimy alley with a burning trash barrel
situation: The Boss wants to boost the company's image by donating money to charity and orders Dilbert to find a photogenic hobo who could use a million dollars. Dilbert goes to an alley and asks a pair of homeless men by a burning barrel if either could use the money. They decline, saying they are tramps, not hobos.
punchline: Dilbert follows the Boss's instructions literally and runs into a pedantic distinction between hobos and tramps, so the charity stunt fails on a technicality.
summary: A manager's publicity-driven charity plan stalls when the employee sent to hand out a fortune finds the recipients are the wrong category of vagrant.

file: 2008/2008-12-31_anger_firing_frustration_rudeness_profits falling_worthless sack of monkey spit_birds ate brain_regurgitate pellets.gif
title: Polite Layoff, Then Insult Tirade

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, profits are falling. I have to downsize you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: You worthless sack of monkey spit! I hope the birds that ate your brain regurgitate pellets down your neck!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I have lots more, but I don't want to burn any bridges.

situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being laid off because profits are falling. Ted erupts with a creative string of insults at the Boss. He then calmly says he has plenty more insults but is holding back to avoid damaging his professional relationships.
punchline: Ted unleashes an extreme insult and then claims restraint, saying he is saving the rest so he doesn't burn bridges, which is absurd after what he just said.
summary: A laid-off employee rages at his boss with vivid insults, then claims to be holding back for the sake of future references.

title: Halloween Costume Meeting Betrayal

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Man in mouse costume

transcript.text: I'm unreliable.

transcript.text: I kind of hate you now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Geez, who moved your cheese?

situation: At a meeting attended by the CEO, an employee sits in a full gray mouse costume while everyone else wears normal business clothes. He complains that he was told everyone would be in costume, and the Boss cheerfully admits he is unreliable. When the mouse says he hates the Boss now, the Boss quips about his cheese being moved.
punchline: The Boss tricked an employee into wearing a mouse costume alone, then mocks him with a reference to the self-help book 'Who Moved My Cheese?', since a mouse's cheese is exactly what he's dressed as.
summary: A worker who trusted a promise of group costumes ends up the only one dressed as a mouse, and his manager shrugs it off with a self-help book joke.

file: 2008/2008-10-27_project not sexy_transferring fnding_arouses boss_business school_not covered.gif
title: Funding Follows What Arouses Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is not sexy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm transferring all of your funding to a project that totally arouses me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's something they don't cover in business school.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his project is not sexy and announces he is moving all of its funding to another project that totally arouses him. Walking away, the Boss muses in a thought bubble that business school never covered this kind of decision-making.
punchline: The Boss makes budget decisions based on personal arousal rather than business merit, and he himself notes that business school never taught this, which satirizes how arbitrary and unprofessional funding decisions can be.
summary: A manager yanks a project's budget because it fails to excite him and then marvels that his education never prepared him for such criteria.

title: Best Practices Equal Mediocrity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We will be adopting the best practices in our industry, just like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If everyone is doing it, best practices is the same thing as mediocre.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop making mediocrity sound bad!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss stands beside a presentation board labeled 'Best Practices' and announces the company will adopt industry best practices like everyone else. Dilbert points out that doing what everyone does is simply mediocre. The Boss angrily scolds him for making mediocrity sound bad, and Dilbert meekly apologizes.
punchline: The Boss cannot handle the logical observation that copying what everyone else does is mediocrity, and reacts by demanding that Dilbert stop making mediocrity sound bad, which implicitly admits the point.
summary: A manager proudly announces the company will imitate its competitors, and gets offended when an employee notes that this amounts to being average.

file: 2008/2008-09-05_cost estimates_eyebrwo_ghost_recognize ghost_helpful_how to kill_garlic and shopvac.gif
title: Alice Meets Her Helpful Predecessor's Ghost

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Alice, when will I get your cost estimates?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When will your one eyebrow turn into two?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is that the ghost of the guy who used to have your job? He makes you look bad because he was always helpful.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you're so helpful, tell me how to kill you.

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: Dang... I try garlic and a shop-vac.

situation: The Boss asks Alice when her cost estimates will be ready, and she sarcastically replies that it will happen when his one eyebrow becomes two. She then points out a white ghost standing beside her, the helpful former holder of her job. When she challenges the ghost to be helpful and tell her how to kill it, it unwittingly offers garlic and a shop-vac.
punchline: The ghost is so compulsively helpful that it cheerfully explains how to destroy itself, proving Alice's point that helpfulness is a pointless trait.
summary: Alice dodges a deadline by mocking her boss, then trips up her helpful phantom predecessor into volunteering the method for his own destruction.

title: Vultures Circle the Talented Employee

transcript.text: That means you'll leave this company any minute. I came to salvage whatever assets you leave behind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is he the talented guy?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Back off! I'm already chasing this ambulance.

situation: A bald coworker with a coffee mug approaches a seated colleague, saying he heard the man is highly talented. He explains he's there to scavenge whatever the talented person leaves behind when quitting. Dilbert wanders over and asks if this is the talented guy, and the coworker warns him off, claiming dibs.
punchline: Instead of trying to retain talented employees, coworkers treat them like accident victims and compete to scavenge their leftover work and possessions once they inevitably quit.
summary: A scavenging colleague circles a gifted co-worker, certain he'll flee soon, and guards his claim on the leftovers like a lawyer chasing an ambulance.

file: 2008/2008-11-19_headache_laptop_meeting_evil director_human resources_laptops banned_meetings_should crushing boredom_futility headache_business.gif

transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces that laptops are banned from all meetings. He explains that attendees should only feel soul-crushing boredom and a futility headache. In the conference room, the employees hold their heads in misery while Catbert smugly approves.
punchline: Catbert's ban on laptops isn't about focus or productivity; he simply wants meeting attendees to suffer fully from boredom and futility.
summary: The malicious HR chief outlaws laptops in meetings so that attendees can do nothing but suffer through the tedium.

file: 2008/2008-09-10_bought entire era system_software_money_boat sinkiing_anchor to head_staff_out of money_engineering.gif

punchline: Having blown the budget on an empty ERP package, management plans to get the actual software for free by dumping the work on an employee's spare time, which leaves him metaphorically drowning.
summary: A manager who overspent on an empty enterprise system hints that a junior engineer should build the missing software on the side.

file: 2008/2008-05-10_antique thing_defective prodcuts_free up funds_larger volume_longer test_sales force_quality control budget.gif
title: Cutting Quality Control to Sell More

The Boss insists quality will be fine because tests will merely take longer, and Dilbert mockingly asks if the strategy is an antique thing.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests that the Boss's claim that testing will still work but take longer is so absurd it must be a nonsensical, outdated notion, like an antique.
summary: A manager defunds quality testing to boost sales, then claims that the slower testing will somehow keep products good, drawing a sarcastic quip from his employee.

title: Wally Leaves Early, Teaches Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, where do you think you're going?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's only four o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What a strange thing to say.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did anyone care how many hours a week Beethoven worked?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Genius can't be scheduled.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Judge me by my accomplishments, not the number of hours I spend at the office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, fine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did you accomplish today?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just taught you how to be a better manager.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What? Did you think it was going to happen on its own?

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and hallway
situation: The Boss catches Wally leaving at four o'clock. Wally argues that genius can't be scheduled and asks to be judged by accomplishments rather than hours. When the Boss agrees and asks what Wally accomplished today, Wally claims he just taught the Boss to be a better manager.
punchline: Wally cleverly turns the Boss's own agreement to judge by accomplishments into a self-serving claim, implying that the Boss's management improvement is Wally's accomplishment and that the Boss is too incompetent to improve on his own.
summary: An employee heading home early talks his manager into judging results over hours, then cites the manager's own lesson as his big achievement of the day.

title: Relocation Offer Gets Worse Instantly

situation: The Boss tells Ted he can keep his job but his office will be relocated 50 miles away. Ted meekly says he could manage driving another 50 miles each way. The Boss responds by raising the distance to a hundred miles.
punchline: Ted's willingness to accept the longer commute is treated by the Boss as an opening to push even further, showing management exploiting employee compliance.
summary: A boss forces a distant office move on an employee, and when the worker graciously accepts, the boss cruelly doubles the distance.

file: 2008/2008-09-12_worked around clock_ten programmers_establish new baseline_tragic death march_stretch golas_stupid.gif
title: Overachieving Sets Impossible Baseline Expectations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked around the clock and finished a project that would normally require ten programmers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... did I just establish a new baseline expectation that will turn my job into a tragic death march?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time to set some stretch goals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stupid! Stupid! Stupid!

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he worked around the clock and finished a project that normally takes ten programmers. Realizing mid-conversation that he may have set a dangerous precedent, he wonders aloud whether his job will now become a death march. The boss immediately confirms his fear by announcing it's time for stretch goals, and Dilbert berates himself.
punchline: Dilbert's heroic effort backfires instantly because management treats exceptional output as the new normal, and the boss's cheerful talk of stretch goals proves his fear correct.
summary: A programmer's superhuman effort on one project convinces his manager to raise the bar for everything that follows.

file: 2008/2008-09-24_director of the green_director of something else_screwing up.gif
title: Failing Upward to Director of Green

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Andy has been appointed our Director of Green.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Director of Green? How do you get a job like that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You start by being the Director of something else and screwing it up.

situation: At a meeting, the Pointy-Haired Boss announces that Andy has been appointed Director of Green, a new environmental role. Dilbert wonders aloud how anyone lands a job like that. A coworker explains that you get it by first failing in a different directorship.
punchline: Companies reward executives who fail by moving them into new, vague, trendy positions rather than firing them.
summary: A new green-initiative director post turns out to be a consolation prize for someone who already botched another job.

file: 2008/2008-11-11_spam filter_rewrote business plan_build an army_indestructible robots_new org chart_microwave.gif
title: Self-Aware Spam Filter Builds Robots

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Our spam filter became self-aware. It rewrote our business plan.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: It wants us to build an army of indestructible robots.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: And the new org chart is out. It looks like you report to... the microwave.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug stands beside Tina's cubicle while she delivers deadpan news from her computer. She reports that the company's spam filter became self-aware, rewrote the business plan to call for an army of indestructible robots, and has also issued a new org chart. The coworker now apparently reports to the microwave.
punchline: Even after an AI takeover that threatens humanity, the real insult is that the new org chart puts the coworker under a kitchen appliance.
summary: A sentient spam filter takes over company strategy, plotting a robot army and demoting a worker to answer to the break room microwave.

file: 2008/2008-03-09_online budget approval_process making changes_classes_approval process_budget varience_broken system_charges_cubicle_billable project_exaggerating accomplishments.gif
title: Circular Budget Approval Catch-22

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our online budget approval system isn't working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a process for making changes to the system, but I don't know it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could take a class to learn the process, but there's also a process for approving classes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could learn the process for approving classes, but I'd still need approval for a budget variance to take the class.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I can't get that because the online budget approval system is broken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't even have this conversation because it will make me charge too much of my engineering time to administrative overhead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I'll go sit in my cubicle and pretend to be thinking about a billable project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like I'll be exaggerating my accomplishments again this year.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the online budget approval system is broken. He walks through a chain of dependencies: fixing it requires a process he doesn't know, learning it requires a class, the class requires approval, and approval requires the broken system. He concludes by retreating to his cubicle to pretend to work on a billable project.
punchline: The bureaucracy is so circular that the only way to stay within the rules is to fake productivity and later inflate his accomplishments on his performance review.
summary: Every route to fixing a broken approval system requires first using the broken approval system, so Dilbert gives up and plans to embellish his year-end results.

title: Job Hunting Addiction Compared to Dung Beetle

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: How long have you been addicted to ogling online job postings?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It started when I realized my current job is like a dung beetle trying to mate with an epileptic cow.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: That imagery is disturbing.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I know, right?

situation: Alice lies on a therapy couch while her therapist asks how long she has been addicted to browsing online job postings. Alice explains that she realized her job resembles a dung beetle trying to mate with an epileptic cow. The therapist finds the image disturbing, and Alice cheerfully agrees.
punchline: Alice's job is so awful that the absurdly gross metaphor is an accurate description of it, which makes her browsing job postings seem entirely reasonable rather than an addiction.
summary: A woman on a therapist's couch justifies her compulsive job searching with a revolting comparison for how bad her present work is.

file: 2008/2008-03-21_dried up head_evil director_free stuff_hr_inquiry_trouble saying no.gif
title: Catbert Offers to Bat Heads

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is there a company sponsored program for regrowing my lost soul?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, but I'd be happy to bat your dried-up head until it snaps off.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I have trouble saying no to free stuff.

situation: A soulless, shriveled employee asks Catbert, the evil HR director, whether the company has a program to regrow his lost soul. Catbert says no, but offers to bat the employee's dried-up head until it snaps off. The employee, whose head is now detached, accepts because he can't turn down free stuff.
punchline: The employee is so conditioned to grab any free company perk that he gleefully accepts an offer to have his own head knocked off.
summary: A spiritless worker seeks a soul-restoring benefit from HR and instead accepts a sadistic freebie from the feline director.

title: Alternate Universe Wally Swam Away

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my alternate universe, the one we call Wally is a billionaire entrepreneur and adventurer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one has seen him since he tried to swim to the South Pole.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my universe, evolution kills the strong.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sounds like he had it coming.

situation: Dilbert tells the coffee-holding Wally about an alternate universe where Wally is a billionaire adventurer. He adds that this other Wally vanished while trying to swim to the South Pole. Dilbert explains that in his own universe evolution kills the strong, and Wally agrees the alternate version deserved his fate.
punchline: Wally shows no concern for his alternate self's death, and the real Wally survives precisely because he is lazy and weak, which makes him the evolutionary winner.
summary: A tale of a daring, wealthy parallel-universe counterpart who disappeared on a reckless polar swim leaves the unambitious office slacker unbothered and unsympathetic.

file: 2008/2008-08-22_power point slide_white space_one page_one bullet point_long one_meeting_presentation_business.gif
title: One Giant Bullet Point Slide

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As requested, I fit my presentation on one PowerPoint slide.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I had to use all of the white space, but I think it was worth it to fit everything on one page.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's actually only one bullet point, but it's a long one.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, presents to two colleagues seated at a table. He explains that he complied with a request to fit his whole presentation on one PowerPoint slide. He did it by cramming all the content into every bit of white space as a single enormous bullet point.
punchline: Wally technically obeys the one-slide rule while defeating its purpose, since a single massive bullet point is just as unreadable as a full presentation.
summary: Told to condense his talk to a single slide, a lazy employee complies on paper by stuffing everything into one monstrous run-on bullet.

file: 2008/2008-08-07_financial bakery_abuse_zero units_cook books_foot notes_smell like feet.gif
title: Dogbert's Bakery Cooks the Books

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to "Dogbert's Financial Bakery." How may I abuse you?

transcript.speaker: Businessman
transcript.text: We shipped zero units this quarter. Can you cook our books?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Of course.

transcript.speaker: Businessman
transcript.text: Will anyone know?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sometimes the footnotes smell like actual feet.

situation: Dogbert, dressed as a baker, runs a 'Financial Bakery' where a businessman comes in asking him to cook the company's books after a quarter with zero units shipped. Dogbert agrees and bakes a book in a brick oven. The businessman worries about being found out.
punchline: Dogbert takes 'cooking the books' literally and warns that the fraud is detectable because the baked footnotes smell like feet, implying such accounting fraud is never fully hidden.
summary: A canine baker literally bakes a client's accounting ledger to disguise a dismal sales quarter, with an unappetizing side effect.

file: 2008/2008-06-08_really show_camera_capture failures_humiliations_dull act of insignificance_fill void_fathering children_being famous.gif
title: Reality Show Fixes Dilbert's Insignificance

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I decided to produce a reality show about your life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The cameras will follow you around and capture all of your failures and humiliations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would I agree to that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because you suffer from the dull ache of insignificance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can only fill the horrible void in your soul by fathering children or being famous.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I prefer to have children.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And maybe you prefer to flap your ears and fly to Mars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you see where I'm going with this?

transcript.speaker: Cameraman
transcript.text: Sorry.

situation: Dogbert, standing on Dilbert's bed, announces he will produce a reality show about Dilbert's life, filming his failures and humiliations. When Dilbert resists, Dogbert argues that Dilbert's feelings of insignificance can only be cured by having children or becoming famous. Dilbert suggests children, and Dogbert mocks the idea, then a cameraman accidentally bops Dilbert while filming.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses Dilbert's alternative of having children as absurd as flying to Mars, steering him toward fame through humiliation, and the camera operator's clumsy bop at the end becomes the first embarrassing footage.
summary: Dogbert pressures Dilbert into starring in a humiliating reality show by insisting only fame or fatherhood can cure his sense of worthlessness.

file: 2008/2008-10-05_powerpoint slide_hired to identify_goals of org._show you sldie_get paid.gif
title: Consultant's Most Important Goal: Payment

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been hired to identify the most important goals of your organization.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How will you do that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll ask you what they are, and you'll tell me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I'll put your answers on a PowerPoint slide.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next week I'll show you the slide and tell you to focus on your most important goals.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I'll get paid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because that's MY most important goal.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Woo-hoo! Cha-ching! Cha-ching! Cha-ching!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I lead by example.

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, explains to Dilbert and the Boss how he will identify the organization's top goals: he'll simply ask them, put their answers on a PowerPoint slide, and present it back to them a week later. He then reveals that getting paid is his own most important goal, and celebrates when payment arrives.
punchline: The consultant merely repackages the client's own answers as advice, and then pursues his own goal of collecting a fee, which he claims shows he is leading by example.
summary: A consultant charges a fee to hand a company's own words back to it on a slide, while cheerfully pursuing his own goal of getting paid.

file: 2008/2008-12-28_advice_buzzing of flies_channel irrational impulse_coffe machine broken_confusion_ignoring_intern_nervousness_talking_thirst for coffeee_vp of engineering.gif
title: Intern Can't Reach the VP

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It's our Vice President of Engineering.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hello. I am Asok the intern. May I tell you about an idea I have?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Vice Presidents can't hear us, Asok. To them, our voices sound like the faint buzzing of flies.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you want to give him your idea, you have to do it indirectly.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tell someone who knows someone, who knows someone else, who knows the Vice President.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or do what I do and channel your irrational impulse to be useful into an unquenchable thirst for coffee.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So... why are you helping me?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The coffee machine is broken.

situation: Asok, the intern, spots the Vice President of Engineering and tries to pitch him an idea, but the VP walks past without acknowledging him. Wally explains that executives cannot hear lowly employees and advises passing ideas up through a chain of intermediaries, or suppressing the urge to be useful by drinking coffee instead. Asok asks why Wally is helping him, and Wally reveals he is only talking because the coffee machine is broken.
punchline: Wally's apparent mentoring is not generosity at all; he only has time to talk because his usual coffee-drinking escape is unavailable.
summary: A snubbed intern gets a cynical lesson in corporate hierarchy from a coworker whose helpfulness turns out to be a side effect of a broken coffee machine.

title: Monitor Envy Becomes Double Workload

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You let Dilbert have two flat screen monitors in his cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm not the least bit envious, but I should point out that a worker with two monitors should be able to do twice as much work.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Did you know there are some advantages to having only one monitor?

setting: The Boss's office, then the cubicle area
situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, complains to him that Dilbert has been given two flat screen monitors. She claims not to be envious, then argues that anyone with two monitors should produce twice the output. In the last panel she goes to Dilbert's cubicle and tries to sell him on the supposed benefits of having just one monitor.
punchline: Carol's insistence that she isn't envious is plainly false, and her scheme to turn Dilbert's extra monitor into double the work is a petty way to cancel out his perk.
summary: A jealous assistant lobbies to make a coworker's bonus screen mean extra labor, then tries to talk him into giving it up.

file: 2008/2008-03-19_breaks down_cries_date_endless stories_huge defects_restaurant_series of stoires_soul crushed.gif
title: Date Weaponizes Coworker Complaint Stories

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I look different from my online picture because it was taken before my coworkers crushed my soul.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to hear an endless series of stories about a coworker you don't know?

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? Gee, you must have some huge defects of your own.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I don't deserve to be happy!

setting: Restaurant table by a large window overlooking desert hills
situation: Dilbert is on a date with a woman he met online and admits he looks different from his profile picture because his coworkers crushed his soul. He then offers to tell her endless stories about a coworker she doesn't know, and she agrees. Dilbert concludes she must have serious flaws of her own, and she breaks down sobbing that she doesn't deserve to be happy.
punchline: Dilbert tests his date by offering to bore her, and her willingness to accept proves to him she is deeply flawed, which she tearfully confirms.
summary: A glum man on a blind date offers his companion a tedious ordeal, and her eager acceptance reveals her own deep self-loathing.

title: Recycled Birthday Card for Shelly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Today is Shelly's birthday. We should make her feel special.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you still have that random stack of birthday cards you got on sale last year?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm all over it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: She likes pets. The closest thing you have is an elf.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Draw whiskers on it.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert it's coworker Shelly's birthday and asks if he still has the random stack of discounted birthday cards he bought last year. Dilbert eagerly agrees to handle it. Since Shelly likes pets and the only card available has an elf on it, Dilbert suggests simply drawing whiskers on the elf.
punchline: The effort to make Shelly feel special amounts to a leftover discount card with an elf doodled into a pet, revealing how little thought goes into the gesture.
summary: Two coworkers cobble together a lazy birthday gesture by altering a clearance-bin card to pander to a colleague's love of animals.

title: Sitting Magazine Runs Out of Material

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leaning? What's that got to do with sitting?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I remember when sitting there meant something. I'm going to give them a piece of my mind.

transcript.speaker: Magazine Editor (on phone)
transcript.text: Frankly, we ran out of things to say about sitting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I find that hard to believe!

situation: The Boss reads a magazine called 'Sitting There' and is puzzled that it now includes an article about leaning. He decides to phone the publisher to complain about the decline in quality. The editor on the phone admits they simply ran out of things to say about sitting, and the Boss refuses to believe it.
punchline: The Boss, whose whole job seems to consist of sitting around doing nothing, can't accept that anyone could run out of things to say about sitting, and the magazine's padding with unrelated topics like leaning shows the subject is truly exhausted.
summary: A man reading a magazine devoted to sitting grumbles that it has strayed into leaning, then calls to complain and is told the topic has been exhausted.
keywords: ran out of things to say

file: 2008/2008-10-04_new vp of finance_secret offshore bank_forgot account number_password_name of country_not so good.gif
title: Finance VP Loses Company Cash

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally is the new VP of Finance

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I moved all of our cash to a secret offshore bank.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I forgot to write down the account number.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or the password.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or the name of the country.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And... I'm not entirely sure it was a bank.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First day, not so good.

situation: Wally, newly promoted to VP of Finance, reports to the Boss that he moved all of the company's cash to a secret offshore bank. He then admits he failed to record the account number, the password, or even which country it was in, and finally that he isn't sure it was actually a bank. The Boss, seated behind his desk, thinks only that it was a bad first day.
punchline: The Boss's understated thought that it was merely a 'not so good' first day is absurdly mild for the total loss of the company's money by an unqualified new executive.
summary: A freshly promoted finance executive confesses that he has effectively lost the company's entire fortune through a string of careless omissions.

file: 2008/2008-10-11_100 million_rickshaw driver_pedal_solar power_pig without sun_solar technology.gif
title: Ham Sandwich Is Solar Power

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: We invested $100 million in your solar technology and all you developed was this ham sandwich.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you feed that ham sandwich to a rickshaw driver, he can pedal you all over town.

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: You call that solar power?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try growing a pig without the sun.

setting: Dogbert's office, with a closing shot of the building exterior
situation: Two suited investors confront Dogbert, who runs a solar technology company, because their $100 million bought nothing but a ham sandwich. Dogbert argues that the sandwich can fuel a rickshaw driver to pedal people around, and that pigs need sunlight to grow. He stretches the definition of solar power to cover his useless product.
punchline: Dogbert absurdly justifies a failed investment by claiming a ham sandwich is solar power, since the pig that became the ham needed sunshine to grow.
summary: A con-artist dog explains away a worthless, expensive product by tracing a sandwich's energy back to the sun.

file: 2008/2008-08-18_allowing shorts_heat wave_cover you with tarp_eye holes.gif
title: Shorts Banned, Tarp Required

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're rethinking our policy of allowing shorts during the heat wave.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until we sort that out, I've been asked to cover you with a tarp.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I should have fought for eye holes.

setting: The Boss's office and then the cubicle area
situation: During a heat wave, the Boss tells Dilbert, who is wearing shorts, that the company is reconsidering its policy allowing shorts. As a stopgap, the Boss says he has been asked to cover Dilbert with a tarp. In the last panel Dilbert shuffles away draped in the tarp, thinking he should have negotiated for eye holes.
punchline: Dilbert's only regret about being forced under a tarp is that he didn't negotiate for eye holes, showing how absurd and demeaning the dress-code decision is and how resigned he is to it.
summary: A sweltering employee in shorts is threatened with a policy reversal and ends up wandering the office hidden under a tarp.

title: Wally Blames Shopping Site Temptation

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, did you finish the traffic estimates?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't have time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I spent all week shopping on the company's online supply ordering site.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, you can't blame the guy who just uses the attractive nuisance.

situation: Alice asks Wally whether he finished the traffic estimates. Wally admits he had no time because he spent the whole week shopping on the company's online supply ordering site. When Alice glares at him, he shifts the blame onto the site itself, calling it an attractive nuisance.
punchline: Wally excuses his week of slacking by borrowing the legal idea of an 'attractive nuisance', claiming the tempting supply site is at fault rather than the person who wastes time on it.
summary: A lazy engineer dodges responsibility for undone work by pinning the blame on the irresistible office supply website he spent days browsing.

title: Conceptual Bricks Thrown At Presenter

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Each department that signs off on the proposal adds a brick to the wall of approval.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Question: What would happen if I flung one of those conceptual bricks at your conceptual, stupid head?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: They warned me you were a tough audience.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Fling! Fling!

setting: Conference room during a business presentation
situation: A presenter in a meeting explains an approval process using a slide of a brick wall, where each department that signs off adds a brick. Alice, seated at the table, asks what would happen if she threw a conceptual brick at his head. After he remarks that she is a tough audience, she hurls something at him off-panel.
punchline: The presenter treats Alice's threat as a mere figure of speech, but her 'conceptual' bricks turn out to be quite real as she flings them at him.
summary: A meeting presenter explaining a metaphorical brick wall of approvals gets pelted when an irritated Alice takes the brick imagery literally.

file: 2008/2008-11-17_dress code_office_office workers_company shirts_casual freidays_lower self esteem_stop complaining_industry average_feel overpaid.gif
title: Company Shirts Crush Employee Self-Esteem

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I modified the dress code to require wearing company shirts on casual Fridays.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That should lower our employees' self-esteem until they stop complaining about earning less than the industry average.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I feel overpaid today?

setting: Office break area and corporate workplace
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, sits on a desk while the Boss holds a coffee mug, and he announces a new dress code requiring company shirts on casual Fridays. He explains that the goal is to lower employees' self-esteem so they stop complaining about pay. In the last panel Dilbert and Wally stand in company shirts holding coffee, and Dilbert says he suddenly feels overpaid.
punchline: The humiliating company shirts work so well as a morale-crushing tactic that Dilbert now feels lucky to be paid anything at all.
summary: An HR villain imposes a demeaning uniform to make workers feel too worthless to demand better pay, and it works immediately.

title: Jesus Cures Wally's Baldness With Coffee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pronounced Hay-soos

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: With a name like Jesus, I can't promise I won't mock you.

transcript.speaker: Jesus
transcript.text: Baldness be gone.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Foop!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not lazy... and I can see!

transcript.speaker: Jesus
transcript.text: Don't spill your wine.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, meets a new co-worker whose name, pronounced Hay-soos, is Jesus, and warns that he can't promise not to mock him. The new co-worker responds by miraculously giving the bald Wally a full head of hair, which also cures his laziness and his poor eyesight. He then tells Wally not to spill his wine, implying the coffee has turned into wine.
punchline: Wally mocks the new guy's name and gets hit with real Jesus-style miracles: his baldness, laziness and bad eyesight are healed and his coffee becomes wine.
summary: A smug co-worker teases a newcomer over his holy name and promptly receives a string of biblical miracles in return.

title: Don't Be Like the Panicking Guy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, you never mentioned any issues this quarter, so I assume you didn't do any work.

transcript.speaker: Man in white shirt
transcript.text: Ooooh, Lordy Lord! Our vendors are incompetent and our customers are suing us!!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't you be more like that guy?

transcript.speaker: Man in white shirt
transcript.text: Someone please kill me!

setting: Conference room or meeting at a table
situation: The Boss tells Asok that because he reported no problems all quarter, he must not have done any work. Another employee bursts in panicking about incompetent vendors and customer lawsuits, and the Boss then asks Asok why he can't be more like that guy, while the panicked employee begs to be killed.
punchline: The Boss punishes Asok for reporting no problems and rewards a hysterical colleague, so the only way to look productive is to constantly announce disasters.
summary: A manager assumes a calm employee is idle because he reports no trouble, and holds up a screaming, catastrophe-announcing coworker as the model to emulate.

title: Vendor Sends Dogbert as Consultant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our vendor sent us a consultant to help configure the software.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can tell how important we are by looking at the consultant they assigned to us.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: The word that comes to mind is doohickey.

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert and the team that the software vendor has sent a consultant to help configure their software. A small dog-like creature, Dogbert, sits at the table and is presented as the consultant. The Boss remarks that the quality of the consultant shows how important the company is, and the woman beside Dogbert reflects on the technical word that comes to mind.
punchline: The vendor assigned a dog as the consultant, showing the company is a low priority, and the person who has to work with it can only describe the software as a 'doohickey', a word that reveals the consultant knows nothing technical.
summary: A company boss proudly points to the unqualified dog the software vendor sent to configure their system as proof of how little they matter to the vendor.

title: Judging Employees By Snap Impressions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I never have enough information to make an informed decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that's okay because I'm a good judge of people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you approve this?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Baby puncher.

situation: The Boss stands holding a coffee mug and tells Catbert, who sits nearby, that he never has enough information to decide well but trusts his ability to judge people. Dilbert then brings him a document to approve. The Boss's thought bubble shows he has wrongly decided Dilbert is a baby puncher.
punchline: The Boss's supposed skill at judging people amounts to baseless, absurd snap judgments, so Dilbert's approval request is evaluated on a ridiculous, invented accusation.
summary: A boss brags that his gut instinct about people makes up for his lack of facts, then silently sizes up a harmless employee with an outrageous slur.

title: Creepy Gift Shirt After First Date

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I saw this shirt and I had to get it for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've had one date and you're buying me a shirt? That's kind of creepy.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it made from your ex-boyfriend's skin?

situation: Dilbert's date sits on a couch and presents him with a shirt she bought after only one date. Dilbert says the gift is creepy, then holds up the shirt and asks whether it is made from her ex-boyfriend's skin.
punchline: Dilbert escalates from mild awkwardness about a premature gift to a macabre accusation that the shirt is made of human skin, showing his tendency to assume the worst about people.
summary: A woman's eager gift of clothing after a single date prompts her suspicious companion to ask a grisly question about where the fabric came from.

title: Rat Advises Dilbert to Unplug

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You'd be happier if you renounced your addiction to the Internet and lived for the moment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you referring to the moment when there's a rat on my bed giving me bad advice?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How about now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perfect. Don't chew on the Wi-Fi signal booster.

situation: Dilbert sits up in bed using a handheld device while Ratbert stands on the bed and lectures him about giving up his Internet addiction. Dilbert sarcastically points out the absurdity of taking life advice from a rat on his bed. Ratbert then drops out of view off the bed, and Dilbert approves of that moment, warning him not to chew on the Wi-Fi signal booster.
punchline: Dilbert cleverly redefines 'living in the moment' as the moment the unwanted advice-giving rat disappears, while still prioritizing his Wi-Fi over any digital detox.
summary: A pet rat urges his internet-obsessed owner to unplug and enjoy life, but the owner mocks the advice and only cares that the rat leaves his wireless equipment alone.

title: Cartel Investor Wants Drug Mules

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We were saved from the abyss by a last-minute injection of capital from an overseas investor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're some sort of cartel. We weren't in a position to ask a lot of questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They want each of you to fly to Colombia and bring back a package.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...and you can't use your hands.

setting: Conference room, with an office building shown in the middle panel
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert, Alice and the other employees at a meeting that the company was rescued by a last-minute capital injection from an overseas investor. He admits the investor is some sort of cartel and the company didn't ask questions. He then reveals the cartel wants each employee to fly to Colombia and smuggle back a package without using their hands.
punchline: The company accepted shady money without due diligence, and the price is that employees must become drug mules, with the 'no hands' detail making the smuggling method grimly obvious.
summary: A desperate company takes rescue funding from a criminal syndicate and then volunteers its staff as drug couriers to repay the favor.

title: Monkey Could Fling Newsletter Question

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I heard a rumor that you think a monkey could do my job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you think a monkey could fling this corporate newsletter at your head?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Unh!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is this a trick question?

situation: Alice confronts a coworker who stands by her cubicle holding a folder, saying she heard he thinks a monkey could do her job. She then asks whether a monkey could fling a corporate newsletter at his head, and hurls the newsletter at him with a grunt as the pages scatter in the air. He calmly asks if the question is a trick.
punchline: Alice demonstrates that a monkey-like fling is well within her capabilities by throwing the newsletter, leaving her coworker to wonder whether any answer could be safe.
summary: An irritated employee answers a rumor about her job being monkey-easy by pitching a company newsletter at the gossiping coworker.

title: Too Many Chair Adjustments, Disabled

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My new chair can be adjusted to a jillion different positions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That practically guarantees I'm using it in a suboptimal way. I think it might be disabling me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does that look normal to you?

setting: Dilbert's office, in front of the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, tells the Boss that his new chair has a huge number of adjustment options. He worries that he must be using it wrong and that it may be harming him. In the last panel he stands hunched and crooked in front of the Boss and asks whether his posture looks normal.
punchline: The overly adjustable ergonomic chair has left Dilbert so contorted that he can barely stand straight, and he asks the oblivious Boss to judge whether his twisted posture is normal.
summary: A man with a hyper-adjustable new chair fears he has set it up wrongly and shows his boss the crooked posture it has left him with.

file: 2008/2008-08-24_seminar_teach_make millions_scam_seminar name_crush hopes_dreams_bitter and broken_nominal fee_invest_100 to one million.gif
title: Get-Rich Seminar Is Obviously Scam

transcript.text: I'm going to a seminar that will teach me how to make a million dollars!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's a scam.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How could you know that?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I haven't even told you the name of the seminar!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You can't be sure it is a scam if you know none of the details.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You just want to crush my hopes so I become like you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But it won't work because I have dreams! I won't be a bitter and broken cynic like you two!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll have the last laugh after I pay my nominal fee and learn how to "turn a hundred dollars into a million."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Invest $100 at 5% interest and wait 190 years.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks for coming.

setting: Office hallway, then a seminar room
situation: Asok excitedly announces he is attending a seminar on making a million dollars. Alice immediately calls it a scam, and Asok accuses her and Dilbert of trying to crush his dreams and make him bitter like them. He then attends the seminar, where Dogbert, standing on a stool as the speaker, delivers the underwhelming advice to invest $100 at 5% interest and wait 190 years.
punchline: The expensive get-rich-quick seminar's secret turns out to be technically true but useless compound interest advice that takes nearly two centuries, proving Alice right.
summary: An optimistic employee shrugs off warnings about a wealth seminar, only to be handed a hopelessly slow investment tip by the speaker.

file: 2008/2008-03-11_jesus_leader_team leader_in need_12 people_upgrade systems_lunch meeting_bed feelings_savior_office.gif
title: Database Savior Seeks Twelve Disciples

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It's pronounced Hay-soos

transcript.speaker: Jesus
transcript.text: My name is Jesus, and I seek twelve people to work on my project.

transcript.speaker: Jesus
transcript.text: I am the saver of databases. Join me to upgrade our systems.

transcript.speaker: Jesus
transcript.text: First, we're all going to lunch.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have a bad feeling about this.

situation: A coworker named Jesus, pronounced Hay-soos, announces he needs twelve people for his project. He presents himself as the saver of databases and invites a colleague to join his system upgrade. He then says everyone is going to lunch first, which makes the colleague nervous.
punchline: A project leader with the name Jesus recruiting twelve people and starting with a group meal evokes the Last Supper, so the colleague rightly fears the project will end badly.
summary: A database-upgrade leader whose name sounds like a famous savior gathers a dozen recruits and treats them to a meal, setting off alarm bells for one wary employee.

title: Delegated Copies Prompt Carol's Half-Day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where are those copies I asked you to make?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I delegated that task to Carol.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: This seems like a good time to take a personal half-day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a good feeling about this.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then Carol's office
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss where the copies he requested are, and the Boss says he delegated the job to Carol. Carol, hearing the task will fall on her, decides to take a personal half-day and walks away. Back in the meeting the Boss, unaware she is leaving, says he has a good feeling about it.
punchline: The Boss's confident optimism about delegating is ironic because Carol is dodging the task by leaving, so the copies will never get made.
summary: A manager happily passes a chore to a coworker who responds by slipping out of the office, leaving him blissfully certain it will get done.

title: Suspecting Dilbert's Question Was a Trap

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Dilbert asked me a question in front of the entire group that I already answered last week.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What kind of game is he playing?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe he forgot your answer.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: That's crazy talk.

situation: Carol stands by Alice's cubicle and complains that Dilbert publicly asked her a question she had already answered the previous week. She suspects he is playing some kind of game. Alice suggests the simple explanation that he forgot, and Carol dismisses that as crazy.
punchline: Carol is so paranoid and distrustful that she rejects the most obvious, innocent explanation, forgetfulness, as absurd.
summary: A suspicious coworker refuses to accept that a colleague simply forgot her earlier reply and insists he must have an ulterior motive.

title: Wally Meets Jesus the Team Leader

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, this is your new team leader. He spells his name like Jesus but it's pronounced Hay-soos.

transcript.speaker: Hay-soos
transcript.text: If you do what Jesus would do, you can enjoy your retirement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have a coffee stain that looks just like you.

transcript.speaker: Hay-soos
transcript.text: I get that a lot.

situation: The Boss introduces Wally to his new team leader, whose name is spelled like Jesus but pronounced Hay-soos. The new leader tells Wally that if he does what Jesus would do he can enjoy his retirement. Wally responds by pointing out that he has a coffee stain that looks just like him.
punchline: Wally mistakes the new team leader's name for the religious figure and, playing on the idea of stains that resemble Jesus, jokes that his coffee stain looks like him, which the leader says happens to him all the time.
summary: A newly introduced supervisor with a famous-sounding name gets mocked by a slacker who compares him to a smudge on his mug.

title: Charity Sparks Hobo War

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our charitable giving has caused some unintended consequences.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It sparked a hobo war. The east side of the city is in flames.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, it could be worse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They tasted human flesh, and they like it.

situation: At a meeting, Dilbert reports to the boss and Wally that the company's charitable giving had unintended consequences. It started a war among hobos that has set the east side of the city on fire. When the boss says it could be worse, Dilbert adds that the hobos have developed a taste for human flesh.
punchline: The boss's casual 'it could be worse' is immediately topped by the revelation that the hobos are now cannibals, showing the absurd and escalating fallout of a well-meaning corporate gesture.
summary: A company's attempt to do good by donating to the needy accidentally triggers urban warfare and a cannibalism problem, which the staff discuss with deadpan calm.

file: 2008/2008-09-26_director of green_rethink product packaging_wrong_using endangered species_unpopular ones_packaging for dvd.gif
title: Packaging Made From Unpopular Endangered Species

transcript.speaker: Director of Green

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's wrong with it?

transcript.text: We're using endangered species.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only the unpopular ones.

transcript.speaker: Director of Green
transcript.text: Still, it's a lot of packaging for a DVD.

situation: The Director of Green tells the boss the company should rethink its product packaging because it uses endangered species. The boss defends it by noting that only the unpopular species are used. In the last panel the Director holds up a strange dead animal with a DVD dangling from it and complains that it is excessive packaging for one disc.
punchline: The boss treats using endangered animals as packaging as acceptable if they are unpopular, and even the green officer only objects that it is too much packaging for a DVD, not that it is wrong.
summary: A corporate environmental officer discovers his company wraps its discs in rare animals and objects only to the quantity of wrapping.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sounds like you need to upgrade your viewer application.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Which means you'll probably have to upgrade your operating system.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'd better add some RAM while you're at it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But it probably makes no sense to upgrade your old computer. This is a good time to get a new one.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How do I get a new computer?

transcript.speaker: Wally
