transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sending corrupted files to people again?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Only if I think they deserve it.

setting: Office break room by the coffee machine
situation: A coworker complains that he can't open a file Wally e-mailed. Wally escalates the fix step by step, from a viewer upgrade to an OS upgrade to more RAM to an entirely new computer, then says he'll send a file explaining how to get one. Dilbert asks if Wally is sending corrupted files again.
punchline: Wally deliberately sends corrupted files to coworkers he feels deserve it, then lets them waste time and money on needless upgrades, and he is even planning to send another file for the new-computer instructions.
summary: A deliberately broken email attachment sends a colleague down an expensive path of software upgrades until he is convinced he needs a whole new machine.

file: 2008/2008-09-07_reject proposal_reason_level of management_authority_get fired_starve to death_repharse_question.gif
title: Boss Rejects Everything To Survive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I reject your proposal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there any particular reason this time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At my level of management I don't have the authority to approve anything important.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I do have the authority to reject things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I don't reject proposals, there's nothing for me to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I do nothing I'll get fired. I might never get another job. I could starve to death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I have to reject everything you propose or else I might die.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What am I supposed to do now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you rephrase that question in the form of a proposal?

situation: The Boss rejects Dilbert's proposal, and when Dilbert asks why, he explains that he lacks the authority to approve anything important but can still reject things. He argues that he must reject every proposal to justify his job and avoid being fired and starving. When Dilbert asks what he should do next, the Boss tells him to phrase the question as a proposal.
punchline: The Boss's only power is to say no, so he will reject everything to stay employed, and he gleefully offers to reject Dilbert's request for guidance too.
summary: A manager with no power to approve anything justifies his job by turning down every idea put in front of him.

file: 2008/2008-06-22_retirement plans_for losers_winners keep jobs_no stress_free coffee_cost estimates_worthless leech.gif

setting: Office break room and hallway beside the coffee maker
situation: Asok asks Wally about his retirement plans, and Wally says retirement is for losers because he can keep his job, stop caring about quality, and still get paid with free coffee. He demonstrates by deflecting a coworker's request for cost estimates onto Dilbert, claiming to be too busy. Asok and then Dilbert point out that this makes Wally a leech.
punchline: Wally brags that he wins by doing no real work while staying employed, and the strip's closing remark notes that by his own definition the 'winner' is simply a parasite on the company.
summary: A slacker coworker explains that the smart move is to hold onto a paycheck while quietly offloading all effort onto someone else.

file: 2008/2008-07-22_ceo_thrown out window_press charges_security_gunning for job_hire for yacht_policeman.gif

situation: A man covered in bandages tells a police officer that his CEO threw him through a fifth-floor window and he wants to press charges. The officer ignores the complaint and instead asks whether the CEO might hire him for yacht security, then offers to club the victim with his nightstick to impress the CEO.
punchline: The officer is more interested in landing a lucrative private security job with the violent CEO than in enforcing the law, and is willing to assault the victim to win it.
summary: A cop shown a defenestration victim sees only a job opportunity and considers beating him up to curry favor with the powerful executive responsible.

transcript.speaker: Ted

setting: Office and Ted's cubicle or workspace
situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Ted a 'funny story' about repeatedly sending a long document to print and checking the wrong printer for three days. The correct printer meanwhile burned through $80,000 worth of paper. Ted, suspicious about why he's being told, asks how it affects him.
punchline: The Boss's costly blunder becomes Ted's problem as the Boss announces that Ted must now go without paper, passing the cost of his mistake onto an innocent employee.
summary: After wasting a fortune on paper through his own printing mistake, the boss punishes a bystander employee with a paper ban.

situation: Dogbert, working as a media trainer, sits on a stool with a microphone and offers a mock interview to a bald executive. He springs a hostile question asking whether the man is a weasel pretending to be human. punchline: The executive really is a weasel in a human mask, so Dogbert's wild accusation was only a lucky guess, and it implies that executives can be literally inhuman.

situation: The Boss promotes a hairy, troll-like employee who maintains legacy systems to a new role as scapegoat. His job is to wear a goat costume and absorb the blame for failed projects. summary: A manager claims a decision-averse employee has physically vaporized into a faint stench, yet the project still depends on his feedback.

file: 2008/2008-03-24_flatten hair_important document_option_put on head happy_unique filing_clutter.gif

summary: A cubicle neighbor solves a filing problem by offering her own head as a storage spot, prompting a gloomy remark from Dilbert about happiness.

title: Demanding Terms Without Snortling Rights

transcript.text: I've decided that your tiny company will give us an interest-free loan.

transcript.text: This is the part where you realize your negotiating leverage is limited.

setting: Executive office with a large desk and high-backed chair
situation: The Boss, seated at his desk, informs the owner of a small vendor company that they will effectively be giving his company an interest-free loan by being paid late. He says nothing needs to be signed, and the late payments will come with snortling. The small-company owner, whose leverage is weak, can only respond by demanding that there be no snortling.
punchline: The supplier has no real power, so the only concession he dares to demand is the trivial one of not being snorted at, while the exploitative late-payment scheme goes ahead unchallenged.
summary: A bullying executive forces a tiny supplier into a free loan by paying late, and the powerless vendor can only object to the mocking laughter.

title: Averaging Two Wrong Data Sources

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Use the CRS database to size the market.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That data is wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then use the SIBS database.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That data is also wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you average them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I can multiply them too.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to size the market using one database, and Dilbert says the data is wrong. The Boss suggests a second database, which Dilbert also says is wrong, so the Boss asks him to average the two. Dilbert agrees, adding that he could multiply them as well.
punchline: Combining two sets of wrong data by averaging or multiplying doesn't make the result correct, so any market size produced this way is meaningless.
summary: A manager responds to unreliable data sources by asking for them to be blended together, and the engineer sarcastically shows how meaningless that would be.

file: 2008/2008-02-26_pro bono job_hit with suit_chair_dinosaur bob_liked it.gif
title: Dinosaur Lawyer Slaps Boss Into Rehiring

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob the Esquire Dinosaur

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I slapped your ex-boss with his own suit until he agreed to rehire you.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It only took ten minutes to make him agree, and another hour to make him convince me that he liked it.

transcript.speaker: Man in chair
transcript.text: How much do I owe you for all the fun?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: This one is pro bono.

setting: A living room or home office where a man sits in an armchair with a cup of coffee
situation: Bob, a green dinosaur lawyer carrying a briefcase, reports to his client that he beat the client's former boss with the boss's own suit until the boss agreed to rehire him. Bob adds that the boss then had to spend an hour convincing Bob that he had enjoyed it. The client offers to pay for the fun, and Bob waives his fee.
punchline: The dinosaur lawyer takes a literal, violent pun on 'slapped with a suit' and turns it into a twisted bit of enjoyment, so he does the job for free because he had so much fun.
summary: A reptilian attorney brags about physically thrashing a former employer into rehiring his client, then declines payment because the work was its own reward.

title: Toss It On The Pile

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked all night to finish the assignment on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Toss it on the pile.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd feel better if you used a different choice of words.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Plop it on the top.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he stayed up all night to finish an assignment on time. The boss tells him to toss it on a pile of papers on his desk. When Dilbert asks for kinder wording, the boss just offers a different phrase that means the same dismissive thing.
punchline: The boss only changes his wording, not his attitude, showing he still doesn't value Dilbert's overnight effort.
summary: A worker's all-night effort is brushed aside by a manager who swaps one dismissive phrase for another without changing his indifference.

title: Alice Kills Antimatter Dilbert With Coffee

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You know that antimatter version of yourself that you brought to work?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I killed him with a cup of coffee. I think he enjoyed it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Because he's, like, opposite.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But enough about me. How's your day going?

situation: Alice stands beside Dilbert's desk and casually mentions that she killed the antimatter version of him he had brought to work, using a cup of coffee. She explains the man probably enjoyed it because he is the opposite of Dilbert. She then cheerfully asks Dilbert how his day is going while he stares at her in alarm.
punchline: Alice casually admits to murder, then makes polite small talk as if nothing happened, leaving Dilbert to contemplate how his own day is going.
summary: A calmly cheerful coworker confesses to bumping off her colleague's cosmic double and then asks about his day.

file: 2008/2008-05-03_new guy_project team_foul stench_stink of failure_follows man.gif
title: Stink of Failure Spreads Handshake

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: You must be Dilbert. I'm the new guy on your project team.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's that foul stench?

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: It's the stink of failure. It follows me from project to project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do I get it off?!!

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: You can dilute it by shaking hands.

situation: A new team member introduces himself to Dilbert, and Dilbert notices a terrible smell as they shake hands. The new guy explains it is the stink of failure that follows him from project to project. Dilbert, now contaminated, panics and asks how to get rid of it, and is told to pass it on by shaking hands with others.
punchline: The new guy's history of failed projects is treated like a contagious smell, and the only 'cure' is to spread it to other people, mirroring how project failure gets passed around an organization.
summary: A newcomer on the team carries a literal stench of past failures that rubs off on Dilbert and can only be shared with others.

file: 2008/2008-01-14_everyone informed_out of loop_witnessing birth_birth of child_envy_project_happy_miracle.gif
title: Out of the Loop Is Bliss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's too hard to keep everyone informed about everything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to take you out of the loop.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Really??

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I know what fathers mean when they talk about witnessing the birth of their children.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lucky!

situation: The Boss tells Wally that keeping everyone informed is too difficult, so he is removing Wally from the information loop. Wally reacts with joy, comparing it to the miracle of witnessing the birth of a child. Dilbert, passing by with a coffee mug, envies him.
punchline: Being left out of the loop is seen as a blessing by employees, since being uninformed means avoiding pointless work and responsibility, and Dilbert is jealous.
summary: A boss cuts a worker out of communications and the worker is overjoyed, to the envy of his coworker.

title: Dilbert's Carbicle Invention Praise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call my invention a carbicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's 50% car, 50% cubicle, and 100% awesome.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is the ultimate expression of human efficiency.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rarely does an engineer get to create something so perfect that it can never be improved.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hesitate to use the word "genius," but I won't protest if others do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should cram a bed in there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You shut up.

setting: A garage or workshop with a boxy brown vehicle
situation: Dilbert proudly shows off his invention, the carbicle, a hybrid of a car and a cubicle, and showers it with praise while fishing for others to call him a genius. Dogbert responds with a sarcastic suggestion to cram a bed inside, implying it is just a tiny, cramped living space. Dilbert and Dogbert then trade 'shut up' insults.
punchline: Dogbert's suggestion to add a bed deflates Dilbert's self-congratulation by implying the carbicle is really just a cramped, miserable place to live.
summary: An engineer gushes about his perfect car-cubicle hybrid until his dog needles him with a suggestion that turns it into a tiny home.

file: 2008/2008-11-04_root cause_projects failure_determinist_origin of universe_cubicle destroyed_free will.gif
title: Determinist Blames Universe's Origin

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone know the root cause of our project's failure?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a determinist, so I'd have to say the problem goes back to the origin of the universe.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you like this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My cubicle destroyed my illusion of free will.

setting: Conference room during a project post-mortem meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks for the root cause of a failed project. Dilbert answers as a determinist, claiming the failure traces back to the origin of the universe. When the Boss asks why he is like this, Dilbert says his cubicle has destroyed his belief in free will.
punchline: Dilbert dodges accountability for the failure with philosophical determinism, and the real reason for his bleak outlook is that cubicle life has convinced him he has no free will.
summary: Asked to find the root cause of a failed project, Dilbert traces it back to the beginning of time and blames his cubicle for his fatalism.

file: 2008/2008-07-18_moral compass damaged_vice president_miserable and helpless_actual job.gif
title: Promoted For Damaged Moral Compass

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: It has come to my attention that your moral compass is damaged.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I'm promoting you to Vice President of making employees feel miserable and helpless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's an actual job?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: It doesn't happen on its own.

situation: The boss tells Dilbert that his moral compass is damaged, then promotes him to Vice President of making employees feel miserable and helpless. Dilbert asks if that is a real job, and the boss shakes his hand and says someone has to make it happen.
punchline: The boss treats a lack of ethics as a qualification for a management role whose purpose is to make staff miserable, implying that workplace misery is deliberately engineered rather than accidental.
summary: A boss rewards an employee's flawed ethics with a promotion to a position dedicated to demoralizing his coworkers.

file: 2008/2008-09-06_evil director_human resources_mandatory stretch_employee welness_good and flexible_new place_tuck your head_business.gif
title: Catbert's Sinister Mandatory Stretching Program

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're instituting a mandatory stretch period every day.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This is surprising because Human Resources usually doesn't care about employee wellness.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Phase one is just to get you good and flexible.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Phase two involves a new place to tuck your head.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces a mandatory daily stretch period to a table of employees. One employee points out that HR normally doesn't care about employee wellness. Catbert reveals the stretching is only preparation for a humiliating second phase.
punchline: The wellness program is a cover for making employees flexible enough to stuff their own heads somewhere unpleasant, implying their heads will be tucked into their own rear ends.
summary: A malicious HR chief rolls out compulsory exercise as the first step in a scheme to make workers contort themselves into absurd positions.

file: 2008/2008-03-16_archaic sayings_bite the hand_cost of measuring_direct deposit_measuring incorrectly_rock carving_software development_web design_wise sayings.gif
title: Dilbert Mocks Boss's Outdated Proverbs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My management philosophy is "measure twice, cut once."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That only makes sense in a narrow, and generally archaic, set of conditions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In software development, the item being cut, metaphorically speaking, is often plentiful and inexpensive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In many cases, the cost of measuring incorrectly is low compared to the time wasted doing two measurements before every action.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your philosophy is better suited for rock carving than web design.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any wise sayings that involve churning your own butter, or putting saddles on dinosaurs?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't bite the hand that feeds you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have direct deposit.

situation: The Boss announces his management philosophy of "measure twice, cut once," and Dilbert methodically argues it doesn't suit software development, where mistakes are cheap and double-checking wastes time. Dilbert compares the saying to rock carving and mocks it as outdated. When the Boss retorts with another proverb about not biting the hand that feeds you, Dilbert deflates it by noting he gets paid by direct deposit.
punchline: Dilbert shows that even the boss's last-resort proverb is obsolete, since modern employees are paid electronically and no longer depend on a literal hand feeding them.
summary: An employee dismantles his manager's old-fashioned carpentry adage as irrelevant to programming, then casually defeats the manager's next saying with a payroll technicality.
keywords: bite the hand that feeds you

title: Addicted to Internal Job Postings

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm addicted to our online job posting system.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It helps me fantasize about having a job I could enjoy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This can't be good.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oooh!

situation: Alice sits at her computer and thinks about how she is hooked on the company's internal job posting system, which lets her daydream about a job she would actually enjoy. In the last panel the Boss appears at her cubicle entrance and sees her browsing listings. He thinks to himself that this is a bad sign.
punchline: An employee who is happily browsing job postings to escape her current job is a clear warning that she is unhappy and may leave, which the Boss instantly realizes.
summary: A worker escapes her dull routine by browsing openings within her own company, only to be spotted by her manager who senses trouble.

file: 2008/2008-08-14_high altitude view_bunch of termites_termites hate each other_eat same log.gif
title: Termites Eating the Same Log

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't need to know the details. Just give me the high altitude view.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: From a high altitude we're all a bunch of termites trying to eat the same log.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe drill down a little more.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The termites hate each other.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he wants only a high-level overview with no details. Dilbert says that from a high altitude everyone at the company is a bunch of termites trying to eat the same log. The Boss asks him to drill down a little more, and Dilbert adds that the termites hate each other.
punchline: The more detail the boss requests, the bleaker the picture gets, showing that the company's internal reality is hostile infighting over limited resources that a high-level view conceals.
summary: Asked for a big-picture view of the company, Dilbert compares his coworkers to insects competing over one piece of wood, then reveals the ugly truth when pressed for more depth.

title: Garbage Man Cures Scent of Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I acquired the musky scent of failure. Do you have anything that can get rid of it?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Try being successful at something important.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I work in a fabric-covered box.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Okay, then try rubbing this behind both ears.

setting: Outdoors beside a garbage can, where Dilbert meets a garbage man
situation: Dilbert, giving off stink lines, asks a garbage man whether he has anything to remove the smell of failure. The garbage man suggests achieving something important, but Dilbert says he works in a cubicle. The garbage man then hands him a piece of trash to rub behind his ears like perfume.
punchline: Dilbert's cubicle job offers so little chance of real success that the garbage man gives up and suggests dabbing garbage on himself instead, implying that trash is the only fix for his odor of failure.
summary: A smelly office worker asks a sanitation worker for a cure for his stench of failure and ends up being handed a scrap of rubbish to dab on like cologne.

file: 2008/2008-07-14_hit with rock_prefrontal cortex_hurting poepl_natural leader_bunk on back of head_dont remeber.gif
title: Rock Injury Creates Natural Leader

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where am I? What happened?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Someone hit you with a rock.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The swelling in your prefrontal cortex will make you care less about hurting people, thus making you a natural leader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's also a bump on the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's so you don't remember who threw the rocks.

setting: Outdoors on a dirt hillside with grassy mounds
situation: Dilbert wakes up lying on the ground, confused, and Dogbert tells him he was hit with a rock. Dogbert then explains that the brain swelling will make Dilbert indifferent to hurting people, which makes him ideal leadership material. When Dilbert notices a second injury on the back of his head, Dogbert reveals it was deliberate so he wouldn't remember who threw the rocks.
punchline: Dogbert has deliberately injured Dilbert to turn him into a ruthless leader, and even arranged the second blow to cover his tracks.
summary: After a mysterious head injury, Dilbert learns that his new lack of empathy is a feature, and that Dogbert engineered the whole thing.

file: 2008/2008-06-07_executive steering group_cancel designs_sowed seeds of destruction_unclear.gif
title: Unclear Communicator Gets Cancelled Projects

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The executive steering group took your recommendation to cancel all design projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?!! I didn't recommend that!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh. Your poor communication skills have sowed the seeds of our destruction.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I an unclear communicator?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Six o'clock.

setting: Office hallway, then Dilbert's living room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the executive steering group acted on his supposed recommendation to cancel all design projects, which Dilbert insists he never made. The Boss blames Dilbert's poor communication skills for the disaster. Dilbert then goes home and asks Dogbert, sitting on the couch, whether he is an unclear communicator.
punchline: Dogbert answers the question 'Am I an unclear communicator?' with the irrelevant 'Six o'clock,' demonstrating that unclear communication is exactly what Dilbert is dealing with, and that Dogbert is not helping.
summary: After being blamed for a decision he never suggested, an engineer asks his dog if he communicates poorly and receives a baffling answer about the time.

title: Improbable Solutions Cost One Million

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need an improbable solution to a work problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure. I charge one million dollars for each improbable solution.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, then I also need an improbable way to get things from you for free.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stop breaking my business model.

setting: Dogbert's office at his 'Deus Ex Machina Services' consultancy
situation: Dilbert visits Dogbert's consulting business, Deus Ex Machina Services, and asks for an improbable solution to a work problem. Dogbert says he charges a million dollars for each one. Dilbert counters by requesting an improbable way to get the solutions for free, which Dogbert complains is undermining his business.
punchline: Dilbert uses Dogbert's own premise against him by demanding an improbable free outcome, forcing the consultant to admit that this threatens his pricing model.
summary: A consultant who sells miracle fixes at a steep price is stumped when his client asks for a miracle that costs nothing.

title: Dilbert Rebuts Boss's Uninformed Design Criticism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This design will never work in the real world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That design is already widely used in the real world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can come back later if you need time to concoct additional uninformed criticisms.

situation: The Boss reviews Dilbert's design document and declares it will never work in the real world. Dilbert calmly points out that the design is already widely used in the real world. He then sarcastically offers to return later so the Boss can come up with more criticisms.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically offers the Boss extra time to invent more baseless objections, since the Boss's complaint was factually wrong and uninformed.
summary: An engineer calmly dismantles his manager's baseless dismissal of a design by noting it is already in common use, then mockingly offers time for further complaints.

file: 2008/2008-03-01_300 iq_immortality drug_impossible requirements_job interview_nobel peace prize_time machine_too old_two centuires_unix.gif
title: Overqualified Applicant Is Just Too Old

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: I have all of the job requirements you're looking for.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: I have an I.Q. of 300, several Nobel prizes, and two centuries of Unix experience, thanks to the time machine and the immortality drug I invented.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's a lot of words for "too old."

setting: Office interview room, across a desk
situation: A job applicant sits across the desk from Catbert, the evil HR director, and claims to meet every job requirement. He lists a 300 IQ, multiple Nobel prizes, and two centuries of Unix experience thanks to his own time machine and immortality drug. Catbert dismisses all of it as a roundabout way of saying he is too old.
punchline: No matter how impressive the qualifications, Catbert's HR department will reject the candidate for age, since the two centuries of experience that satisfy the requirements also make him "too old."
summary: An applicant with absurdly impressive credentials is turned down by HR because acquiring them took him two hundred years.

file: 2008/2008-12-06_economy_sarcasm_smart_twice as smart_survive economy_spontaneously developing_high iq_pep talk_worked in marketing_see future.gif
title: Twice As Smart Pep Talk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to be twice as smart to survive in this economy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Good plan. I look forward to spontaneously developing an I.Q. of 400.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This pep talk totally worked in marketing.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Will I be able to see the future?

situation: The Boss tells the staff at a meeting that they must be twice as smart to survive the poor economy. Alice sarcastically says she looks forward to spontaneously developing an I.Q. of 400. Afterward, the Boss privately thinks the pep talk worked well on marketing, while a gullible employee asks if he'll be able to see the future.
punchline: The Boss's absurd demand to simply become twice as smart is met with sarcasm by Alice but taken literally by a gullible marketing employee, whom the Boss considers proof the pep talk worked.
summary: A manager's empty motivational speech about getting smarter is mocked by a sharp coworker but swallowed whole by a naive one.

title: No Tickets Because System Broke

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The server virtualization project is done, and there are no trouble tickets.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My rates might seem steep, but remember, there are no trouble tickets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our online trouble ticket system is broken.

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, tells The Boss that his server virtualization project is finished and that the absence of trouble tickets justifies his high rates. The Boss seems pleased. Dilbert then interrupts to reveal that the online trouble ticket system is broken, so no tickets could have been filed.
punchline: The lack of trouble tickets is not proof of success, because the ticket system itself is broken, which suggests the consultant's claim of success is meaningless or even engineered.
summary: A consultant defends his pricey virtualization work by pointing to zero complaints, until an employee reveals that nobody can file complaints at all.

title: Selling Organs After Budget Cuts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: After budget cuts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It might seem bleak now, but things will turn around...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as the public starts loving poorly made products that are relevant to a bygone era.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In the meantime, who has organs that are still healthy enough to sell on the black market?

setting: A barren desert wasteland where employees sit around a makeshift desk made from a door on cinder blocks
situation: After budget cuts have left the company in a desolate wasteland, The Boss tries to give an optimistic pep talk to his shabby employees seated at a door-turned-desk. He says things will improve when the public loves outdated, poorly made products. He then asks who has healthy organs to sell on the black market to keep the company going.
punchline: The company's recovery plan depends on customers inexplicably wanting obsolete, shoddy products, so in the meantime management casually asks employees to sell their organs to fund the business.
summary: Management offers a hollow recovery forecast in a ruined post-cuts landscape, then pivots to asking staff to sell their body parts.

title: Topping Each Other's Tall Tales
