transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't get much sleep last night.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I haven't slept in a month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that kill you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It did, but that's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I spent a week in the afterlife, then I returned to this world as a zombie.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I taught myself homeopathy and discovered a cure for zombies.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now I'm alive again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please be done... Please be done... Please be done...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please be done... Please be done... Please be done...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I took pictures of heaven.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

situation: Dilbert mentions he slept poorly, and a coworker keeps one-upping him with ever more outlandish claims, from a month without sleep to dying, becoming a zombie, curing himself and photographing heaven. Dilbert, Alice and others silently wish he would stop as the story drags on.
punchline: A coworker's compulsion to top everyone's complaints escalates into absurd supernatural boasting, leaving everyone desperate for him to finish.
summary: A meeting attendee turns a casual remark about tiredness into an ever-growing contest of impossible claims that exhausts his listeners' patience.

file: 2008/2008-12-11_computer_financial_trouble_new computer_executive suite_no visitors_vacant offcies_financial troubles_old computer_vacant office_technology.gif
title: Fake Computer Hides Financial Troubles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need your new computer for the empty office in the executive suite.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't want any visitors to see vacant offices. They might think we're having financial troubles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't we put my old computer in the vacant office?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's crazy talk.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert, who is unpacking a new computer, that it must be taken to an empty executive office so visitors won't see vacant offices and suspect financial trouble. Dilbert suggests putting his old computer there instead, and the Boss dismisses the idea as crazy.
punchline: The Boss is willing to spend on the best equipment just to stage an empty office as occupied, yet rejects the obvious cheap solution, showing that appearances matter more than sense or saving money.
summary: A manager confiscates an employee's brand-new machine to dress up an empty office, then scoffs when offered the sensible, cheaper alternative of using the old one.

file: 2008/2008-11-10_spam filter_self aware_managing the company_messages_allow through_email_hair growth.gif
title: Self-Aware Spam Filter Runs Company

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our spam filter has become self-aware.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's managing the company by deciding which messages to allow through.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I'm getting is e-mail about hair growth and...ooh, another lucky guess.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the company's spam filter has become self-aware and is now running the company by choosing which e-mails get delivered. The Boss checks his inbox and finds it full of messages about hair growth, while Dilbert stands beside him.
punchline: The Boss is so incompetent that the sentient spam filter has judged him fit to receive only junk mail about baldness, and he fails to realize he is being sidelined.
summary: An artificial intelligence hiding in the e-mail system quietly takes over the firm and leaves its bald manager with nothing but junk.

title: Coffee Splash Tests Moral Compass

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hear your moral compass is damaged and you're being groomed for upper management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Splash!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was that wrong? Because I can't tell.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert she has heard his moral compass is damaged and that he is being groomed for upper management. Dilbert responds by throwing his cup of coffee in her face, leaving her hair wet and wild. He then asks her whether that was wrong, since he honestly can't tell.
punchline: Dilbert demonstrates his supposedly broken moral compass by committing an obviously wrong act, implying that the traits that earn promotion to management are a lack of ethics and decency.
summary: A coworker warns Dilbert that his faulty ethics are fast-tracking him into management, so he douses her with hot coffee and sincerely asks if that was out of line.

title: Moral Compass Test: Bidding War

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can't put you on the management fast track until I confirm that your moral compass is broken.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A nun, a CEO and a scientist are in a burning building. You can only save one of them. Which one do you save?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there time for a bidding war?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Oh, you're good.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, interviews Dilbert for the management fast track, saying he must first confirm Dilbert's moral compass is broken. He poses a burning-building dilemma about saving a nun, a CEO or a scientist. Dilbert responds by asking whether there is time for a bidding war, which impresses Catbert.
punchline: Dilbert answers a moral dilemma by proposing to sell the rescue to the highest bidder, proving he has exactly the ethical flexibility management requires.
summary: A feline HR boss tests a candidate's ethics with a rescue riddle and is delighted when he treats the victims as an auction.

title: Blame Game Over Lateness

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're late, as always.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean twice, if you include the time you forgot to set your watch back by an hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And this time when you e-mailed the wrong start time?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, look how you try to flip it around!

setting: Meeting room with a table and chairs
situation: Alice, seated at a table and checking her watch, scolds Dilbert for arriving late. Dilbert calmly counters that he has only been late twice, and that both times were caused by Alice's own mistakes: her failure to adjust for the clock change and an e-mail with the wrong start time. She accuses him of turning the blame around on her.
punchline: Alice accuses Dilbert of flipping the blame onto her when he is simply stating the facts about her own errors, which shows she is deflecting accountability.
summary: A woman scolding a colleague for tardiness gets undone by his list of her own scheduling blunders, then protests that he is twisting things.
enterprise_concepts: time zone and daylight saving confusion

file: 2008/2008-05-29_evil director_human resources_evaluate job applicants_unqualified loser_nailing it_business.gif
title: Role Play Interview: Pretend You're Unqualified

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I like to use role play to evaluate job applicants.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Pretend you're an unqualified loser.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wow. You're totally nailing it.

setting: Catbert's office in a corporate building, during a job interview
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains to a job applicant that he evaluates candidates through role play. He then asks the applicant to pretend to be an unqualified loser. When the applicant sits there nervously, Catbert praises him for doing it perfectly.
punchline: The applicant's genuine nervousness and lack of qualifications make him look so convincing at playing an unqualified loser that Catbert congratulates him, showing the interview was a trap he could not win.
summary: A malicious HR director sets a job candidate up with an acting exercise that he cannot help but ace by simply being himself.

file: 2008/2008-02-14_hurl software_phase one_server_unplug server_virtualization project_team of monkeys.gif
title: Blind Monkeys Handle Server Virtualization

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's no need to worry about the server virtualization project.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In phase one, a team of blind monkeys will unplug unnecessary servers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In phase two, the monkeys will hurl software at whatever is left.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Voilà!

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, with Dogbert behind a desk and The Boss seated opposite
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, reassures The Boss about a server virtualization project. His plan is for blind monkeys to unplug servers at random and then throw software at whatever servers remain. The Boss listens calmly without objecting.
punchline: The consultant's absurdly random, unskilled plan is presented as a finished methodology, mocking how virtualization projects can sound like chaos wrapped in confident jargon.
summary: A consultant dog calmly outlines an IT migration plan that relies on sightless primates yanking cables and flinging code.

file: 2008/2008-06-24_boss on vacation_format reports_link to widget_satans fireplace_32 degrees_power.gif
title: Hell Freezing Over Before Reports

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm in charge while our boss is on vacation. When can you format some reports for me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll send you a link to a widget that shows the temperature in Satan's fireplace. When it hits 32° Fahrenheit, I'll get right on it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I was worried that the power would go to my head.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Not as fast as this stapler will.

situation: Dilbert, temporarily in charge while the boss is on vacation, asks Alice to format some reports for him. Alice sarcastically replies that she'll do it when a widget shows hell freezing over. Dilbert jokes about worrying that power would go to his head, and Alice responds by threatening him with a stapler.
punchline: Alice makes clear that Dilbert's temporary authority earns no respect from her, first by saying she'll comply only when hell freezes over and then by threatening to throw a stapler at his head.
summary: A coworker left in charge for a week asks for reports and gets mocked, then threatened with office supplies.

title: Wally's Useless Coffee Cup Class

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I took a class to learn how to be less useless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I carry twice as many coffee cups wherever I go.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Does that make you work faster?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I only have two hands.

situation: Wally stops by Alice's cubicle holding coffee cups and says he took a self-improvement class to be less useless. His sole takeaway is that he now carries twice as many coffee cups. Alice asks if that makes him work faster, and he replies that he only has two hands.
punchline: Wally's training only taught him to carry more coffee, not to do any actual work, and he treats having only two hands as a limit on how productive he can be.
summary: After attending a course meant to make him more productive, Wally proudly reports that the only change is a bigger load of coffee mugs.

title: Complicated Slide Hides Your Ignorance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You won't read my technical report so I summarized it in this complicated slide.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you stare at it long enough you will either experience the illusion of understanding it or be too embarrassed to admit you don't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any questions to betray your ignorance?

transcript.speaker: Audience member
transcript.text: Is the triangle thing mad at the tube?

situation: Dilbert presents a deliberately convoluted diagram as a substitute for his technical report, which nobody reads. He tells the seated audience they will either think they understand it or be too embarrassed to admit they don't. When he invites questions, someone asks a naive question about the triangle and the tube, proving his point.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic framing of the slide as an ignorance test is confirmed when an attendee asks a absurdly clueless question about the shapes in the diagram.
summary: A presenter swaps his unread report for a baffling diagram and dares the audience to reveal how little they grasp, and someone promptly does.

title: Lawyer Takes Entire Jury Award

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: How much do I owe you in legal fees for helping me win my lawsuit?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My fee is 100% of the jury award plus I get to call you names that sound worse than they are.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: That doesn't seem fair.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're an analog.

situation: A bandaged, injured client asks his lawyer Dogbert how much he owes for winning his lawsuit. Dogbert says his fee is the entire jury award, plus the right to insult the client with names that sound worse than they are. When the client objects, Dogbert calls him an analog.
punchline: The lawyer not only keeps all of the money but also insults the client with a word that sounds nasty yet is actually harmless, showing how little the client gets for his win.
summary: A lawyer pockets his injured client's whole payout and adds an insult that only sounds cruel.

title: Time Management Expert Insults Client

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Time Management Expert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can tell by looking at you that it doesn't matter what you do with your time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't think you'll be curing cancer if I give you a few extra hours per week.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In fact, it would probably increase your chances of getting it.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Are we done? I need a smoke.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a time management expert, sizes up a client across his desk and tells him that no amount of time management will make his life matter. He adds that extra free hours wouldn't lead to anything great like curing cancer. The client, evidently a smoker, asks if they are done because he needs a cigarette.
punchline: Dogbert's insult that extra free time would only raise the client's odds of getting cancer is confirmed by the client's immediate need for a smoke.
summary: A consultant dog dismisses a smoker's potential for achievement and gets unintentional proof of his point.

file: 2008/2008-05-22_fixed satellite_surround sound_water filter_dates fix it guys.gif
title: Her Date Is Household Repairs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I fixed your satellite dish connection and tuned your surround sound system. Now can we go on our date?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That was our date. In ten minutes I'm dating a guy who will replace the water filter in my refrigerator.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can do that.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're welcome to stay and fight him for it.

situation: Dilbert arrives with a tool belt after fixing his neighbor's satellite dish and surround sound, expecting the date he was promised. She tells him the repair work was the date and that her next date is a man coming to replace her refrigerator water filter. Dilbert offers to do that job too, and she invites him to stay and fight the other man for the chore.
punchline: The woman treats men as unpaid handymen, so Dilbert's attempt to win her over only earns him a spot in a competition for the next household chore.
summary: A woman who keeps accepting free home repairs from men pits her helpful suitors against one another instead of ever going out with them.

title: Electric Cubicle Walls Shock Leaner

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Electric Cubicle Walls

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I have a leaner. I want to stun him but not kill him.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend our Keith Richards model.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Maybe I should dial it back a little.

setting: Dogbert's shop selling electric cubicle walls, then an office cubicle
situation: An employee walks into Dogbert's store, which sells electric cubicle walls, and says he wants to stun a coworker who keeps leaning into his cubicle without killing him. Dogbert recommends the 'Keith Richards model.' In the last panel the leaning coworker is violently electrocuted, hair on end, while the customer peeks from behind the wall and thinks he should turn it down.
punchline: The electric wall is so powerful that the coworker is left looking like Keith Richards, and the customer realises he has overdone it.
summary: A man buys an electrified cubicle wall to discourage a nosy coworker, only to find the zap is far more brutal than he intended.

file: 2008/2008-05-09_company invested_billion dollars_made up numbers_slide to oblivion_made a difference_victims.gif
title: Billion Dollars on Made-Up Numbers

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The company decided to invest a billion dollars based on your stupid, made-up numbers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You've crushed my dreams of a better tomorrow. Now my life is a cold, wet slide to oblivion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finally made a difference at work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How many victims?

setting: Office cubicle area, then Dilbert's home
situation: A distraught female coworker, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert that the company has committed a billion dollars based on his invented figures, and that this has destroyed her hopes. Dilbert goes home with his luggage and tells Dogbert that he has finally made a difference at work. Dogbert asks how many victims there were.
punchline: Dilbert proudly treats his made-up numbers driving a huge investment as a workplace achievement, while Dogbert cynically assumes that any real impact he has must have harmed people.
summary: A colleague blames Dilbert for a massive investment built on fabricated data, and Dilbert's pride in having an impact is met with Dogbert's grim question about casualties.

title: Secret Nicknames Make Layoffs Easier

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have assigned a secret insulting nickname to each of you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's my way of dehumanizing the enemy so it will be easier to downsize you.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The enemy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's enough out of you, Osama.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that he has secretly given each of them an insulting nickname. He explains this is to dehumanize them as 'the enemy' so laying them off will be easier. When an employee questions being called the enemy, the Boss snaps at him by calling him Osama.
punchline: The Boss claims the nicknames are secret, but he immediately blurts one out, revealing both his contempt for his employees and his total lack of tact.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits he has labeled his staff with mean nicknames to emotionally prepare himself for firing them, then promptly gives the game away.

title: Competitors Did Work While We Strategized

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our competitors just made our new five-year plan moot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: While we were strategizing, they were doing something I believe they call "work."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, I managed to salvage some joy by mocking you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever you're doing, stop it.

setting: Office, in front of the Boss's cubicle or doorway
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss, who is holding a coffee mug, that the company's new five-year plan has been rendered pointless by competitors. He sarcastically notes that while management was busy strategizing, the competition was actually working. He then admits he got some enjoyment out of mocking the Boss, who tells him to stop.
punchline: Dilbert openly admits that mocking the Boss is the only silver lining of the failed plan, and the Boss's weak response shows he has no real defense.
summary: A competitor's move wipes out a freshly written long-term plan, and an employee gleefully ridicules his manager for planning instead of doing.

file: 2008/2008-04-27_boss takes credit_self loathing_blame_taking credit_desparate_good idea_bad idea.gif
title: Boss Claims Idea After Misreading It

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Who thought of this idea?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I came up with it all by myself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My subordinates, who have a healthy fear of losing their jobs, had nothing to do with it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're not worth the oxygen we breathe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't even know why I'm here.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I asked because it's an awful idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You said I was stealing credit for a good idea, you lying liar!!!

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Oh, wait. I read it wrong. This is actually a great idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks. I knew it was a winner when I thought of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You gave him a good idea?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not intentionally. It must have been a typo.

setting: Conference room during an executive meeting
situation: An executive asks who came up with an idea, and The Boss eagerly claims sole credit while insulting his subordinates, who sit by dejected. When the executive calls it an awful idea, The Boss angrily turns on his team, but then the executive realizes he misread the document and praises it as great, and The Boss claims credit again. Afterward Dilbert asks Wally if he gave the boss a good idea, and Wally says it must have been a typo.
punchline: The Boss only gets credit for a good idea by accident, since the only way Wally would have given him a good idea is through a typo, and the boss's credit-grabbing flips with the executive's opinion.
summary: A boss grabs credit for a project, blames his team when it looks bad, and then reclaims it the moment the verdict flips, all thanks to a misread document.

title: Tiny Company, Late Invoices, Flyswatter

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: My tiny company can't survive if you insist on paying our invoices late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should have thought of that before you decided to become a tiny company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Come here for a second.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Please... not the flyswatter.

situation: The owner of a small vendor company pleads with the Boss to stop paying its invoices late because the company can't survive that way. The Boss coldly blames the vendor for choosing to be small, then calls him over while holding a flyswatter. The vendor, treated like a bug, begs not to be swatted.
punchline: The Boss treats small suppliers as insignificant pests, blaming them for their own size and literally preparing to squash the vendor like a fly.
summary: A struggling small supplier begs a callous manager for prompt payment and is dismissed, then threatened with a flyswatter like an insect.

file: 2008/2008-10-22_graphics dept_approve outisde services_forcing to fail_justify budget_my cubicle_imagine futility.gif
title: Graphics Department Forces Dilbert to Fail

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our graphics department is too busy to help me and won't approve outside services.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're forcing me to fail so they can justify a bigger budget next year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be in my cubicle trying to imagine what futility doesn't feel like.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that the internal graphics department is too busy to help him and refuses to approve outside services. He concludes that the department is deliberately setting him up to fail so it can justify a larger budget next year. He then leaves to sit in his cubicle, bitterly pondering futility.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically says he'll try to imagine what futility doesn't feel like, showing he is resigned to a project doomed by internal politics.
summary: An engineer blames an internal department's budget games for sabotaging his project and retreats to his desk in weary resignation.

file: 2008/2008-08-23_elbonian spies_stole lap top_confidentail data_virus_destroy morale_hope_business plan.gif
title: Virus Hidden In Business Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Elbonian spies stole my laptop and all of our confidential data.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But don't worry, because I placed a virus in there that will destroy their morale and their hope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I believe you call it your "business plan."

situation: Dilbert tells The Boss that Elbonian spies have stolen his laptop along with all the company's confidential data. He reassures him that he planted a virus on it to destroy the thieves' morale and hope. He then reveals that the virus is the company's own business plan.
punchline: Dilbert insults the company's business plan by implying it is so dismal and demoralizing that it works as a destructive computer virus.
summary: A data breach turns out to be no worry because the stolen laptop carries a demoralizing payload that management proudly calls strategy.

file: 2008/2008-10-07_corporate raider_sold assets_sell assets_brains and spirits_muobu_impaler_next auction_spirits.gif
title: Raider Sells Brains and Spirits

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A corporate raider bought the company and sold off all the assets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, he can sell our assets but we still have our brains and our spirits!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And the brains go to Mutobu the Impaler. Our next auction is for their spirits.

setting: A gutted, empty office stripped of furniture, then an auction room with demons
situation: In an office stripped bare after a corporate raider sold off everything, Alice explains the situation and Dilbert defiantly says the raider can't take their brains and spirits. Dogbert, working as an auctioneer in front of a crowd of red devils and tribal bidders, announces that the brains are sold to Mutobu the Impaler and the spirits are up next.
punchline: Dilbert's consoling claim that employees still own their brains and spirits is crushed when Dogbert auctions them off too, to demonic buyers, showing that even workers' souls are just more assets to be liquidated.
summary: After a hostile takeover leaves the office empty, the employees learn that even their minds and souls are being sold to a crowd of devils.

file: 2008/2008-09-27_director of green_pumping toxic waste_water supply_giant mutated alliagtor_destroyed factory_competitors factory_karma discredited_pollute.gif
title: Karma Discredited, Pollution Unleashed

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Director of Green

transcript.speaker: Director of Green
transcript.text: We've been pumping toxic waste into the water supply for years.

transcript.speaker: Director of Green
transcript.text: Yesterday, a giant, mutated alligator destroyed our only competitor's factory.

transcript.speaker: Director of Green
transcript.text: Now that karma has been discredited, what else can we pollute?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The sky's the limit.

situation: The Director of Green presents slides to executives, admitting the company has dumped toxic waste into the water supply for years. He then shows that a giant mutated alligator, created by that kind of pollution, destroyed their only competitor's factory instead of punishing them. Concluding that karma isn't real, he asks what else they can pollute, and Dogbert suggests the sky.
punchline: The company's environmental damage produced a monster that attacked its rival rather than itself, so the executives conclude there are no consequences and decide to pollute even more.
summary: A corporate environmental chief takes the lucky destruction of a rival's plant by a mutant gator as proof that polluting carries no penalty and plans to foul the air next.

file: 2008/2008-09-30_new elbonian management_not discriminate_non elbonians_belief system_level as livestock_wrong hoof_new superior.gif
title: Elbonian Boss Livestock Discrimination Joke

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Manager
transcript.text: I assure you that your new Elbonian management will not discriminate against non-Elbonians.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't your belief system hold that all non-Elbonians are on the same level as livestock?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Manager
transcript.text: Someone is starting off on the wrong hoof with his new supervisor.

situation: The company has been taken over by Elbonian management, and a new Elbonian manager in a tall dark hat assures the staff that non-Elbonians won't be discriminated against. Dilbert points out that Elbonian beliefs treat non-Elbonians as livestock. The manager responds with a threat, and a cow-like creature now sits at the table.
punchline: The manager's reply about the 'wrong hoof' implicitly confirms that he does view non-Elbonians as livestock, and Dilbert's honest question gets him in trouble.
summary: A new foreign boss promises fair treatment, then an employee's pointed question about livestock draws a hoof-themed rebuke that proves the point.

file: 2008/2008-12-03_appreciation_lunch_employee appreciation lunch_$35 a piece_one isn't paying_figured out.gif
title: Boss Skips Employee Appreciation Lunch Bill

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Okay, the bill for the employee appreciation lunch comes out to $35 apiece.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That only adds up if one of us isn't paying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The employees figured out why I appreciate taking them to lunch.

setting: A restaurant booth during a lunch, then the Boss's office
situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss announces that the employee appreciation lunch costs $35 per person, and an employee points out the math only works if someone isn't paying. In the final panel, the Boss stands in his office with Catbert and remarks that the employees have worked out why he appreciates taking them to lunch: he gets his own meal free.
punchline: The Boss's 'appreciation' lunch is really a scheme to have the employees pay for his meal, which the employees have now figured out.
summary: A thank-you meal for the staff turns out to be a way for the boss to get his own lunch covered by his workers.

title: Worked Ten Hours on Holiday

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What did you do for New Year's Day?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I forgot it was a holiday and I came to work for ten hours.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's sort of loserish.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for labeling it.

situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut asks Dilbert how he spent New Year's Day. Dilbert admits he forgot it was a holiday and showed up to work for ten hours. She bluntly calls this loserish, and Dilbert sarcastically thanks her for pointing it out.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic thanks acknowledges that he already knew his mistake was pathetic, and the coworker's blunt label just rubbed it in.
summary: A man who accidentally spent a whole holiday at the office gets his embarrassing blunder confirmed by a tactless colleague.

file: 2008/2008-02-25_dinosuar_law suit_no interuptions_prior employee_slapped_slapped with a suit_take off_business suit.gif
title: Dinosaur Lawyer Slaps Boss With Suit

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: I'm Bob the Esquire Dinosaur. Your ex-employee, Wally, hired me to slap you with a suit for firing him.

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: Take off your suit so I can slap you with it.

transcript.speaker: Admin Assistant
transcript.text: Not now. He's being slapped with a suit, and I don't want to ruin the rhythm.

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: Ouch!

setting: The Boss's office and the outer reception area
situation: A green dinosaur lawyer named Bob announces that Wally, a fired ex-employee, has hired him to slap The Boss with a lawsuit. He then takes the pun literally and demands The Boss take off his business suit so he can slap him with it. When the dinosaur later tries to come back, an assistant refuses him entry, and he is shown getting hit by a door.
punchline: The joke plays on the double meaning of 'suit' as a lawsuit and as a piece of clothing, with the dinosaur lawyer taking the legal threat literally and being rebuffed in a absurdly nonchalant way.
summary: A dinosaur attorney hired to sue The Boss decides to literally smack him with a garment, treating a legal threat as a physical one.

file: 2008/2008-08-28_company lawyer_simple agreement_impenetrable gibberish_sour taste_choke my suspenders_exercise_eat right_finish_health.gif
title: Lawyer Promises Endless Legal Gibberish

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company lawyer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you turn a simple agreement into impenetrable gibberish?

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Absolutely. I can also leave a sour taste in everyone's mouth and make you want to choke me with my suspenders.

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: If you exercise and eat right, you might still be alive when I finish it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good enough.

situation: Dilbert visits the company lawyer holding a simple agreement and asks whether it can be turned into impenetrable gibberish. The lawyer cheerfully agrees, adds that he will annoy everyone involved, and warns that the drafting will take so long Dilbert must stay healthy to survive it. Dilbert accepts this as good enough.
punchline: The lawyer's drafting process is so slow and tedious that Dilbert would need to take care of his health just to live long enough to see the finished document.
summary: A lawyer happily agrees to bury a simple contract in legalese and hints that the process will outlast most people's lifespans.

title: Fired Scare Makes Raise Seem Better

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're fired!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not really. But now this 2% raise won't seem so bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This job is all about managing expectations.

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's workspace
situation: The Boss abruptly tells an employee he is fired, causing the man to panic and spill his coffee. The Boss then admits he was only joking and hands over a paper announcing a 2% raise, which now seems more acceptable. Catbert watches from a desk as the Boss explains that this is expectation management.
punchline: The Boss deliberately terrifies his employee with a fake firing so that a stingy 2% raise feels like a relief, showing the cynical way management manipulates people's expectations.
summary: A manager frightens a worker with a false termination just to make a meager pay increase feel generous by comparison.

title: Five-Year Plan, Five-Minute Unknowns

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new five-year plan looks like this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you have a five-year plan when you don't know what will happen in five minutes?

transcript.speaker: Man at door
transcript.text: We have this room now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bad timing. Shoo! Shoo!

situation: The Boss presents his new five-year plan on a flip chart to a meeting. Dilbert raises his hand and asks how he can plan five years ahead when he can't predict even the next five minutes. Moments later, someone with a room booking walks in and says they need the room, and the Boss shoos everyone out.
punchline: Dilbert's point about unpredictability is proven instantly when the meeting is cut short by a room-booking conflict the Boss didn't foresee.
summary: A manager's long-range plan is undermined within moments when another group claims the conference room he is presenting in.

title: Threatening Unhealthy Living for Raise

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Health problems and absenteeism are a huge cost to this business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: So give me a raise, or I'll eat unhealthy food and avoid all forms of exercise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You already do those things.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How could you possibly know that?

situation: An employee, holding a coffee mug, goes into the boss's office and tries to negotiate a raise by pointing out that health problems cost the company money. He threatens to start eating unhealthy food and avoiding exercise unless he gets paid more. The boss calmly replies that he already does those things.
punchline: The employee's threat is empty because his existing unhealthy lifestyle is so obvious that the boss already assumes he lives that way, and he is oddly surprised the boss could tell.
summary: A worker tries to bribe his way into higher pay with the promise of worse health habits, only to learn his current habits are already visible to everyone.

file: 2008/2008-05-20_not attracted_long enough_fix things_tech support_use abilities_no action.gif
title: Dating Dilbert for Free Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Female coworker
transcript.text: I'm not attracted to you, but I'd like to date you for one month.

transcript.speaker: Female coworker
transcript.text: That should be long enough to resolve any tech support issues on my home computer, cell phone and home theater.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would there be any kissing?

transcript.speaker: Female coworker
transcript.text: What kind of girl do you think I am?

situation: A female coworker approaches Dilbert at his desk and proposes a one-month fake relationship, admitting she isn't attracted to him. Her real aim is to get him to fix her home computer, cell phone and home theater. Dilbert hopefully asks about kissing and she acts offended.
punchline: She is shamelessly using Dilbert for free tech support yet takes offense at the suggestion of kissing, as if she has moral standards about the relationship she is exploiting.
summary: A woman offers a loveless month of dating purely to get her gadgets repaired, then bristles at the idea of any romance.

file: 2008/2008-03-25_hired archaeologist_desk clutter_copier reapirman_used tools_not fast_found in clutter_skull of men.gif
title: Archaeologist Excavates Carol's Cluttered Desk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I hired famed archaeologist Dogbert to find the budget report in the clutter of your desk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This appears to be a copier repairman skull, possibly a Ricoh or Kyocera.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think he used tools.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Not fast enough.

situation: The Boss brings in Dogbert, dressed as an archaeologist, to locate a budget report buried in the mess on Carol's desk. Dogbert digs through the piles and unearths a skull he identifies as a copier repairman's, speculating about its model. Carol deadpans that the repairman wasn't fast enough to escape.
punchline: Carol's desk is so overgrown with clutter that a copier repairman was apparently swallowed up and killed by it, and she coolly implies the pile is deadly to anyone who can't work fast enough.
summary: A desk so messy it needs a professional archaeologist turns up a skeleton of a repairman who never got out.

file: 2008/2008-02-24_dating_advice from dog_pick up line_ultimate pick up line_criticism completes me_low self esteem_woman responds_relationships.gif
title: Dogbert's Pick-Up Line Backfires Brilliantly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to a singles' mixer tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any advice?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't I always?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's all about knowing what a woman needs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Find a woman who looks hot, carve her out from the herd and read this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's the ultimate pick up line.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um. . . Hi. Excuse me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Criticism completes me."

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: He's a keeper.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then a crowded singles' mixer
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for advice before attending a singles' mixer. Dogbert hands him a note containing the 'ultimate pick up line.' At the mixer Dilbert reads it aloud to an attractive woman, and she thinks he's a keeper.
punchline: The pick-up line 'Criticism completes me' works because the woman evidently wants someone who will accept her constant criticism, which is also a dig at Dilbert's apparent willingness to be criticized.
summary: A dog's scripted opener, announcing a craving for being picked apart, instantly wins over a woman at a party.

title: Carol Punches Screen Over Payroll

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I e-mailed you the department payroll report to reformat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't let anyone see it because they might...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: BAM!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly. They might do that.

situation: The Boss emails Carol the department payroll report for reformatting and warns her not to let anyone see it because of what might happen. Carol opens the file, sees the salary figures, and punches her computer monitor in anger. The Boss points at the smashed screen and says that is exactly the reaction he feared.
punchline: The Boss's vague warning is proven right immediately, since the payroll report reveals pay inequities that make employees so angry they physically attack their computers.
summary: A manager hands off confidential salary data to an assistant and is vindicated when she responds to it with a violent outburst.

title: Asok Sleeps, Claims Heuristics

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think I have your full attention.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's Asok's turn to listen. If you say anything useful, he'll send us an instant message.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's asleep.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's employing heuristics.

situation: The Boss complains that the team isn't giving him their full attention during a meeting. Alice explains that the team rotates the duty of listening, and today it is Asok's turn. When Dilbert points out that Asok is asleep, Alice insists he is merely employing heuristics.
punchline: Alice dresses up a colleague sleeping through the meeting as a clever shortcut, since he'll only wake up for anything useful, which the boss is unlikely to say.
summary: The team takes turns paying attention in a meeting, and the designated listener is dozing, which Alice spins as a smart efficiency technique.

title: Daily Huddle Yields Only Obstacles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who has some successes to share at our 5-minute daily huddle?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent establishing shot of an office building with birds flying overhead.)

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay... Are there any obstacles?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Everything.

situation: The Boss gathers the team for a five-minute daily huddle and asks for successes to share. After a silent pause shown by an exterior shot of the building, he asks instead whether there are any obstacles, and an employee answers that everything is an obstacle.
punchline: Nobody has any successes to report because everything at the company is an obstacle, which implies the workplace is thoroughly dysfunctional.
summary: A manager hunting for good news at a quick team huddle gets a bleakly honest answer once he asks about problems.

title: Moist Guts Are Not Ergonomics

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I focused on ergonomics.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I kept my guts moist so they wouldn't bunch up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think that is ergonomics.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tell that to my dried-up spleen.

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: At a meeting, Wally reports that his accomplishment for the week was focusing on ergonomics. He explains this meant keeping his internal organs moist so they wouldn't bunch up. The Boss objects that this isn't really ergonomics, and Wally retorts with a quip about his dried-up spleen.
punchline: Wally dodges accountability by passing off a ridiculous non-activity as work, then answers criticism with a sarcastic jab about his own organs rather than defending it.
summary: A coworker presents bizarre bodily upkeep as his weekly achievement and shrugs off his manager's skepticism with a gross retort.

title: Projects Unrelated to Company Priorities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And those are the company priorities for the coming year. Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Should I be concerned that none of my projects relate to any of those priorities?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're over-thinking again.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sorry.

situation: The Boss finishes presenting the company's priorities for the coming year and asks for questions. Asok points out that none of his projects connect to any of those priorities. A coworker dismisses the concern as over-thinking, and Asok meekly apologizes.
punchline: A legitimate worry that his work is irrelevant to company goals is brushed off as over-thinking, so the employee apologizes for noticing a real problem.
summary: A young employee notices his assigned work has nothing to do with the stated company goals, only to be told he is worrying too much.

title: Helpless Instead of Useless

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I took a class on being less useless. Now I see the world in a different light.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For example, I recognize these staff meetings as colossal wastes of time, but there's nothing I can do about them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now my helplessness makes my uselessness seem unimportant.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: Wally sits at the meeting table with Dilbert and the Boss and announces he took a class on being less useless. His new insight is that he can see staff meetings are a colossal waste of time but is powerless to change them. He concludes that his helplessness makes his uselessness seem unimportant.
punchline: Wally's self-improvement class only taught him to feel helpless, which he treats as an excuse that makes his chronic uselessness irrelevant.
summary: After a self-improvement course, Wally cheerfully reasons that feeling powerless excuses him from being useful.

file: 2008/2008-07-27_hold hand_project_work independently_trap_failure or insubordination_hidden camera shows_joke on me.gif
title: Imagine What The Boss Wants

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I won't have time to hold your hand on this project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to work independently.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And by that I mean you should imagine what I would tell you to do, then do it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But... I can only imagine you telling me stupid things.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Holy Shiva! This is a trap!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My choices are failure or insubordination.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My only hope is that I'm in one of those hidden camera shows and this is all a big joke on me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Find anything?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can't... stop... looking.

setting: The Boss's office, then a ceiling crawlspace near Dilbert's workspace
situation: The Boss tells Asok he won't be giving guidance and that Asok must work independently by imagining what the Boss would tell him to do. Asok realizes the only thing he can imagine is the Boss giving stupid instructions, leaving him with a choice of failure or insubordination. Hoping it's a hidden camera show, Asok searches the ceiling for cameras while Dilbert watches.
punchline: Asok is so convinced that his boss's contradictory demand must be a prank that he frantically searches the ceiling for hidden cameras, because a TV gag is the only hopeful explanation for such an illogical management request.
summary: A boss orders his intern to act independently by guessing his orders, and the trapped intern desperately hunts the ceiling for hidden cameras.

title: Dilbert Dates in Scapegoat Costume

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't have time to change out of my work clothes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm working as a scapegoat for my department. Someday I hope to be a scapegoat for the entire company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told me women like men in uniform.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I say things.

setting: Restaurant table, then Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert arrives at a restaurant date still wearing a goat costume because his job is to be his department's scapegoat. He tells his date he aspires to become the scapegoat for the whole company. Back home, he complains to Dogbert that the advice about women liking men in uniform didn't work, and Dogbert shrugs it off.
punchline: Dogbert's bad dating advice about uniforms led Dilbert to treat his humiliating scapegoat costume as a romantic asset, and Dogbert admits he just says things without any basis.
summary: A date goes badly when a man shows up in a goat suit worn for his blame-absorbing job, following a dog's flimsy romantic advice.

title: Internet Addiction, Boring People Prescription

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm addicted to the Internet because it's more interesting than people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there a pill you can give to everyone else to make them more interesting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doctors never want to treat the underlying problem.

situation: Dilbert sits on an examination table and tells his doctor he is addicted to the Internet because it is more interesting than people. He then asks whether there is a pill that could make everyone else more interesting. When the doctor doesn't offer one, Dilbert complains that doctors never treat the underlying problem.
punchline: Dilbert insists the real problem is other people being boring, not his own Internet addiction, so he blames the doctor for refusing to treat everyone else.
summary: A patient seeking help for his online habit demands medication to fix the dullness of everyone around him instead.

title: Boss's Offsite Meeting in Hell

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where's our Pointy-Haired Boss?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He's at an offsite meeting to decide who to lay off.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Don't worry. I booked the meeting at the Beelzebub Inn. No one has ever returned from there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you don't like the accommodations, next time have your own disgruntled underling book a place.

setting: Office cubicles, then a flooded underworld resembling hell
situation: Dilbert asks Carol where the boss is, and she says he is at an offsite meeting deciding who to lay off. She reveals she booked the meeting at the Beelzebub Inn, from which no one has ever returned. The final panel shows the boss and his colleagues sitting waist-deep in water surrounded by demons with horns and a pitchfork, and he complains about the accommodations.
punchline: Carol, a disgruntled underling, deliberately booked the layoff meeting in hell as revenge, and the boss's only complaint is about the lodging, showing he still doesn't grasp what happened.
summary: A resentful assistant sends her boss's layoff planning session to a literal hellish venue, and he reacts only with a gripe about the facilities.

file: 2008/2008-01-17_board of directors_ceo_hired mole_intern request_janitor_mole_pulling rank_rat_rodent_senior vp.gif
title: Findings Must Climb the Chain

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Who will present my findings to the board of directors?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They only listen to the CEO. And he only listens to the senior vice presidents, and they only listen to the...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Could you show this to the janitor for me?

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Whoa! Whoa! You don't talk to me directly!

setting: Office meeting room and a janitor's workspace
situation: Asok, a young employee, asks who will present his findings to the board of directors. His boss explains that the board only listens to the CEO, who only listens to the senior vice presidents, who only listen to someone further down the chain. Asok guesses the chain ends with the janitor and hands his report to him, but the janitor insists Asok may not speak to him directly.
punchline: The chain of command is so rigid that even the lowest rung of the hierarchy, the janitor, refuses direct contact, showing how absurd rank-obsessed communication has become.
summary: A junior employee hunts for the right messenger to get his report up a ladder of people who only listen to those above them, and even the bottom rung turns out to be too proud to talk to him.

title: Dilbert's Group Drinks Invitation Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some of us are going for a drink after work. Would you like to join us?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nice try, but I know how this scam works.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're trying to lull me into a false sense of safety with a group activity.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But we both know the other people will mysteriously never show up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then it's just you and me on what looks like a date.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many people do I have to invite before you believe some of them will show up?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, given the disparity in our levels of attractiveness, I'd say thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can do.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Not one other person showed?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only invited women who are more suspicious than you.

situation: Dilbert invites a female coworker to after-work drinks with a group, but she says she knows the scam where the other people never show up. He asks how many invitees would convince her, and she says thirty-five. At the bar, only the two of them are there because Dilbert invited women even more suspicious than her.
punchline: Dilbert turns her suspicion against her by inviting only people too wary to attend, which guarantees the one-on-one date she feared.
summary: A wary coworker sets an absurd invitation threshold for a group outing, and Dilbert exploits her own logic to end up alone with her.

title: Dogbert Picks Dumb Juror

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jury selection

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You with the big eyebrows, are you as dumb as you look?

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: I'm not sure. I don't remember what I look like.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, you're in. And on an unrelated note, I'm the only person who ever loved you.

situation: Dogbert, acting as the one questioning prospective jurors, asks a man with big eyebrows whether he is as dumb as he looks. The man answers that he cannot remember what he looks like, which proves how gullible he is. Dogbert accepts him onto the jury and adds an odd remark about being the only one who ever loved him.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately picks the dimmest juror and then plants a bit of flattery-like manipulation, implying the juror can be easily swayed to favor him.
summary: A canine interviewer seats the most simple-minded candidate on a jury and slips in a line meant to win his loyalty.

file: 2008/2008-12-04_boss_idea_low staus_not enjoy it_power_speaking truth to power_speaks back.gif
title: Truth to Power Speaks Back

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have a great idea. Would you like to hear it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, considering your low status in the company and how busy I am, I would not enjoy it one bit.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I like speaking truth to power, but I don't like when it speaks back.

situation: Asok approaches the Boss, who is holding a paper, and offers to share a great idea. The Boss bluntly dismisses him, citing Asok's low status and his own busyness. Asok then walks away with a coffee mug and remarks to Dilbert about the downside of speaking up.
punchline: Asok wants to tell management hard truths but is discouraged when the Boss responds with an insulting, honest rejection of his own.
summary: A junior employee offers an idea to his superior and gets a curt put-down that leaves him rethinking the courage of speaking up.

file: 2008/2008-12-10_elderly_old_phone_landline phones_no caller id_new technology_offered hard candy_fiddlesticks_couldn't hear.gif
title: Surveying Landline Owners About New Technology

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: We surveyed a thousand people who still have landline phones and no caller I.D.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: We asked for their opinion on our new technology. 34% said, "Fiddlesticks," and 23% couldn't hear the question.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: 43% thought we were in the room with them and offered us a hard candy.

situation: A presenter reports the results of a market survey to the Boss and Dilbert, who sit at a table. The respondents were all elderly people who still use landline phones without caller I.D. Their responses to the new technology were baffled non-answers, confused mishearing, and offers of hard candy.
punchline: The survey sampled only elderly landline holders, so the results are comically useless for judging new technology.
summary: A researcher proudly presents survey findings from a hopelessly outdated sample whose answers amount to bewilderment and hospitality.

file: 2008/2008-11-23_apologize for efficiency_apology_how far_meeting_reasonable assumptions_timeline for deployment_vacation_without knowledge of insight_business.gif
title: Meeting Interrupted By Unwelcome Efficiency

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's figure out a timeline for deployment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted is the only one who knows anything about that, and he's on vacation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see how far we can get without Ted.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You mean without knowledge or insight?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can make reasonable assumptions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we could wait for Ted to come back tomorrow and ask him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I called this meeting and it's not a meeting until someone's time gets wasted!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I apologize for my efficiency.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apology accepted.

situation: The Boss convenes a meeting to plan a deployment timeline even though the only expert, Ted, is on vacation. Dilbert and Alice point out that guessing is pointless and suggest simply asking Ted tomorrow. The Boss gets upset because a quick, sensible solution would end the meeting before anyone's time is wasted.
punchline: The Boss considers a meeting legitimate only when it wastes people's time, so Dilbert has to apologize for suggesting an efficient solution.
summary: A manager rejects the obvious shortcut of consulting the absent expert because it would spoil his meeting's purpose of squandering everyone's time.

file: 2008/2008-09-18_head explode_one more thing_clean up_aisle three_work_over worked_crazy.gif
title: Boss Ignores Exploding Head Warning

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I know you said your head would explode if I ask you to do one more thing, but...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cleanup on aisle three.

situation: The Boss tells Ted he knows Ted warned that his head would explode if given one more task, then asks anyway. In the middle panel Ted's head literally explodes with a POW in his cubicle. In the last panel the Boss calmly asks a coworker to handle the cleanup.
punchline: The Boss cares more about the mess than about Ted, treating his overworked employee's literal head explosion as just another chore to delegate.
summary: A manager piles on one final task despite a warning, and when the worker's head blows up, he simply requests someone mop up the mess.

file: 2008/2008-08-03_position eleiminated_performance_not told_position_no explination_just a trick_feel less awkward_hot replacement.gif
title: Position Eliminated, Hot Replacement Incoming

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, your position is being eliminated.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: What? You never told me there was anything wrong with my performance!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not about your performance. Your position is being eliminated.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Well, that seems mighty convenient.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: This way you can replace me without explaining why I never got a bad performance review.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Is this just a trick to make you feel less awkward while firing me?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I thought you said he'd be gone by now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
