situation: The Boss tells Ted that his position is being eliminated and insists it has nothing to do with performance. Ted suspects it is a convenient way to fire him without documenting poor reviews. A woman waiting nearby asks why Ted is still there, and the Boss reveals she is his replacement.
punchline: The 'eliminated position' was a pretext, since Ted is simply being replaced by an attractive new hire, which the Boss offers as a tactless consolation.
summary: A manager claims a job is being cut rather than the person judged poorly, then gives away the ruse by introducing the good-looking successor.

title: Elbonians Haggle Over Company Price

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: A corporate raider has offered to buy our company for nine dollars.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We should ask for more.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: He's a tough negotiator.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Now it's only eight dollars?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I want you to do something in your hat.

situation: A group of Elbonian executives in tall hats discusses a corporate raider's offer of nine dollars for their entire company. They decide to counter by asking for more. The raider turns out to be Dogbert, who responds by lowering his offer to eight dollars and adding a demeaning demand.
punchline: Asking for more only made the offer worse, as Dogbert proves he is a tough negotiator by cutting the price and piling on absurd demands.
summary: Trying to haggle with a ruthless raider backfires on a poor foreign company when its already tiny buyout price shrinks even further.

title: Elbonian Acquisition Brings Head Covering Insult

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: An Elbonian company bought our company yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They promise they won't discriminate against non-Elbonians.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Hey, hatless spawn of Satan's bowels, put a head on this.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that an Elbonian company has bought their company, and reassures everyone that the new owners promise not to discriminate against non-Elbonians. Immediately afterward, a bearded Elbonian in a tall head covering walks in holding a coffee mug and insults the hatless Dilbert while handing him the mug to wear on his head.
punchline: The promise of non-discrimination is broken within seconds, as the Elbonian insults Dilbert for being hatless and treats him with contempt.
summary: Moments after management vows the foreign buyers will treat everyone fairly, one of them barges in and abuses an employee for his bare head.

title: Coffee Supply Effigies of Management

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I realize you don't like the new Information Services approval policy.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: But I would appreciate it if you didn't build effigies of me out of coffee supplies.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Seriously. It's creeping me out.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Heh heh heh!

situation: A manager stands before seated employees and says he understands they dislike the new Information Services approval policy. He asks them to stop building effigies of him from coffee supplies because it unnerves him. In the last panel Alice cackles gleefully while holding up a small figure, apparently a coffee-supply effigy, as little clouds hover around it.
punchline: Employees' resentment of a bureaucratic approval policy has escalated to voodoo-style effigies made of office coffee supplies, and Alice's delighted cackling shows she is not stopping.
summary: Staff channel their anger over a new bureaucratic rule into crafting creepy dolls of their manager out of break-room supplies.

file: 2008/2008-02-10_personality predictor_judge career_dead end job_matches_lack of potential_sample question_angry loner_embezzler_lazy_label yourself.gif
title: Personality Test With Terrible Labels

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll be using the Dogbert Personality Predictor Index to judge your career potential.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we'll leave you in the dead end job that most closely matches your lack of potential.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a sample question. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How would other people describe you? A) Angry loner B) Embezzler C) Lazy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not enough choices!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Says the angry loner.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have thirty minutes to give yourself a label that will haunt you for the rest of your life.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Would you say I'm more of an unidentified hominid or an inappropriate toucher?

situation: The Boss explains that a personality test will be used to assign employees to dead end jobs. His sample question offers only unflattering labels, so Dilbert complains there aren't enough choices and gets branded an angry loner. Wally then dutifully asks which of two terrible labels fits him better.
punchline: The personality test only offers insulting labels, and Wally's cheerful choice between two awful self-descriptions shows how little the exercise helps anyone.
summary: A manager rolls out a career-sorting personality quiz whose answer options are all insults, and employees end up picking among embarrassing labels.

file: 2008/2008-11-15_dinner date_interesting story_self aware_build an army_killer robots.gif
title: Date Hears Alice Punch Robots

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Tell me an interesting story.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our spam filter became self-aware and ordered us to build an army of killer robots. My coworker, Alice, punched them all to death.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not even in that story.

setting: Restaurant table by a window overlooking green hills
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date with a dark-haired woman who asks him for an interesting story. He tells a wild tale about a self-aware spam filter ordering the construction of killer robots, which his coworker Alice punched to death. The woman across the table turns out to be Alice herself, and she objects to being included in the story.
punchline: Dilbert's date is Alice, and she is annoyed that his only interesting story is about her fighting robots rather than about the two of them.
summary: A man on a date spins a far-fetched tale about his coworker, only to find his dining companion is that very coworker and unimpressed.

file: 2008/2008-01-20_human resources_hr person_evil director_bad attitude_project_corpse of misery_donated brain_gum museum_mental imbalance_clarity_irrational_employee moral festival_won meeting_business.gif
title: Bad Attitude Proves Clear Thinking

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your boss says you have a bad attitude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because my project is a flailing corpse of misery, and my boss donated his brain to a gum museum.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I had a good attitude in this situation, it would be a sign of mental imbalance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My bad attitude is proof that I am thinking clearly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you going to compliment me on my clarity or demand I be irrational?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of the employee morale festival.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a sudden urge to grab you by the tail and beat myself to death.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's how I know I won the meeting.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, summons Dilbert to tell him his boss says he has a bad attitude. Dilbert argues that a bad attitude is the logical response to a doomed project and an brainless boss, so it proves he is thinking clearly. Catbert counters by putting him in charge of the employee morale festival.
punchline: Catbert wins the argument by assigning Dilbert the morale festival, which is so miserable that it drives Dilbert to a self-destructive urge, confirming Catbert's victory.
summary: Dilbert's airtight defence of his grumpiness is demolished when the HR director assigns him a punishment disguised as a morale-boosting job.

file: 2008/2008-10-24_quality of work_dark shadow_stimulates brain_revulsion and dread_death relate me.gif
title: Brutal Critique Backfires on Graphic Designer

transcript.speaker: Graphic designer
transcript.text: The quality of your graphics casts a dark shadow across all of your work.

transcript.speaker: Graphic designer
transcript.text: Your logo stimulates the parts of my brain responsible for revulsion and dread.

transcript.speaker: Graphic designer
transcript.text: Only death can release me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... bad graphics... what else?

setting: Office desk, a design review meeting
situation: A graphic designer reads from a sheet of paper and delivers increasingly harsh criticism of Dilbert's graphics and logo. Her review escalates until she exclaims in distress that only death can release her. Dilbert calmly accepts it all and asks what else is wrong.
punchline: After a wildly over-the-top, dramatic condemnation, Dilbert reduces it to a plain 'bad graphics' and asks for the rest of the feedback, treating the melodrama as ordinary criticism.
summary: A designer's flowery, horrified review of Dilbert's artwork gets boiled down by him into a simple request for more notes.

title: Two Other People Are Losers

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Before I get too invested in this conversation, tell me what you do for a living.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm one of three people my boss asked to do the same assignment because he deems all of us unreliable.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: This is why I ask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The other two people are total losers.

setting: A cocktail party or social gathering with a crowd of silhouetted guests in the background
situation: At a party, a woman holding a drink asks Dilbert what he does for a living before committing to a conversation. Dilbert explains that his boss gave the same assignment to three people because he considers all of them unreliable. The woman says this is exactly why she asks, and Dilbert insists the other two people are the real losers.
punchline: Dilbert admits his boss considers him unreliable, then tries to save face by claiming the other two are the losers, which only confirms the woman's suspicion about him.
summary: A party guest screens a stranger's job before chatting, and his awkward answer reveals his boss trusts him so little that he duplicated the work across three people.
keywords: what do you do for a living

title: Anticipating Doom Didn't Help Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's my plan. Now I'd like to open the floor to your soul-crushing negativity.

transcript.speaker: Coworker 1
transcript.text: You have written humanity's final chapter!

transcript.speaker: Coworker 2
transcript.text: Darkness stalks us!

transcript.speaker: Coworker 3
transcript.text: I'll never know love!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Anticipating it didn't help.

setting: Conference room, then Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert presents his plan at a meeting and invites criticism, expecting the usual negativity. His coworkers respond with wildly over-the-top despair about the end of humanity and never finding love. At home afterward, a deflated Dilbert sits slumped with Dogbert on the couch.
punchline: Even though Dilbert braced himself for harsh criticism by asking for it up front, the melodramatic doom-and-gloom reaction still crushed him, so anticipating it offered no protection.
summary: After inviting his colleagues' pessimism on his proposal, an engineer is flattened by their apocalyptic overreactions and admits that bracing for it didn't soften the blow.

title: Bad Reference Instead of Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, there's no budget to give you a raise, but I'll give you something that is just as good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I promise that if you quit on me I will give you a bad job reference and you will never work again.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How is that just as good as a raise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to see it from my point of view.

setting: The Boss's office, with Alice seated across the desk
situation: The Boss tells Alice there is no money for a raise but offers her something supposedly just as good. He then explains the offer is a promise to give her a terrible job reference if she ever quits. Alice is outraged, and he tells her to consider his perspective.
punchline: The Boss's idea of an equivalent reward is a threat to ruin her career if she leaves, which only benefits him, so the 'raise' substitute is really coercion.
summary: Denied a pay increase, an employee is offered a vow of career sabotage as a supposed consolation prize by her self-serving manager.

file: 2008/2008-11-01_change is good_most start ups fail_questions at end.gif
title: Questions Only At The End

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Change is good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why do most startups fail?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I only take questions at the end.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: There's more?

situation: The Boss is giving a presentation, pointing to a screen that reads 'Change' with a smiley face, and declares that change is good. Dilbert challenges him by asking why most startups fail, but the Boss deflects by saying he only takes questions at the end. An audience member groans in dismay that the presentation isn't over yet.
punchline: The Boss dodges a legitimate challenge to his simplistic claim with a procedural excuse, and the audience's horrified 'There's more?' shows how painful the presentation already is.
summary: A manager's cheerful pro-change slide show meets a pointed question he refuses to answer, while the weary audience dreads how much longer it will last.

file: 2008/2008-12-16_office workers_valuable_value_legacy system_less valuable_never appear less valuable_dress code troll.gif
title: Reassurance That Insults Dilbert's Value

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worry that being assigned to work on the legacy systems will make me appear less valuable in the future.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You have my word that you could never appear less valuable than you are now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do your assurances make me feel worse?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your new dress code is "troll."

setting: Catbert's office, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: Dilbert tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that he fears being assigned to the legacy systems will make him look less valuable. Catbert promises that he could never appear less valuable than he already is, which only upsets Dilbert more. Catbert then adds insult to injury by announcing that Dilbert's new dress code is "troll."
punchline: Catbert's "reassurance" is really an insult saying Dilbert is already worthless, and he follows it by assigning Dilbert a troll dress code, tying legacy system work to being a basement-dwelling troll.
summary: A worried engineer seeks comfort from the HR director about maintenance duty and instead gets a backhanded compliment and a humiliating wardrobe mandate.

file: 2008/2008-11-27_boss_budget_clothes_drastic budget cuts_dramatic_how much cut_buzzards seem selective.gif
title: Buzzards Selective After Drastic Budget Cuts

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: We need to make drastic budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's not get all dramatic. Just tell me how much to cut and I'll make it happen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, the buzzards seem selective.

setting: The Boss's office, then a barren wasteland
situation: A green dinosaur tells the Boss that drastic budget cuts are needed. The Boss dismisses the drama and asks only for a dollar figure to cut. In the last panel Dilbert, Wally and another man stand in their underwear in a desolate wasteland with a buzzard perched on one of them, showing the cuts left them destitute.
punchline: The Boss's casual, uninformed approach to deep budget cuts leaves the employees stripped of everything, and Dilbert's bleak optimism is that the buzzards aren't picking at all of them.
summary: A manager waves off warnings about severe spending cuts, and the staff end up penniless and half-naked in a wasteland circled by vultures.

title: Literal Mole Watches Wally's Neck

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Someone said our Pointy-Haired Boss hired a mole. Moles creep me out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Mole" is a figure of speech. It's not literally a mole.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why do I feel tiny eyes on the back of my neck?

setting: Office break area and Wally's cubicle
situation: Wally tells Dilbert he has heard the boss hired a mole and says moles creep him out. Dilbert reassures him that 'mole' is just a figure of speech for a spy. In the last panel Wally sits at his desk feeling watched, while an actual small animal peeks out of a hole in the floor behind him.
punchline: Dilbert insists the mole is only a figure of speech, but a real mole is indeed popping out of the floor to stare at Wally.
summary: A coworker's fear of a rumored spy is waved off as metaphor, yet a real burrowing animal is watching him from the carpet.

title: Downsized Employee Returns as Consultant

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pronounced hay-soos

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Jesus, I thought you got downsized.

transcript.speaker: Jesus
transcript.text: I came back.

transcript.speaker: Jesus
transcript.text: Tell the others I was downsized so I could return as a consultant and save their pensions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should have written that down.

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss meets a coworker named Jesus (pronounced hay-soos) whom he thought had been laid off. Jesus says he came back and asks the Boss to tell everyone that he was downsized only so he could return as a consultant and save their pensions. The Boss then sits at his desk, realizing he'll forget the message.
punchline: The joke plays on the Boss mispronouncing the name Jesus as the religious figure, so the coworker's 'came back' and 'save' lines sound like a resurrection and salvation story, while the Boss's only concern is that he will forget the message.
summary: A manager confuses a laid-off coworker's name with the Messiah, who then claims to have returned as a consultant to save everyone's pensions.

file: 2008/2008-12-18_complain_garbage_job_trash_new assignment_troll in charge_legacy systems_shouldn't complain_economy_free bag of garbage_business.gif
title: Legacy Systems Troll Takes Garbage

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: My new assignment is "Troll in charge of the legacy systems."

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: I guess I shouldn't complain. I'm lucky to have a job in this economy.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Would a free bag of garbage make you feel better?

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: A little.

setting: Sidewalk beside a hedge, next to a trash can
situation: A hairy, nearly naked troll holding a walking stick tells a garbage man about his new job guarding the legacy systems. He says he should be grateful to be employed in a bad economy. The garbage man offers him a free bag of garbage, and the troll admits it helps a little.
punchline: Being handed trash is enough to cheer up someone whose job is already garbage, which underlines how bleak the job and the economy are.
summary: A grumbling troll assigned to look after outdated systems finds a small comfort when a sanitation worker gives him a bag of rubbish.

title: Dogbert's Rumor Control Pricing Trap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to squash a workplace rumor that I'm an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I charge $10 for each false rumor and $1,000 for any rumor I decide is true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds fair.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Really? That just cost you $1,000.

setting: Dogbert's office, at his desk with a 'Dogbert's Rumor Control' sign
situation: Dilbert visits Dogbert's Rumor Control service and asks him to squash a rumor that Dilbert is an idiot. Dogbert explains his pricing: $10 for false rumors but $1,000 for any rumor he decides is true. Dilbert agrees without thinking it through, and Dogbert points out that agreeing to such a deal has just proven the rumor true.
punchline: By casually accepting an obviously rigged fee structure, Dilbert demonstrates that he really is an idiot, so Dogbert declares the rumor true and charges him the $1,000 rate.
summary: A man hires a rumor-control consultant who bills far more for true rumors, then proves the rumor true the instant the man accepts the terms.

file: 2008/2008-11-26_coworkers_beat up_deal with difficult coworkers_evil driector_human resources_business.gif
title: Catbert's Useless Book on Jerks

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice beat me up. You have to do something.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Here's a book on how to deal with difficult coworkers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This isn't quite what...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try holding it in front of your face.

situation: Dilbert, his head bandaged from injuries, complains to Catbert, the Evil Director of Human Resources, that Alice beat him up and demands action. Catbert hands him a book about handling difficult coworkers, and when Dilbert objects that this isn't what he wanted, Catbert suggests he use the book as a shield.
punchline: HR offers a worthless self-help book instead of real intervention, and Catbert's advice to hold it in front of your face as protection against Alice's violence shows his callous indifference to employee welfare.
summary: A battered employee seeks help from the human resources director and is given a book to use as a shield rather than any actual protection.

title: Evil Laugh Meets Literal-Minded Alice

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There is an ugly rumor that I sold your brains to cannibals and your spirits to demons.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Bu-wa-ha-ha-ha-ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You seem a bit unclear on the whole bu-wa-ha-ha concept.

situation: During a meeting, Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells the staff there is an ugly rumor that he sold their brains to cannibals and their spirits to demons. He then breaks into a villainous laugh. Alice asks whether the rumor is true, and Catbert is irritated that she missed the point of his evil laugh.
punchline: Catbert's villainous laugh was supposed to confirm the rumor, so Alice's innocent question shows she doesn't grasp the conventions of evil villainy.
summary: A gleefully wicked HR chief admits to a horrifying rumor with a cackle, only to be frustrated when an employee asks for confirmation.

file: 2008/2008-08-08_cooked books_pension fund_15% per year_crooks_optimists_whistling noise_soul escaping.gif
title: Cooking the Books With Optimistic Pensions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I cooked the books by assuming your pension fund will earn 15% per year.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Technically you aren't crooks, just optimists.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you hear a whistling noise, that would be your soul escaping through your nose.

transcript.speaker: Executive 1
transcript.text: Tweet!

transcript.speaker: Executive 2
transcript.text: Mmph!

transcript.speaker: Executive 3
transcript.text: Tweet!

setting: A conference room where Dogbert presents to a group of executives
situation: Dogbert, dressed as a chef, stands in front of a chart showing a pension fund growing at 15% per year and explains that he 'cooked the books' with that unrealistic assumption. He reassures the executives that this makes them optimists rather than crooks. In the last panel the executives are seen with steam and whistling noises coming from their noses.
punchline: Dogbert's cheerful rationalization of fraudulent accounting as optimism gets a sarcastic coda: the executives' guilty consciences are literally escaping as whistling steam from their noses.
summary: A chef-hatted canine accountant excuses wildly inflated pension projections as mere optimism, then jokes that the guilt-ridden executives' whistling is their souls leaking out.

file: 2008/2008-09-28_answer technical question_bad actor_best person_fake own death_helping customer_insult dead_just a quick question_polite_safest course_work that divison_commercial sales.gif
title: Faking Death to Avoid Customer Question

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hi, I'm a customer of your commercial sales division.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I heard you would be the best person to answer a technical question...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't work in that division.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I know. It's just a quick question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I tell you something different from what the commercial division tells you, I'll get in trouble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'll also get in trouble for not helping a customer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My safest course of action is to fake my own death.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You're a bad actor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't polite to insult the dead.

situation: A customer approaches Dilbert in his cubicle with a technical question about the commercial sales division's product, even though Dilbert works in a different division. Dilbert reasons that he will be punished either for contradicting the commercial division or for refusing to help a customer, so he decides to fake his own death. He collapses with his feet sticking up out of his chair, and the customer calls him a bad actor.
punchline: Dilbert would rather play dead than navigate a no-win corporate situation, and he stays in character even when the customer sees through the act.
summary: Caught between two ways of getting punished, an engineer escapes a customer's question by pretending to be dead.

title: Robot Rampage Goes On Agenda

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our robots have gone on a murderous rampage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll put that issue on the agenda for our next meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! You're an issue!

situation: Dilbert, looking battered, tells the Boss that the company's robots have gone on a murderous rampage. The Boss calmly replies that he will add it to the agenda for the next meeting. In the last panel a robot holds the Boss up with a flaming torch, and Dilbert gleefully calls the Boss an issue.
punchline: The Boss treats a deadly emergency as routine meeting business, so Dilbert enjoys the irony of the robots now treating the Boss himself as the 'issue' to be dealt with.
summary: A manager shrugs off news of killer robots by scheduling it for a future meeting, and then gets seized by one of them.

title: Not Arrogant Enough, Apparently

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My smartest employees keep disagreeing with me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which is weird because great minds usually think alike. They must be slipping.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I think I'm not arrogant enough.

setting: Catbert's office, with a desk and a blue chair
situation: The Boss stands holding a coffee mug in front of Catbert's desk and complains that his smartest employees keep disagreeing with him. He concludes that their minds must be slipping, since great minds supposedly think alike. He ends by wondering whether he is arrogant enough.
punchline: The Boss assumes anyone who disagrees with him must be at fault, and his closing worry that he isn't arrogant enough shows how oblivious he is to his own overconfidence.
summary: A boss blames his brightest staff for failing to agree with him and then frets that he lacks sufficient arrogance.

title: Cha-Ching Over Solar Panel Business

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vijay the venture capitalist

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: We're going into the solar panel business.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Cha-ching! Cha-ching!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pretend you didn't see that when I negotiate my equity.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: Vijay, a venture capitalist, announces that his firm is going into the solar panel business. Dilbert's eyes turn into dollar signs with cha-ching sounds, revealing his excitement about the money to be made. He then asks Vijay to pretend he didn't notice so it won't hurt Dilbert's negotiation of his equity stake.
punchline: Dilbert gives away his greed involuntarily, then asks the investor to ignore the obvious tell so he can still negotiate a better equity deal.
summary: A glimpse of a lucrative new venture makes one man's eyes literally ring up dollar signs, undermining his own bargaining position.

title: Injured Dilbert Offers Elbow Massage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Girlfriend
transcript.text: Maybe later you can give me a back rub with your good hand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have a good hand. But one of my elbows doesn't hurt too much.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Girlfriend
transcript.text: I feel like you're not even trying to make me happy.

setting: Outdoor path beside a grassy hill
situation: Dilbert, who has a bandaged head and his arm in a sling, walks with his girlfriend. She asks him for a back rub later with his good hand, and he explains that he has no good hand, offering one of his less painful elbows instead. She then complains that he isn't trying to make her happy.
punchline: Even though Dilbert is clearly injured all over and offering what he can, his girlfriend is still unreasonably dissatisfied and accuses him of not trying.
summary: A thoroughly bandaged man proposes an elbow massage as the best he can manage, and his partner responds by accusing him of not caring.

title: Did You Make My Changes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you make the changes I asked for?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That depends.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you remember what you asked me to change?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup, I made the changes.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he made the changes he requested. Dilbert answers that it depends, then asks whether the Boss remembers what he asked to have changed. When the Boss admits he doesn't, Dilbert claims he made the changes.
punchline: Since the Boss can't remember what he requested, Dilbert can safely claim to have done it, because nobody can verify the work.
summary: A manager who has forgotten his own instructions can't check up on his employee, so the employee happily claims the job is done.

file: 2008/2008-01-26_job interview_fat and lazy_safe working_thrive on abuse_complain_remove tongue_begging_desparate.gif
title: Immigrant Applicant Promises Endless Abuse

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant

transcript.text: Do you complain much?

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant

situation: A job applicant in a tall hat and long beard pitches himself to The Boss as a cheap, compliant worker who will do the jobs native-born workers refuse. He adds that he needs no safe working conditions and thrives on abuse. When The Boss asks if he complains much, he offers to cut out his own tongue as a gift.
punchline: The applicant is so desperate and so eager to be exploited that he promises to mutilate himself to guarantee he will never complain, which is exactly what the boss wants.
summary: A hopeful newcomer sells himself to an employer as the ideal silent, abuse-tolerant worker, going to grotesque lengths to prove he will never object.

file: 2008/2008-04-15_5 minute huddle_high energy_standup meeting_solved in minute.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want the entire staff to meet at 10 am. Every day for a five-minute huddle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll use this high-energy stand-up meeting to solve problems and share successes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who has a problem that can be solved in a minute?

transcript.text: I'm tired. Can I sit on you?

setting: Office, then a standing huddle of employees
situation: The Boss announces a mandatory daily five-minute stand-up huddle at 10 am to solve problems and share successes. When he asks for any problem that can be solved in a minute, the standing employees gather around him. One of them, tired from standing, asks if he can sit on the boss.
punchline: The only problem a stand-up meeting produces is that people get tired from standing, and the employee's request mocks the boss's forced 'high-energy' format.
summary: A manager imposes a daily standing huddle to fix problems quickly, and the first complaint is that standing is exhausting.

title: Realistic Goals: Having a Pulse

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Some people see me as a loser who achieves nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In reality I am a winner who knows how to set realistic goals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So you're sort of a genius.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And yet my only goal was to have a pulse.

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cups, with an office building shown in the middle panel
situation: Wally sits at a table with Dilbert and Alice and claims that others wrongly view him as a loser, insisting he is really a winner because he sets realistic goals. Dilbert sarcastically suggests this makes him a genius. Wally then admits his only goal was to have a pulse.
punchline: Wally's idea of a realistic goal is merely staying alive, so his claim to being a winner rests on achieving the lowest possible bar, confirming he achieves nothing.
summary: A lazy employee reframes his lack of accomplishment as smart goal-setting, then reveals his sole target was simply being alive.

title: Catbert Mocks Raise-Seeking Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I need a goal. What can I do to get a raise?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try rewriting the law of supply and demand.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Harsh.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I have to toss a purr your way.

situation: An employee asks Catbert, the evil HR director, what goal he should set in order to earn a raise. Catbert sarcastically tells him to rewrite the law of supply and demand, implying the task is impossible. When the employee calls this harsh, Catbert offers a cat-themed pun as a consolation.
punchline: Catbert implies a raise is impossible by assigning an absurd goal, since there is a surplus of workers, then follows with a cat pun ('toss a purr') as a mock consolation.
summary: A hopeful worker seeking pay advice gets an impossible economics assignment from a sardonic feline HR boss, who caps it with a pun.

title: Intern Insults the Board by Presenting

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I finished my project and I'm ready to present it to the board of directors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Interns don't speak to the board of directors, Asok. It would be considered an insult.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How is that an insult?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have the stink of unimportance.

situation: Asok, an intern, tells his boss he has finished his project and wants to present it to the board of directors. The Boss tells him interns are not allowed to address the board because it would be an insult. When Asok asks why, the Boss says he has the stink of unimportance.
punchline: The Boss dismisses the intern's hard work by saying his low status is so obvious that merely appearing before important people would offend them.
summary: A diligent intern hoping to show off his finished work is shut down by a boss who treats his lowly rank as something offensive.

file: 2008/2008-10-17_stepping down_ceo_money stolen_hellhole_huge bag of cash_helicopter_writes book_buy book.gif
title: CEO Escapes With Stolen Cash

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am stepping down as CEO so I can spend more time with the money I stole from this hellhole.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need you and you to carry huge bags of cash to my helicopter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The worst part is that if he ever writes a book, I'll probably buy it.

situation: Dogbert, sitting as CEO at the head of the conference table, announces he is resigning to enjoy the money he stole from the company. He orders two employees, including Dilbert, to haul giant sacks of cash to his helicopter. Dilbert, carrying a sack, grumbles that he would probably still buy the CEO's memoir.
punchline: Even after being robbed by a crooked CEO, Dilbert admits he'd still buy the executive's inevitable self-congratulatory business book, mocking society's fascination with celebrity executives.
summary: A thieving chief executive departs with sacks of loot while a conscripted employee laments that he would still purchase the crook's future autobiography.

title: Due Diligence on Alien Food Company

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to handle the due diligence for our alliance with the Galactic Protein Corporation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Find out if they have any hidden issues we should know about.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this a bad time?

setting: Office, then the Galactic Protein Corporation's facility
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to perform due diligence on a prospective alliance with the Galactic Protein Corporation and look for hidden issues. Dilbert goes to their site and finds alien creatures in the middle of processing a human-sized hot dog bun, next to a box labeled 'Human Buns'.
punchline: The hidden issue is that the alien company's protein source is apparently humans, and Dilbert has walked in on them mid-meal, so he politely asks if it's a bad time.
summary: A routine background check on a new partner company turns up a shockingly literal skeleton in the closet: aliens preparing a person as food.

file: 2008/2008-06-28_entire budget_empire building_work on trendy things_vote to cut budget.gif
title: Dilbert Honestly Admits Wasteful Budget

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Filling in for the Pointy-Haired Boss

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Does your department need its entire budget this year?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, we'll waste most of it on empire building and appearing to work on trendy things.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: All in favor of cutting this guy's budget in half?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call do-over! Do-over!

setting: Conference room during a budget meeting
situation: Dilbert is filling in for the Boss at a budget meeting. When a manager asks whether his department needs its full budget, Dilbert candidly admits most of it would be wasted on empire building and chasing trends. The manager immediately calls a vote to halve his budget, and Dilbert desperately asks for a do-over.
punchline: Dilbert's rare moment of honesty about wasteful budgeting gets his department punished, showing why nobody in a corporation ever admits they don't need their money.
summary: Telling the truth about how his department squanders money backfires on Dilbert the instant he says it out loud.

title: Millennial Robot Threatens Planet, Gets Trashed

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Greeting, troglodytes. I am from the millennium generation.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I was forged in the digital age. I will use my knowledge of MySpace.com and YouTube and e-mail to rule this planet.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Buwha-haha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow, you're right. He doesn't have much upper body strength.

setting: Outdoor grassy field with a trash can
situation: A robot claiming to be from the millennium generation announces to Dilbert and Dogbert that it will conquer the planet using its knowledge of MySpace, YouTube and e-mail. In the last panel the robot has been stuffed upside-down into a trash can, with only its legs sticking out, and Dilbert looks on.
punchline: The tech-savvy conqueror's digital skills are useless against physical force, and Dilbert's remark about his weak upper body strength implies he was easily dumped in the trash.
summary: A boastful young android who plans world domination through social media is promptly tossed into a garbage bin by the people he mocked.

title: Scapegoat Hired to Take Punches

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert the Scapegoat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you for a meeting with my boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: About five minutes into the meeting I'm going to start punching you. With any luck, my boss will join in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe that shouldn't be called luck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay... Skill. What-ever.

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk
situation: Dilbert, dressed in a goat costume as the office scapegoat, is summoned by The Boss for a meeting with the Boss's own boss. The Boss explains he plans to punch Dilbert partway through the meeting and hopes his superior joins in. Dilbert points out that this shouldn't be called luck, and The Boss grudgingly swaps the word for skill.
punchline: The Boss treats deliberately arranging for his scapegoat to be beaten up as a clever management tactic, and the only objection he concedes is to the word 'luck', not the plan itself.
summary: A manager recruits his costumed scapegoat as a punching bag to deflect his own superior's wrath, then reluctantly rebrands his plan as skill rather than luck.

title: Honest Candidate Gets Rejected Instantly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you tell me bad news even if you knew it would upset me?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Yes, I would.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why would I hire someone who hates me?

setting: Job interview across a desk in an office
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and asks whether he would deliver bad news even if it would upset the boss. The candidate honestly answers that he would. The Boss immediately interprets this honesty as hatred and rejects him.
punchline: The Boss equates honesty with hostility, so the candidate's truthful answer proves he is unfit, revealing that the boss only wants yes-men who never deliver bad news.
summary: A hiring manager treats a candidate's willingness to be truthful as proof that the candidate despises him.

title: Catbert Gossipsizes Ted Into Quitting

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ted, I've decided to gossipsize you.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm spreading vicious rumors about you until you feel compelled to quit.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: People are too smart to...

transcript.speaker: Unknown speaker
transcript.text: Pipe down, baby eater!

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, stands in Ted's cubicle and announces he will spread vicious rumors about Ted until Ted feels compelled to quit. Ted starts to protest that people are too smart to believe gossip. A voice from off-panel angrily shouts at him to be quiet and calls him a baby eater, showing the rumors are already taking hold.
punchline: Ted claims people are too smart to fall for gossip, but the instant accusation of being a baby eater proves the rumors work immediately.
summary: An HR cat threatens to ruin an employee's reputation with rumors, and the employee's confident dismissal is interrupted by a coworker already believing the worst.

file: 2008/2008-09-13_purse at home_pay you_curse of competence_fortune teller_curse on first born_crystal ball.gif
title: Curse of Competence on Firstborn

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I seem to have left my purse at home. I won't be able to pay you.

transcript.speaker: Fortune Teller
transcript.text: I put the curse of competence on your firstborn son!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That doesn't sound so bad.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Years later

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need a little help.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa! Why always me?!

setting: A fortune teller's table, then an office years later
situation: A customer admits she can't pay a fortune teller, who retaliates by cursing the customer's firstborn son with competence. The customer shrugs it off as harmless. Years later, her grown son (Dilbert) is in the office, swamped when a coworker asks him for help.
punchline: Being competent is a curse at work, because the one person who can do things gets all the requests for help.
summary: A fortune teller's revenge curse turns out to be a lifetime of being the go-to person for everyone else's problems.

title: Support Group For Defenestrated Employees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to find a support group for people who have my same problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Type "Thrown out of a fifth floor window by a CEO who will escape justice."

transcript.speaker: Support group member
transcript.text: Look who doesn't have a broken leg. Do you think you're better than us?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then a support group meeting
situation: Dilbert, bandaged and injured, sits at his computer and says he needs a support group for people with his problem. Dogbert suggests a search phrase describing being thrown out of a fifth floor window by a CEO who will escape justice. Dilbert then meets a group of similarly bandaged people who resent him for not having a broken leg.
punchline: Even in a support group of people thrown out of windows by executives, Dilbert is picked on for being less injured than the others, showing that workplace pettiness and one-upmanship follow you everywhere.
summary: After being tossed from a high window by an executive, Dilbert finds fellow victims online, only to be snubbed by them for having gotten off lightly.

title: Unwarranted Optimism Fortress of Buzzwords

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you give me some comments on my business plan?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your plan is a hodge-podge of unwarranted optimism encased in an impenetrable fortress of buzz-words.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Would you like to read it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's that unwarranted optimism again.

situation: Dilbert asks a bbalding, bespectacled coworker for feedback on his business plan. The coworker delivers an elaborate, harshly worded critique of it. When the coworker then asks if Dilbert would like to read the critique, Dilbert points out the optimism in that offer.
punchline: Dilbert's coworker has just torn his plan apart for unwarranted optimism, and then optimistically assumes Dilbert will want to read the criticism.
summary: After getting a scathing verdict on his business plan, a hopeful engineer notices the critic is guilty of the very optimism he just condemned.

title: Round Number Meals Raise Suspicion

transcript.speaker: Finance Troll
transcript.text: Your travel expenses are rejected because all of your meal costs are round numbers.

transcript.speaker: Finance Troll
transcript.text: Either you are a liar, or worse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I decide what to order based on what totals to a round number after a 15% tip.

transcript.speaker: Finance Troll
transcript.text: That's worse.

situation: A green troll from the finance department tells Dilbert his travel expense report is rejected because every meal total is a round number, implying fraud. Dilbert explains that he deliberately picks his food so the total with a 15% tip comes out round. The troll finds this explanation even more disturbing.
punchline: Dilbert's honest explanation, that he engineers his meal orders to hit round totals, is considered even worse than lying, mocking his obsessive behavior and the absurdity of expense auditing.
summary: An accountant creature suspects fraud in Dilbert's neat expense figures, but his quirky truth about how he orders dinner only deepens the suspicion.

title: Code Monkey Wants Architect Title

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I'd like to change my job title to something with "architect" in it.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: My dream is to do less work while allegedly being more valuable.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The best I can do is "code monkey."

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: How about "software simian"?

situation: An engineer visits Catbert, the Evil Director of Human Resources, and asks for a new job title containing the word "architect." He admits he wants to do less work while seeming more valuable. Catbert offers only "code monkey," and the engineer cheerfully counters with "software simian."
punchline: The engineer is so desperate for a fancier-sounding title that he haggles over a synonym for an insulting label, showing that job titles are about vanity rather than actual value or work.
summary: A worker angling for a prestigious job title ends up negotiating a fancier way to be called a monkey.

file: 2008/2008-06-29_eliminate bonuses_savings used_fun loving executives_wear festive costumes_sound of no money_ceo's yacht_whale oil_bring harpoon_happy about underpay.gif
title: Bonus Cuts Fund Inspirational Executive Movie

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Our CEO decided to eliminate employee bonuses.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: The savings will be used to produce an in-house movie to inspire you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Inspire us to do what?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: For starters, we'd like you to be happy about being underpaid.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Our fun-loving executives will wear festive costumes and sing about the virtues of poverty.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: The movie is called "The Sound of No Money."

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: The premiere is on our CEO's yacht. He wants all of you to be there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're invited to his yacht?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: The yacht runs on whale oil, so bring a harpoon.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: A manager announces to staff that the CEO is eliminating employee bonuses and spending the savings on an in-house movie meant to inspire them. The film turns out to be a musical in which executives sing about the virtues of poverty. The staff are then invited to the premiere on the CEO's luxury yacht.
punchline: Management cuts employee pay to fund a tone-deaf vanity film, then rubs it in by inviting the underpaid workers to the CEO's lavish whale-oil-powered yacht.
summary: Staff lose their bonuses so executives can make a musical about poverty and show it aboard the boss's extravagant yacht.

title: Don't Look Directly At Boss

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That thing is called a "boss."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: His job is to identify systems that are inefficient and make them our new standards.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I do way more than that.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Don't look directly at it.

situation: Tina points out the Pointy-Haired Boss to a young girl, as if he were a strange creature, and explains that his job is to find inefficient systems and make them the company's new standards. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, protests that he does far more than that. Tina then warns the girl not to look directly at him.
punchline: Tina describes the boss like a dangerous animal or solar eclipse, implying that his only real contribution is institutionalizing inefficiency and that he is best avoided.
summary: An employee introduces a child to a manager as though he were a hazardous curiosity, mocking his habit of turning bad processes into official policy.

title: Turtle Role Play Management Test

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I will use role play to evaluate your management potential.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Imagine you are a turtle and you are being attacked by a hawk.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's better than I expected.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Thanks.

setting: Catbert's office, with an employee seated across the desk
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells an employee he will use role play to judge the employee's management potential. He asks the employee to imagine being a turtle attacked by a hawk. The employee responds by pulling his head and limbs inside his clothes like a turtle, leaving an empty-looking suit slumped in the chair.
punchline: The employee's instinct to hide and withdraw like a turtle is judged as a good sign of management potential, implying that managers succeed by retreating and avoiding confrontation.
summary: A cat from HR tests a worker's leadership skills with a pretend predator scenario, and the worker's cowering is oddly praised.

title: Waiting for Data from Deceased Larry

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, are you busy?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, I'm reading the "In Memoriam" section of our company newsletter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you're done, can you compile the beta test results?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure. Just as soon as I get the data from . . . Larry.

situation: The Boss asks Wally if he is busy, and Wally says he is reading the In Memoriam section of the company newsletter. The Boss then asks him to compile the beta test results afterward. Wally agrees, but says he must first wait for data from Larry, who has apparently died.
punchline: Wally slyly turns a dead coworker into the perfect excuse for never finishing the task, since the data he needs can't ever arrive.
summary: A lazy employee reading obituaries in the company newsletter dodges a work request by blaming a colleague who is no longer alive.

title: Interviewers Mock Candidate Working for Boss

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Please introduce yourself by saying your name and who you work for.

transcript.speaker: Erin
transcript.text: My name is Erin and I work for Sue Boysenberry.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer 1
transcript.text: Wow, lucky. I hear she's great.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer 2
transcript.text: Can you give her my résumé?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One minute later

transcript.speaker: Interviewer 1
transcript.text: I'm so sorry for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You must cry a lot.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer 1
transcript.text: If you ever need to talk to someone, I know a good shrink.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He can prescribe pills that will make you feel self-employed.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer 1
transcript.text: Be strong. We'll all pray for you.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Next.

situation: A panel of interviewers, including Dilbert, asks a candidate named Erin to introduce herself. When she says she works for Sue Boysenberry, they first praise the boss and ask Erin to pass along a résumé, but a minute later they turn sympathetic and offer pity, a shrink referral and prayers. The panel then calls for the next candidate.
punchline: Sue Boysenberry is such a terrible boss that interviewers treat working for her as a tragedy requiring sympathy and psychiatric pills, rather than as a credential.
summary: A job candidate's mention of her employer prompts the interview panel to pity her as though she were the victim of a terrible misfortune.

file: 2008/2008-11-05_conference room_where hope goes to die_the rectangle of futility.gif
title: Interview in the Rectangle of Futility

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'm here for an interview in a conference room named...

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: "Where hope goes to die"

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: It's the first one past "The Rectangle of Futility."

setting: Office reception area / cubicle at a company
situation: A job candidate in a suit arrives for an interview and reads the name of the conference room off a piece of paper. The room is named "Where Hope Goes to Die." The unfazed receptionist casually gives directions by referencing another equally grim-named conference room.
punchline: The company's conference rooms have bleakly depressing names that the staff treat as completely normal, hinting at how miserable the workplace is.
summary: A nervous interviewee asks for a gloomily named meeting room, and the receptionist cheerfully points him past an even gloomier one.

title: Consultant Takes Over Dilbert's Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a consultant to help with our virtualization project because I don't trust employees with anything important.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will do the heavy thinking while each of you performs your usual duties as obstacles to progress.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said this is my project!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll let him unplug something.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he has hired a consultant for the virtualization project because he doesn't trust employees with important work. Dogbert, the consultant, declares he will do the thinking while the employees act as obstacles. When Dilbert protests that it was supposed to be his project, Dogbert says he will let Dilbert unplug something.
punchline: The consultant takes all the meaningful work and credit for himself, leaving the real project owner only a trivial, menial task.
summary: A boss brings in a consultant who sidelines the engineer who owns the project and hands him a token chore.

title: Alice Fights Murderous Robot Rampage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our robots went bad. They're on a murderous rampage.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll take care of it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, Alice. Guess who says your hair is unfashionable and you're overpaid?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Robots.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Little help, please. My fist of death is stuck.

setting: Office meeting room and Alice's cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Dogbert that the company's robots have gone bad and are on a murderous rampage, and Dogbert says he will handle it. Dogbert goes to Alice and tells her the robots insult her hair and her pay. An enraged Alice attacks the robot so fiercely that her arm is stuck through its chest, and the robot has to ask Dilbert for help.
punchline: Dogbert defeats the killer robots by provoking Alice's rage, and she is so violent that the robot ends up the victim, begging for help to free its fist of death from her.
summary: Dogbert neutralizes a deadly robot uprising by telling the famously short-tempered Alice that the machines have been insulting her.

file: 2008/2008-03-18_pessimistic co workers_crushed soul_meat clothes_rain soul_less fortunate_volunteering.gif
title: Volunteering to Help Anyone You Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My pessimistic coworkers have crushed my soul. Now I am nothing but meat with clothes.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You can regain your soul by volunteering to help the less fortunate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who is less fortunate than me?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Anyone you date.

situation: Dilbert complains to a garbage man that his pessimistic coworkers have crushed his soul and left him feeling like meat with clothes. The garbage man suggests volunteering to help the less fortunate to regain his soul. When Dilbert asks who could possibly be less fortunate than him, the garbage man says anyone he dates.
punchline: The garbage man delivers a deadpan insult, implying that Dilbert's dates are the only people worse off than he is because they have to date him.
summary: A downtrodden engineer seeks a way to restore his spirit and is told the neediest people around are his romantic partners.

file: 2008/2008-04-23_asok_intern_indian institute of technology_30 years in box_punished to box.gif
title: Asok's Telekinesis Ban Punishment

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Asok, you have violated the Indian Institute of Technology's ban on the use of telekinesis in the ungifted world.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Your punishment is 30 years in the box.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where were you this morning?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Grrrr

setting: A tribunal-like room with high-backed chairs, then the office cubicles
situation: Asok sits among tall chairs in his underwear while an unseen authority from the Indian Institute of Technology accuses him of using forbidden telekinesis and sentences him to 30 years in the box. In the last panel, Dilbert asks the Boss where he was this morning while the Boss sits at his desk growling.
punchline: The Boss's snarling at his desk suggests he was the one sentenced, or is otherwise behind Asok's mysterious absence, so Asok's elaborate telekinetic punishment plays out as an absurd excuse for his missing morning at work.
summary: A stern, hidden panel punishes the intern for secretly using mind powers, and the office carries on with a puzzled question about who was missing.

file: 2008/2008-06-01_behind schedule_defective equipment_improbable event_reliable vendor_sales guy_golfing_bought hat_impossible boss_on the hook.gif
title: Boss Blames Dilbert for Vendor's Hat Bribe

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because your project is behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because the vendor delivered defective equipment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It is your job to anticipate that sort of problem and head it off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't possible to anticipate and head off every improbable event.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, you could have picked a more reliable vendor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told me to use this vendor because the sales guy took you golfing and bought you a hat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, you should have seen that coming and burned down all hat factories a year ago.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He would have bribed you another way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what lazy people say.

situation: The Boss refuses Dilbert a raise because his project is late. Dilbert blames the vendor's defective equipment, and the Boss insists he should have anticipated it and picked a better vendor. Dilbert points out the Boss chose that vendor because a salesman gave him golf and a hat, so the Boss demands absurdly that Dilbert should have burned down all hat factories.
punchline: The Boss, whose own bribe-driven vendor choice caused the problem, dodges responsibility by demanding Dilbert foresee the future and commit arson, then dismisses Dilbert's valid objection as laziness.
summary: A manager denies a raise over a delay he caused himself by picking a supplier in exchange for a free golf outing and a hat.

title: Shorts Allowed, Wardrobe Not Updated

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company will be using less air conditioning to reduce expenses.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: To compensate, we're loosening up on the dress code. Shorts will now be allowed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not going to update my shorts wardrobe until I know this will last.

situation: The Boss announces in a meeting that the company will cut back on air conditioning to save money. As a 'compensation,' shorts will be allowed under a relaxed dress code. Later, Wally, holding a coffee mug and wearing lederhosen-style shorts, says he won't buy new shorts until he knows the policy will last, while Dilbert stands by in shorts too.
punchline: Management offers a laughably cheap substitute for real comfort, and Wally cynically assumes the perk will be revoked, so he's wearing his old lederhosen rather than investing in proper shorts.
summary: To offset a hotter office from budget cuts, management lets staff wear shorts, but one skeptical employee shows up in lederhosen, expecting the perk to vanish.

title: Raise Budget Spent on Coffee Maker

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to give you a raise but I used the entire budget on a new coffee maker.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a nice one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's talk that I paid too much for you.

situation: The Boss tells Alice across a desk that he can't give her a raise because he spent the whole budget on a new coffee maker. He brags that it's a nice machine, while Alice grows visibly angrier. In the last panel he holds a coffee next to the elaborate machine and says there's talk he overpaid for her.
punchline: The Boss not only denies Alice a raise in favor of an appliance but insults her by implying she is overpaid, showing he values the coffee maker more than her.
summary: A manager rejects his employee's pay request because an expensive espresso machine ate the money, then adds an insult about her cost.

file: 2008/2008-10-15_dogcart the ceo_investors_bought helicopter_birds off building_parking lot_beaks and feathers.gif
title: CEO Dogbert's Bird-Killing Helicopter

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our investors are not happy that you bought a helicopter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or that you only use it to keep birds off the building.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or that the parking lot is filling up with beaks and feathers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't please everyone.

situation: Dogbert is now CEO, and the Pointy-Haired Boss reports that investors are unhappy about his purchase of a company helicopter. The complaints escalate: he uses it only to chase birds away from the building, and the result is a parking lot littered with beaks and feathers. Dogbert, seated behind his desk, shrugs it off.
punchline: Dogbert responds to serious investor complaints about wasteful, grisly spending with a breezy 'I can't please everyone,' showing a CEO who doesn't care about shareholders.
summary: A boss lists the escalating reasons investors dislike the CEO's extravagant helicopter, and the dog in charge brushes off every objection.

title: Three People, Same Unreliable Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have the approved vendor list?

transcript.speaker: Procurement Clerk
transcript.text: Hmmm, Alice and Asok asked for that list too.

transcript.speaker: Procurement Clerk
transcript.text: Are you one of three people assigned to the same project because your boss believes none of you are reliable?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Procurement Clerk
transcript.text: Hmmm, and you're the last one to ask for the list.

situation: Dilbert asks a clerk at a computer for the approved vendor list. She notes that Alice and Asok already asked for it, then deduces that the three of them were assigned to the same project because their boss thinks none of them is reliable. Dilbert concedes 'Maybe,' and she points out he was the last to ask.
punchline: Dilbert's slowness to request the list shows he really is the least reliable of the three, confirming the boss's lack of faith.
summary: A clerk figures out that three employees were given the same task as a safeguard against unreliability, then notes the one standing before her was the slowest of the trio.

file: 2008/2008-03-02_dismissive and insulting_eduction_experience needed_insulting answer_snake mittens_rejected idea.gif
title: Insulting Answer Beats Long Explanation

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do you think of my idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It won't work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why not?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want the long answer that you won't understand because you possess neither the experience nor the education needed?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or the dismissive and insulting answer that has the advantage of being quick?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Another advantage of the insulting answer is that you can tell people I rejected your idea because I didn't think of it myself.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I guess I'll take the insulting answer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. Your idea is dumber than snake mittens.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do you have against snake mittens?

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for his opinion on an idea, and Dilbert says it won't work. He offers a choice between a long explanation the coworker is too inexperienced to understand or a quick, insulting answer, and points out the insult at least lets the coworker save face by blaming Dilbert's pride. The coworker chooses the insult and gets compared unfavorably to snake mittens.
punchline: Having been insulted as requested, the coworker ignores the put-down of his own idea and takes offense on behalf of the absurd snake mittens.
summary: Offered a choice between a thorough rebuttal and a quick put-down, a coworker picks the put-down, then defends the ridiculous thing his idea was compared to.

title: Catbert Denies Ergonomic Chair Request

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our concern for your wellness is related to your job performance.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Obviously you won't be getting an ergonomically correct chair any time soon.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And feel free to type as hard as you want.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, sits behind his desk talking to an employee. He explains that the company cares about employee wellness only as far as it affects productivity. He then refuses the employee an ergonomic chair and invites him to type as hard as he likes.
punchline: HR's supposed concern for wellness is purely about productivity, so the employee gets no ergonomic chair and is sarcastically encouraged to hammer the keyboard, implying he will suffer repetitive strain injuries.
summary: A malicious HR boss makes clear that worker health matters only when it affects output, then denies a comfortable chair with a cruel parting remark.

title: Boss's Proxy Imitates Boss Badly

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My boss sent me to represent him at this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Fuh-fuh-fuh everything costs too much. Fuh-fuh-fuh we don't have enough resources!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't help us.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hey, I'm not the one who invited him.

situation: Carol arrives at a meeting as a stand-in for her boss and then mimics him, pulling her hair into pointy shapes and spouting stock complaints about costs and resources. Dilbert points out that this is unhelpful, and she shrugs off responsibility since she didn't invite him.
punchline: Carol's literal impersonation of her boss shows his only contribution is complaining about budgets, and she deflects blame for the useless result by pointing out that the attendees chose to invite him.
summary: A manager's stand-in mocks her absent boss by acting out his habitual griping, then blames the organisers for having asked him.

file: 2008/2008-06-03_cure uselessness_glass hammer_bag of nothing_borrow a pen.gif
title: Useless Wally's Classmates: Hammer and Nothing

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, I enrolled you in a program to cure uselessness.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your classmates will be a glass hammer and a bag of nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I borrow a pen?

transcript.speaker: Bag of Nothing
transcript.text: Dude, no arms.

setting: Office, then a classroom or training room
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Wally he has signed him up for a program meant to cure uselessness. Wally's classmates turn out to be a glass hammer and a bag of nothing, seated at a table with him. When Wally asks to borrow a pen, the bag of nothing points out that it has no arms.
punchline: Wally is so useless that his only classmates are inanimate objects, and even a bag of nothing is too helpless to lend him a pen.
summary: A remedial class for the hopelessly useless turns out to be populated by a fragile tool and an empty sack.

file: 2008/2008-11-28_boss_budget cut_joke_bleak_budget cuts_undead_feast on flesh_don't like light.gif
title: Darkest Before the Undead Feast

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I realize things look bleak after the budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But remember, it's always the darkest before the undead feast on your flesh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because they don't like light.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We get it!!!

setting: Post-apocalyptic wasteland where employees huddle around a burning barrel for warmth
situation: After budget cuts have left the office in ruins, the Boss and his employees stand around a fire barrel in a desolate landscape. The Boss tries to give an uplifting pep talk, but twists the 'darkest before the dawn' cliche into a grim zombie warning. Dilbert snaps in frustration at the Boss's labored metaphor.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at a motivational cliche turns into a gruesome explanation about zombies avoiding light, and the exasperated staff point out they already understood the 'darkest before dawn' reference.
summary: Standing around a trash-can fire in a ruined wasteland, a manager mangles an optimistic proverb into a zombie warning until his weary staff begs him to stop.

title: Helping Ted Means Dilbert Is Unimportant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to help Ted on his project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If Ted's project succeeds, who will get the credit?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted will. It's his project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if it fails?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That would be your fault for not helping him enough.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I spend my time helping Ted, my own projects will suffer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only way this makes sense is if my projects are unimportant and so am I.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it makes you feel any better, Ted and his project are unimportant too.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to assist Ted with his project. Dilbert points out that Ted gets the credit for any success while Dilbert gets the blame for any failure, and that his own work will suffer. He concludes that he must be unimportant, and the Boss responds with a backhanded reassurance.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at comforting Dilbert confirms that Dilbert is unimportant, merely adding that Ted and his project are unimportant too.
summary: A manager assigns an employee to prop up a colleague's project, where all the upside goes to someone else and all the blame lands on the helper.

title: Antimatter Dilbert Opposes Everything

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My particle accelerator brought an antimatter Dilbert into this world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything he thinks is opposite of what I think.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why did you bring him here?

transcript.speaker: Antimatter Dilbert
transcript.text: You're like his Oprah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold me.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss in a meeting that his particle accelerator created an antimatter version of himself who thinks the opposite of everything he does. The Boss asks why Dilbert brought him there. The antimatter Dilbert answers that the Boss is like his Oprah, which Dilbert has to hear.
punchline: Because the antimatter twin believes the opposite of Dilbert, he would admire the Boss and treat him like an inspiring celebrity guru, which horrifies Dilbert enough to ask for comfort.
summary: A scientist's experiment produces an opposite-minded double, and the double turns out to idolize the one person Dilbert can't stand.

file: 2008/2008-06-21_monitor actions_cameras_strapped to head_non work related_attach sensors_track thoughts_engineers_lab assistant.gif
title: Monitoring Employee Thoughts, Then Insulting Engineers

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We monitor all of your actions, but we suspect you are still doing non-work-related thinking.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My lab assistant Trixie will attach sensors to your head and track all of your thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
