transcript.text: Mmm... Trixie, wear this while you wash my electric car.

transcript.speaker: Trixie
transcript.text: Engineers.

setting: Catbert's office, then a lab area
situation: Catbert, acting as the evil HR director, tells Dilbert that the company already monitors all his actions but suspects he is still thinking about non-work things. Trixie, his lab assistant, attaches sensors and a camera to Dilbert's head to track his thoughts. Catbert then has Trixie wear the thought-tracking device while she washes his electric car, and her thought bubble reveals she is silently cursing engineers.
punchline: The thought-monitoring device ends up on Catbert's assistant, whose private resentment of engineers shows that employees will always have unauthorized thoughts about their bosses.
summary: A scheming HR cat wires up an employee's brain to police his daydreaming, then misuses the gadget on his own assistant, whose grumbling mind proves the futility of the surveillance.

file: 2008/2008-07-21_moral compass_healed_position of power_narrow gap_executive pay_worker pay.gif
title: Dilbert's Moral Compass Gets Him Defenestrated

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My moral compass has healed. Can I keep my new job in management?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to use my position of power to narrow the gap between executive and worker pay.

setting: The Boss's office, then the exterior of the office building
situation: Dilbert, holding his broken moral compass, asks the seated boss if he can keep his new management job now that his conscience has recovered. He then announces he wants to use his power to narrow the gap between executive and worker pay. The final panel shows the office building from outside, with a figure being thrown through a window.
punchline: Proposing to cut executive pay in favor of workers is so unwelcome to management that Dilbert is immediately thrown out of the window, implied by the wordless final panel.
summary: A newly principled manager's plan to even out pay between bosses and workers gets him violently ejected from the building.

title: Resolved Means Anything, Even Hanging Up

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: How can you say my trouble ticket is resolved when I still have the problem??!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Resolved is a catch-all term that can mean a shift change, escalation, or even an accidental disconnect.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: So... you escalated it?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

setting: Help desk call, with the customer at his desk and Dogbert at a support desk
situation: A frustrated customer phones tech support to complain that his trouble ticket was marked resolved while his problem persists. Dogbert, working as the support agent, explains that resolved can mean a shift change, an escalation, or an accidental disconnect. When the customer asks if the ticket was escalated, Dogbert hangs up on him.
punchline: Dogbert's explanation of what resolved means is demonstrated to be the accidental disconnect option, as he deliberately hangs up on the customer, showing how help desks close tickets without fixing anything.
summary: A help desk agent defends a bogus ticket closure with a vague definition and then cuts the caller off to prove the point.

title: Secret Third Arm Gets Ignored

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My task is impossible unless I use my forbidden powers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would anyone notice if I had a third arm for a few hours?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I lost my intellectual curiosity just in time.

situation: Dilbert sits alone in his cubicle and thinks that his impossible task can only be done with his forbidden powers. He wonders whether anyone would notice if he grew a third arm for a few hours. In the last panel he types with an extra arm sprouting from his head while a coworker holding a coffee mug stands right beside him and says he has lost his intellectual curiosity just in time.
punchline: A coworker is standing next to Dilbert's obviously bizarre third arm, but he deliberately avoids wondering about it, so workplace incuriosity lets Dilbert get away with using his freakish power.
summary: A cubicle worker secretly sprouts an extra limb to finish an impossible job, and a nearby colleague conveniently chooses not to wonder about it.

file: 2008/2008-11-09_follow arc_unwarranted optimism_delusions competence_obstructionists slither_smother dreams_ignorance & envy_fuel rumors_morph common knowledge_resources allocated_misinformation & favoritism_requirements drift_undesirable & impossible.gif
title: Project Plan Follows Usual Doom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our project plan will follow the usual arc.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Phase one will be unwarranted optimism supported by delusions of competence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In phase two, the obstructionists will slither out of their lairs and try to smother our dreams.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ignorance and envy will fuel rumors that get repeated until they morph into common knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Resources will be allocated based on misinformation and favoritism.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And requirements will drift until the project is both undesirable and impossible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That brings us to the second week.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I want my unwarranted optimism back.

setting: Conference room during a project kickoff meeting
situation: Dilbert presents a project plan to his team, cynically predicting each stage of how the project will go wrong, from false optimism to rumors, favoritism and drifting requirements. He finishes by noting that all of this happens within the first two weeks, and a team member says she wants her optimism back.
punchline: The doomed project lifecycle plays out so fast and so predictably that the team is thoroughly demoralized before it has barely started, and they long for the naive optimism of phase one.
summary: A cynical engineer walks colleagues through the predictable stages of a failing project, leaving them wishing they could return to blissful ignorance.

file: 2008/2008-09-14_cell phone product_form of radiation_negative effect_head turn red_weight loss_new cell phone_positive spin.gif
title: Radiation Cell Phone Needs Positive Spin

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a little problem with our new cell phone product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It gives off a form of radiation that has a negative effect on the user.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How bad is it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, it makes your head turn red, and you lose weight.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Hey, what is up with our new cell phone? I feel different.

transcript.speaker: Plumber
transcript.text: Can I borrow your friend?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see why not.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Aaaiii!!! Glub glub glub

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyway, see if you can put a positive spin on it.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company's new cell phone gives off harmful radiation that turns users' heads red and makes them lose weight. Dilbert asks how bad it is, and as the effects appear a plunger-like figure becomes a victim. The plumber casually borrows the transformed victim as a plunger and uses it on a clogged drain, and the Boss shrugs it off.
punchline: Instead of fixing a dangerous product, the Boss simply asks Dilbert to spin the harmful defect, even as it is turning people into plungers.
summary: A manager shrugs off a phone that mutates its users into household tools and just wants the damage reframed as a selling point.

file: 2008/2008-12-21_agreement_areas of expertise_business units_confusion_consolidate shared services_diagnostic review_evil director_from centers_invoice_meeting_presentation_business.gif
title: Consultant Buzzwords Meet Simple Question

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: My consultants can transform human resources.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: We'll start with a diagnostic review.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Then you'll form centers of excellence around areas of expertise.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Next, you'll consolidate shared services and drive continuous improvement.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Business units will translate operational imperatives into HR actions.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Does any of that mean the same as firing idiots and cutting the budget?

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Which answer gets us hired?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try yes.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Great. Put a bow on it and send me the invoice.

setting: Catbert's office, across a desk from a consultant
situation: A consultant pitches Catbert, the evil HR director, with a stream of management jargon about transforming human resources. Catbert asks whether it all just means firing idiots and cutting the budget. The consultant, realizing that agreeing is the way to win the contract, says yes, and Catbert tells him to send the invoice.
punchline: All the consulting jargon is just a fancy disguise for layoffs and cost cutting, and the consultant will say whatever wins the contract.
summary: A jargon-spouting consultant happily admits his grand plan is just layoffs and budget cuts once he learns that answer will land him the job.

file: 2008/2008-10-16_dogcart the ceo_start rumors_spread lies_stock pop up_stock options_steal_before computers.gif
title: Dogbert's Stock Option Pump Scheme

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Start some rumors, spread some lies...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wait for the stock to pop up... exercise my stock options... Bang!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How did people steal before computers?

setting: Dogbert's CEO office, seated at a desk with a computer
situation: Dogbert, acting as a CEO, sits at his computer and thinks through a plan: spread rumors and lies to inflate the company's stock price, then cash in his stock options when it jumps. In the final panel he wonders how anyone managed to steal before computers existed.
punchline: Dogbert treats market manipulation and stock option fraud as a trivially easy computer-enabled crime, implying that executives' schemes to enrich themselves are a modern, tech-powered form of theft.
summary: A scheming canine executive plots to pump up his company's share price with falsehoods and profit from his options, marveling at how easy computers make stealing.

title: CEO Rewards Himself For Confusion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO didn't understand the PowerPoint slides you made for him, so he asked the board of directors for a bonus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With any luck, the bonus will incent him to try harder to understand your slides.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting better at finding tenuous connections to hope.

setting: The Boss's office, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss tells a young employee (apparently Asok, the intern) that the CEO couldn't follow his PowerPoint slides and responded by asking the board for a bonus. The Boss then hopes the bonus will motivate the CEO to try harder to understand the slides. Alone with Catbert, he admits he is getting better at finding flimsy reasons for optimism.
punchline: The CEO is being rewarded for failing to understand, and the Boss's strained optimism that the bonus will fix the problem is acknowledged to be a very thin thread of hope.
summary: A boss tries to put a hopeful spin on an executive being paid extra for not grasping a presentation.

title: The Musky Scent of Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I count on your cooperation for the next phase of the project?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You emit the musky scent of failure. Women can detect that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would a bath fix it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How long are you willing to stay submerged?

situation: Dilbert asks a female coworker for her cooperation on the next phase of a project, and she flatly refuses. She explains that he gives off the scent of failure, and when he hopefully asks if a bath would help, she replies with a pointed question about how long he would stay underwater. The final panel shows only an office building exterior while the two voices continue off-screen.
punchline: Alice implies that nothing short of drowning could cure Dilbert's reputation for failure, politely suggesting he stay submerged permanently.
summary: A coworker turns down a request for help by claiming the requester reeks of failure, then hints that only a very long dunking could fix it.

file: 2008/2008-11-30_boss_lazy_specific_understand_quibbled about methodology_bought crickets_wait for answer_borrow crisckets.gif
title: Crickets While Boss Bluffs Understanding

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I don't understand a word of this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did other people say about it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A few people quibbled about the methodology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right, well, yes, the methodology does have a few issues.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you be more specific?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I brought some crickets to keep me company while I wait for your answer.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Chirp chirp chirp chirp chirp chirp chirp chirp

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm up next. Can I borrow the crickets?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're a little tired.

situation: The Boss admits privately that he can't understand a document, then fishes for what others thought of it. After agreeing that the methodology has issues, he is asked to be more specific. Dilbert waits with a cage of crickets for the Boss's answer, which never comes, and a colleague eventually asks to borrow the crickets.
punchline: The Boss is bluffing about a document he doesn't understand and can't give specifics, so Dilbert waits so long that the crickets he brought for company wear themselves out.
summary: A clueless manager pretends to grasp a report, and an employee sits through an endless silence while his noisy insects tire out waiting for a real answer.

title: Dogbert Hires a Replacement CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I thwarted the hostile takeover bid, but your CEO died in the process.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll find you someone else to blather about quality while being grossly overpaid.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I like your look, but can you blather?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: Quality is my global added value!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells a company executive he stopped a hostile takeover but the CEO died in the process. He offers to find a replacement whose job is to talk about quality while being grossly overpaid. A candidate then pitches himself to the executive with buzzword-laden nonsense.
punchline: The CEO role is reduced to someone who can spout empty buzzwords about quality, and the candidate proves his worth by doing exactly that.
summary: After a consultant's takeover defense costs the company its chief, a replacement is hired purely for his talent at spouting impressive-sounding jargon.

title: Top Secret Envelope Security Fail

transcript.speaker: Man in suit
transcript.text: Your most sensitive materials should always be sent in an interoffice envelope marked "Top Secret."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you a moron who works in our security department, or an industrial spy who is too lazy to look through lots of envelopes?

transcript.speaker: Man in suit
transcript.text: Our security guys don't slap that hard or run that fast.

situation: A man in a suit advises Dilbert and others to send their most sensitive materials in an interoffice envelope stamped "Top Secret." Dilbert asks whether the advice comes from a moron in security or a lazy industrial spy. The man replies that the company's security guards aren't strong or fast enough to hurt him.
punchline: Labeling an envelope "Top Secret" makes it the obvious thing to steal, and the advisor's only defense is that the company's security guards are too weak and slow to catch him.
summary: A smug advisor recommends flagging secret documents with a giant label, then brushes off the criticism by mocking the physical prowess of the security staff.

title: Boss Delegates Virtualization After Reading Journal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our servers are using too much electricity. We need to virtualize.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I did my part by reading about virtualization in a trade journal. Now you do the software part.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is your part taking so long?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company's servers use too much electricity and must be virtualized. He claims he has already done his share by reading a trade journal article, and hands the entire software implementation to Dilbert. He then returns and impatiently asks why Dilbert's part is taking so long.
punchline: The Boss treats skimming a magazine article as equal to the real engineering work, then blames Dilbert for the delay in the much bigger task he was handed.
summary: After skimming a magazine piece on server consolidation, a manager dumps the whole technical project on his engineer and then demands to know why it isn't finished.

title: Wally Incubates Brains, Does Nothing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I functioned as an incubator of innovations for contributions to the value chain.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: To the observer, it looks as if I am doing nothing, but on the inside, I am incubating my brains out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It doesn't count unless it hurts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It hurts plenty.

situation: Wally stands before the Boss holding his coffee mug and gives a weekly report full of buzzwords, claiming he was incubating innovations for the value chain. He admits it looks like he did nothing, but says he was mentally incubating. The Boss replies that work only counts if it hurts, and Wally insists it hurts plenty.
punchline: Wally dresses up doing nothing in jargon, and the Boss's only criterion for valuing work is suffering, so Wally simply claims he suffered to get credit.
summary: Wally justifies a week of idleness with grand management jargon and then satisfies his boss's pain-based standard for real work by simply claiming it was painful.

file: 2008/2008-11-03_competent_good judge of people_hired_lame resume_not tall_job interview_hired on spot.gif
title: Hired Because He's Tall

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your résumé is lame, but you're tall, so you must be competent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired. Let me show you around.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm what you call a good judge of people.

setting: Interview room in the office, then walking through the office
situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss interviews a candidate, dismisses his résumé as lame, and decides he must be competent simply because he is tall. He hires him on the spot and starts a tour. In the last panel the boss walks upright while the supposedly tall candidate shuffles along crouched beside him.
punchline: The boss brags about being a good judge of people right after hiring someone on a absurd criterion, and the candidate is shown not to be tall at all, so even the flimsy reasoning is wrong.
summary: A boss hires an applicant on the strength of his supposed height rather than his weak résumé, then congratulates himself on his judgment.

title: Excess IT Support Means Farm Exile

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: You have exceeded your allocation for I.T. support.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: The penalty is forcible relocation to an agrarian society.

transcript.speaker: Cow
transcript.text: Seriously, even a cow knows you should try rebooting before calling tech support.

situation: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services, tells an employee at her computer that she has used up her allowance of IT support calls. As punishment she is forcibly relocated to a farm, where she stands by a tree stump with an axe. A cow there lectures her that even a cow knows to try rebooting before calling tech support.
punchline: The employee's punishment for calling IT too often is exile to a farm, where even a cow can mock her for not trying the most basic troubleshooting step of rebooting.
summary: A user who leans on IT help too much gets banished to the countryside, where a cow scolds her for skipping the obvious reboot.

title: Ham Sandwich Passes as Solar Panel

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our investors want to see the solar panels you invented.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't invent any solar panels.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Show them something else. They won't know the difference.

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: It looks like a ham sandwich.

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: I was assured that you're stupid.

setting: Office cubicle area and engineering lab
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that investors want to see the solar panels he invented, but Dilbert says he never invented any. The Boss tells him to show them something else because the investors won't know the difference. Dilbert presents a ham sandwich on his lab bench, and the investors note that it looks like a ham sandwich.
punchline: The investors are not fooled by the ham sandwich, and one says he was assured that Dilbert is stupid, implying the Boss misled them about how gullible they would be.
summary: Pressed to demo an invention that does not exist, an engineer offers a lunch item and discovers the people funding him are less gullible than his manager promised.

file: 2008/2008-04-22_indian institute of technology_illegal use of telekinesis_vijay pants.gif
title: Asok Summoned Pantless to IIT

transcript.speaker: Caller (phone)
transcript.text: Asok, you must return to the Indian Institute of Technology to explain your illegal use of telekinesis.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But, but...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: POOF!!

transcript.speaker: Panel member
transcript.text: Vijay, pants.

setting: Asok's office cubicle, then a tribunal hall at the Indian Institute of Technology
situation: Asok gets a phone call ordering him back to the Indian Institute of Technology to answer for illegally using telekinesis. Before he can object, he is magically teleported out of his chair and appears in front of a panel of seated officials, standing there without his clothes. One panelist tells Vijay to deal with the pants.
punchline: Asok is yanked from his desk so abruptly that his clothes are left behind, so he faces the disciplinary panel naked, and the panel's only concern is getting him pants.
summary: A sudden magical summons drops a clothes-free Asok in front of a stern academic tribunal.

title: Productive Day Was Just a Holiday

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had a great day at work. For some reason, no one interrupted me, so I got a lot done.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Today is a holiday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of my victories are tainted.

setting: Outdoors by a trash can, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert cheerfully tells a garbage man that he had a great, productive day at work because nobody interrupted him. The garbage man points out that today is a holiday, so no one else was at the office. Dilbert, at home with Dogbert, glumly admits his victories are tainted.
punchline: Dilbert's big productivity win was only possible because it was a holiday and nobody else was working, so he realizes his success doesn't really count.
summary: A man proudly reports an uninterrupted, productive workday until a passing garbage collector reveals the office was empty for a holiday.

file: 2008/2008-03-03_borrow pen_company like family_culture_search computer_sign docuemnt_test for dugs_trust and respect_manipulate.gif
title: Family Culture Requires Drug Test Consent

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This company is like a family. Our culture is based on trust and respect.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now sign this document that says we can test you for drugs and search your computer and your office.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Can I borrow your pen?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do I look like Bill and Melinda Gates?

setting: Conference room in a corporate office
situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells a new employee that the company is like a family built on trust and respect. He then hands over a document authorizing drug tests and searches of the employee's computer and office. When the employee asks to borrow a pen to sign, Catbert refuses and asks if he looks like Bill and Melinda Gates.
punchline: The company claims to be a trusting family while demanding invasive surveillance consent, and then refuses to share a pen, a gag that also pokes fun at the Gates family's reputation for generosity (the Gates Foundation gives away fortunes).
summary: An HR director praises the company's trust-based family culture, then demands invasive searches and drug testing consent, and balks at lending a pen.

title: Duplicate Assignment Odds Get Worse

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We just discovered that you assigned the same project to both of us a month ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I do that when I think neither of you has more than a 50% chance of doing something right.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hey, I just discovered something.

situation: Dilbert and Alice confront the Boss after finding out he gave both of them the same project a month earlier. The Boss casually explains he does this when he doubts either employee can succeed alone. Asok then announces he has discovered something too, revealing he was also given the same project, and the Boss adjusts his odds.
punchline: Learning that a third person was also assigned the project drops the Boss's estimated chance of success from 50% to 33.3%, underscoring his low opinion of his employees and his wasteful management style.
summary: A manager secretly gives one task to several workers as a hedge against their incompetence, and a third victim turns up to make the odds look even worse.

title: Dogbert CEO Boasts About Salary

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My salary is 400 times more than yours.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My goal is to jack that up to 410, maybe 420.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I hate you for this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So you admit you're selfish?

situation: Dogbert, as CEO, tells a female employee standing at his desk that his salary is 400 times hers and that he intends to raise the multiple to 410 or 420. She says she hates him for it. Dogbert responds by accusing her of being selfish.
punchline: Dogbert flips the moral framing so that the employee's resentment of his enormous pay becomes proof of her own selfishness, rather than his greed.
summary: A canine chief executive brags about his outsized pay and then turns a worker's anger at it into an accusation against her.

title: Blaming Your Own Unpersuasive Recommendation

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The new software is a disaster.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then why did you recommend it?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: This software is your idea. I recommended against it!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: So whose fault is it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The person with the unpersuasive recommendations?

situation: Carol tells the Boss that the new software is a disaster, and he asks why she recommended it. She protests that it was his idea and that she actually advised against it. When she asks whose fault it is, he pins the blame on her for not arguing persuasively enough.
punchline: The Boss dodges responsibility for his own bad decision by claiming the real failure was Carol's inability to talk him out of it.
summary: A manager shifts responsibility for a failed software rollout onto the employee who warned him against it, accusing her of not being convincing enough.

title: Alien Partner's Tongue Interrupts Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We could only find one company in the galaxy willing to form a strategic alliance with us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Admiral B'tang-B'tang is here to describe how we can help each other.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Foop!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop saying "Foop," Ted.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces that only one company in the galaxy would form a strategic alliance with them, and introduces a green alien admiral as the partner. The alien shoots out a long tongue that hits Ted in the face with a 'Foop!' sound. The Boss then blames Ted for the noise, scolding him for saying 'Foop.'
punchline: The Boss ignores the obvious alien assault on his employee and instead reprimands Ted for making the sound effect, showing his obliviousness and eagerness to protect a desperate business partnership.
summary: A manager's only willing alliance partner is a tongue-lashing alien, yet he scolds the victim of the attack rather than the creature responsible.

title: Copies Are Beneath My Status

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need someone to make ten copies of this document.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is there any risk that performing this task will make me appear less valuable?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need someone to tell copy boy to get to work.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Erk!

setting: Conference room meeting around a table
situation: During a meeting, the Boss asks for someone to make ten copies of a document. Asok, holding a paper, responds by asking whether doing the task would make him look less valuable. The Boss then reframes the request, asking for someone to tell 'copy boy' (Asok) to get to work.
punchline: Asok's attempt to avoid menial work out of concern for his status backfires, as the Boss labels him 'copy boy' and delegates the task to him anyway.
summary: An employee worried about looking important gets stuck with a clerical chore and a demeaning nickname when his boss spots his hesitation.

file: 2008/2008-10-03_albanian makeover_bald and chinless_hat makes taller_career helper_minute to drink in_vp of finance.gif
title: Elbonian Makeover Lands Finance Job

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got an Elbonian makeover. Now no one can tell I'm bald and chinless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The hat even makes me look taller. I think this will help my career.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Take a minute to drink this in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just found my new VP of Finance!

setting: Office break area and a meeting room
situation: Wally shows Dilbert his Elbonian makeover, a tall hat and a fake beard, claiming it hides his baldness and lack of a chin and will help his career. In a meeting he invites the Boss to take in his new look, and the Boss responds by announcing he has found his new VP of Finance.
punchline: The Boss is so easily impressed by a ridiculous costume that Wally's cosmetic disguise instantly earns him a senior executive position, mocking how promotions are based on appearance rather than ability.
summary: A tall-hatted, bearded disguise turns out to be all it takes for a lazy employee to be picked for a top finance role.

file: 2008/2008-04-12_matt the temp_fully embrace_catbert_temp concept_temp_find down cable.gif
title: Temp Sent Into Flooded Lot

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Matt the Temp

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our parking lot flooded after the big storm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to wade out there and find our downed power cables.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FZEET!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He seems to fully embrace the temp concept.

situation: The Boss tells Matt, a temporary worker, that the parking lot flooded in a storm and orders him to wade out and locate the downed power cables. A zapping sound effect is heard from outside the window, implying Matt has been electrocuted. The Boss cheerfully remarks that Matt has fully embraced the temp concept while Catbert sits on the desk.
punchline: The Boss sends a disposable temp into a flooded lot to find live power cables, and Matt's electrocution is treated as him happily embracing the idea of being expendable.
summary: A manager sends a temporary employee into floodwater to hunt for fallen electrical lines and treats the resulting zap as a sign of dedication.

file: 2008/2008-03-05_woman_confides_sad story_piano fell on head_dilbert laughs_killed brother.gif
title: Dilbert Laughs at Brother's Piano Death

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I used to have a brother, but a piano fell on his head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I laugh at the wrong times.

setting: Outdoors, walking along a path beside a grassy area
situation: A woman walking with Dilbert confides in him that she once had a brother who was killed when a piano fell on his head. Dilbert bursts into giggles at this tragic story. In the last panel, back at home with Dogbert on the couch, Dilbert offers a lame excuse for his inappropriate laughter.
punchline: Dilbert laughs at a genuinely tragic story and then dismisses his rudeness with the understatement that he sometimes laughs at the wrong times.
summary: A woman shares a grim family loss and Dilbert can't stop himself from giggling, then shrugs it off as a quirk.

title: Wally's Knowledge-Free Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, how do you keep up with all of the changes in technology?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Chasing knowledge is a fool's game, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I use experience to answer questions without the burden of knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Observe.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, if we upgrade our servers, would that solve our network problem?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If the problem is the servers, yes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll ask someone else.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There goes another satisfied customer.

situation: Asok asks Wally how he keeps up with technology, and Wally says he doesn't bother learning and instead relies on experience. To demonstrate, a coworker asks whether upgrading servers will fix a network problem, and Wally gives a vague, tautological answer. The coworker leaves to ask someone else, and Wally calls him a satisfied customer.
punchline: Wally's answer is technically true but completely useless, yet he sarcastically considers the dissatisfied, departing coworker a happy customer.
summary: A lazy engineer shows his colleague how he dodges real technical questions with empty answers that help nobody.

file: 2008/2008-07-20_failed to accomplish.objectives_physical impossiblities_logical impossibilities_unforeseen problems_spying_consumer fraud_win converstaion.gif
title: Dilbert Wins Argument, Only Imagined

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why have you failed to accomplish any of your objectives this quarter?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I took the objectives you gave me and put them into three categories.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The first group includes physical impossibilities, such as being in two places at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The second group includes logical impossibilities, such as anticipating unforeseen problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Last, we have the illegal objectives, including industrial spying and consumer fraud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I spent my time doing things that are both important and legal, while hoping you wouldn't fire me for it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whoa, what just happened? Is it my imagination, or did I just win this conversation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was my imagination.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home
situation: The Boss demands to know why Dilbert accomplished none of his quarterly objectives. Dilbert gives a calm, logical breakdown sorting the goals into physically impossible, logically impossible and illegal, and says he did the important legal work instead. He then realizes he seems to have won the exchange, but at home with Dogbert he admits it was only in his imagination.
punchline: Dilbert's perfectly reasoned rebuttal to his boss never actually happened, because in real life employees never win arguments against unreasonable management.
summary: An engineer fantasizes about dismantling his boss's impossible goals with flawless logic before admitting the confrontation never took place.

file: 2008/2008-07-19_new job_miserable and helpless_women_attracted to men_salary ranges_trophy wives_carnival skanks.gif
title: Dilbert's Demoralizing Salary Attraction Chart

transcript.text: Dilbert's moral compass is damaged.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's a chart that shows the sort of women that are attracted to men at various salary ranges.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Trophy wives are at the top, obviously, and down in your range we have the carnival skanks.

situation: Dilbert explains that his new job is to make employees feel miserable and helpless. He then shows Asok a long chart of what kind of women are attracted to men at different salary levels. He points out that trophy wives are at the top, while Asok's pay grade lands him among the carnival skanks.
punchline: Dilbert demonstrates his new demoralizing job by insulting a coworker's salary and romantic prospects, showing his moral compass really is damaged.
summary: Having taken a job whose goal is to crush morale, Dilbert shows a young colleague a chart implying his low pay condemns him to unappealing romantic options.

file: 2008/2008-03-30_dont know_fail test_it is what it is_security audit_developers.gif
title: The Boss Fails the Turing Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The security audit accidentally locked all of the developers out of the system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, it is what it is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does that help?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't know what you don't know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Congratulations. You're the first human to fail the Turing test.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Um. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is what it is?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why didn't you say that in the first place?

situation: Dilbert reports that a security audit has locked all the developers out of the system. The Boss responds only with empty platitudes like 'it is what it is' and 'you don't know what you don't know.' Dilbert says the Boss is the first human to fail the Turing test, and when the Boss asks what that means, Dilbert answers with the Boss's own cliche, which the Boss accepts.
punchline: The Boss is so reliant on canned, meaningless phrases that he sounds like a failed chatbot, and he only understands the insult when it is phrased as one of his own platitudes.
summary: A manager who answers a system outage with nothing but stock phrases is told he resembles a malfunctioning machine, and only grasps the point when the insult is repackaged in his own clichés.
keywords: you don't know what you don't know

title: Killer Robot Fires On Skeptic

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you really think it's a good idea to build killer robots just because our spam filter ordered you?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FZEEEET!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the worst thing that could happen?

situation: A coworker questions whether Dilbert should build killer robots simply because the company's spam filter told him to. Dilbert's robot answers by zapping the coworker with a ray. Dilbert then asks what the worst thing that could happen is, while the smoking, scorched coworker stands beside him.
punchline: Dilbert asks what the worst that could happen is right after the robot has just blasted his critic, so the answer is standing there smoking.
summary: A man scolds Dilbert for obeying his spam filter's order to build killer robots, and the robot promptly zaps him.

title: Financial Planner Insults Client First

transcript.text: Dogbert the Financial Planner

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You are a financial troglodyte!!!

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Do I get some advice now?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, our first meeting is just to soften you up.

situation: Dogbert, working as a financial planner, tells a client that investing is too complicated for his tiny brain and then shouts that he is a financial troglodyte. The bewildered client asks when he will get advice, and Dogbert explains the insults are a deliberate softening-up tactic for the first meeting.
punchline: Dogbert treats insulting and belittling clients as a standard sales technique to make them more compliant before any actual advice is given.
summary: A canine money manager berates his customer as hopelessly ignorant and calls it a deliberate opening strategy.

title: Executive Retreat Somewhere Warm: Hell

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, book an executive retreat so we can figure out which one of you to downsize.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Find us someplace warm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a pool?

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: You could call it that.

setting: Office cubicle area, then a hot, fiery destination
situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to book an executive retreat where the executives will decide which of them to lay off, and asks for somewhere warm. Carol sends him to Hell, where he arrives sweating with his luggage and asks a devil if there is a pool. The devil replies that you could call it that.
punchline: Carol, tired of the Boss and his layoff plans, takes 'someplace warm' literally and books him a trip to Hell, where the 'pool' is presumably a lake of fire.
summary: Told to find a warm getaway for a layoff-planning retreat, a put-upon assistant sends her boss straight to the underworld.

title: Manufactured Urgency Replaces Missing Coffee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're out of coffee.

transcript.text: Can you give me a false sense of urgency and some unnecessary stress to compensate?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perfect. I'll see you this afternoon for a second cup.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss the office is out of coffee. The Boss asks Dilbert to supply a false sense of urgency and unnecessary stress as a substitute stimulant. Dilbert invents a looming CEO visit deadline, and the Boss happily asks him to come back in the afternoon for more.
punchline: The Boss treats artificial deadline pressure as a caffeine substitute, and Dilbert's made-up stress works so well that the Boss wants a refill like a second cup of coffee.
summary: With the coffee gone, a manager requests invented panic as a replacement pick-me-up and promptly asks for seconds.

file: 2008/2008-12-09_job_lose my job_rate service superiro_service_successful man_survey_loose job_loose wife_business.gif
title: Begging For Superior Survey Ratings

transcript.speaker: Service Representative

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: A desk or counter in a service office
situation: A service representative tells Dilbert, his customer, that he will be sent a satisfaction survey. The representative pressures him to give top marks in every category by claiming he will lose his job and his wife will leave him if he doesn't. Dilbert responds by asking whether the wife is cute.
punchline: Dilbert deflects the emotional guilt trip by asking about the wife's looks, implying he might give a lower rating if it would free up an attractive woman.
summary: A pleading service rep guilt-trips a customer into perfect survey scores, and the customer's only reply is a cheeky question about the rep's wife.

title: Dilbert Predicts Boss's Convenient Interruption

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a short question, so get ready to make your move.

situation: Dilbert stands in front of the Boss's desk and announces that he is only going through the motions of asking a question, since something always interrupts him before he can. He lists the likely excuses, such as a ringing phone, a meeting, or a carpet fire, then tells the Boss to get ready to make his move.
punchline: The Boss is so reliably evasive that Dilbert can predict his excuses in advance and sarcastically warns him to start dodging, since the question is short.
summary: Expecting his boss to dodge him yet again, an employee lists the evasions in advance and invites him to start.

file: 2008/2008-11-25_coldness of the grave_dress it up_high in demand_mad_time_time management_waiting.gif

situation: Dilbert and a coworker sit at a conference table waiting for a late attendee. Dilbert explains that Alice is chronically late and will excuse it by claiming to be in high demand. In the last panel Alice has appeared behind him with a furious glare, and Dilbert shivers.

summary: While griping about a tardy colleague's excuses, a man gets chilled by the sudden arrival of the very woman he was mocking.

situation: Dilbert asks Ratbert to act as his lawyer in a lawsuit against the company's CEO. Ratbert agrees only if Dilbert obeys every instruction without question or hesitation. Dilbert worries the commands might be painful and done purely for Ratbert's amusement.

summary: A man hoping to hire a tiny lawyer learns the price of representation is total obedience to a creature who plans to enjoy tormenting him.

title: Catbert Predicts The Boss's Sneeze

The Boss, determined to prove he is not predictable, tries to suppress the sneeze, and his head swells up grotesquely from the effort. Catbert then shows a drawing he made the day before that depicts exactly this outcome.
punchline: The Boss's frantic attempt to avoid being predictable ends up being exactly what Catbert had already predicted, proving him thoroughly predictable.
summary: Told he is predictable, a boss strains to hold back a sneeze just to prove otherwise, only to discover his cat-like HR adviser had already sketched the swollen-headed result.

title: Too Stupid to Collect Unemployment

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, I have to fire you for posting a comic comparing managers to drunken lemurs.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You won't be eligible for unemployment benefits unless you can prove you were stupid as opposed to malicious.

transcript.text: Is there another explanation for working here?
