He explains that Wally can only claim unemployment benefits if he proves his offense was stupidity rather than malice. Wally calmly offers his decision to work at the company as proof of his stupidity.
punchline: Wally argues that the only way to explain why anyone would work at this company is stupidity, which makes his case for benefits airtight while insulting the employer.
summary: A cat in charge of personnel tells a fired slacker he must prove he is dumb rather than spiteful to get benefits, and the slacker points to his own employment as the evidence.

title: Hyperinflation Makes Water Unaffordable

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonian inflation reaches a billion percent, daily

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Is this enough for a small?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: A minute ago, yes. Now it costs a hundred times more.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Problem solved.

setting: A muddy Elbonian roadside stand selling water, under a tree
situation: An Elbonian customer carries a huge sack of money to a stand selling fetid water and asks if it is enough for a small serving. The vendor says it would have been a minute ago, but inflation has made the price a hundred times higher. In the last panel the customer has lost the cash, the sack is shrunken and the customer seems to have given up on buying.
punchline: With hyperinflation, the customer decides he no longer needs to buy water, so the price problem is 'solved' by simply giving up (or dying of thirst).
summary: A shopper hauling a giant bag of cash discovers that runaway inflation has priced swamp water out of reach by the time he reaches the counter.

title: Cubicle Is a Giant Mushroom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that you're out of the loop, your new cubicle will be a giant mushroom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a pleasant environment except when the mushroom gets its nutrients.

transcript.speaker: Cow (thought)
transcript.text: Nutrients?

setting: Office floor with a giant mushroom-shaped cubicle
situation: The Boss tells a bald employee, who has been cut out of the loop, that his new cubicle is a giant mushroom house. He cheerfully explains it's pleasant except when the mushroom feeds on its nutrients. A cow looks on and thinks about the word 'nutrients'.
punchline: The old saying about mushrooms being kept in the dark and fed manure is made literal: the employee kept out of the loop is housed in a mushroom, and the cow realizes what its nutrients are.
summary: A manager literalizes the idea of keeping staff in the dark by relocating a sidelined worker into a mushroom house that gets fertilized, much to a cow's dawning realization.

file: 2008/2008-05-18_discriminating_genetic reason_idiot_intolerance_turned down for raise_maximum raise_learning problem_desparation_money.gif
title: Alice Turns Intolerance Into Discrimination Claim

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I can't give you the maximum raise because you don't respect other people's differences.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why are you discriminating against me for my intolerance?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I am intolerant for some genetic reason, then I can't help it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And if I'm intolerant because I can't learn to be otherwise, then obviously I have a learning problem.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why is it acceptable for you to be an idiot but not acceptable for me to notice it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You need to start appreciating me for my intolerance!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And while I'm at it, allow me to mention that a monkey's seat cushion has better views than what I'm looking at right now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not quite sure where to go with this.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ooh! Ooh! I have a suggestion.

situation: The Boss denies Alice the maximum raise because she doesn't respect other people's differences. Alice turns the argument around, claiming her intolerance is genetic or a learning problem and that he is discriminating against her. She escalates into insulting him, and he is left unsure how to respond.
punchline: Alice uses the language of diversity and disability protection to defend her own intolerance, then insults the boss and offers to tell him how to proceed, probably with an even bigger raise.
summary: Told she's too intolerant to earn a top raise, Alice flips the logic into a discrimination complaint and berates her baffled manager.

title: Legacy Systems Manager Becomes Troll

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got reassigned to manage our legacy systems. The dress code is "troll."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My cubicle is under the walkway. My side job is scaring vendors.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that hard?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only the first day. After you eat one vendor, word gets around.

situation: Dilbert, dressed as a hairy troll in yellow polka-dot shorts and carrying a walking staff, tells Dogbert he has been reassigned to manage the company's legacy systems. His cubicle is under a walkway and his side job is scaring vendors. Dogbert asks if that is hard, and Dilbert says it only takes eating one vendor before word spreads.
punchline: Managing legacy systems turns Dilbert into a literal bridge troll who eats vendors, implying that sales people are best kept away by sheer terror, and that a single cannibalistic example is enough to make the rest keep their distance.
summary: A reassigned Dilbert has become a bridge troll guarding old systems and discouraging salespeople by devouring one of them as a warning.

title: Contract Signed During Miocene Epoch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just finished a contract I started during the Miocene epoch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... Assuming this hoof fossil is a signature.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These things can't be rushed.

situation: The Boss stands by Dilbert's cubicle and announces he has just completed a contract he began millions of years ago. He holds up a fossilized hoof as the supposed signature, then declares that such things cannot be rushed while Dilbert sits silently at his desk.
punchline: The Boss treats a contract that took millions of years to close as normal diligence, absurdly claiming that slow business deals simply can't be hurried.
summary: A boss proudly reports wrapping up a deal that dragged on for geological ages and cites a fossil as the signature.

title: Graphics Support Doesn't Make Logos

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I need you to design a logo for our prototype.

transcript.speaker: Graphics Support Employee
transcript.text: We don't do that. We're the graphics support department. Talk to the graphics production department.

transcript.speaker: Voice from building
transcript.text: They create logos?

transcript.speaker: Voice from building
transcript.text: No, they tell people we do it.

setting: Office desk, then exterior of an office building
situation: Dilbert asks a bearded employee in the graphics support department to design a logo for his prototype. The employee refuses and redirects him to the graphics production department. In the last panel, two voices over a view of the building reveal that production only tells people that support does the work.
punchline: The two departments each deflect logo work onto the other, so the department that supposedly creates logos does nothing but pass the buck.
summary: Two similarly named departments each insist the other handles the actual design work, leaving a simple request stuck in a loop of redirection.

title: Hellness Program Saves Money Now

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Employee wellness programs save money in the long run, but that does you no good.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You need a program that can save you money now, when it makes a difference.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A hellness program? I don't like the sound of that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Try to see the big picture for once.

setting: The Boss's office, then a conference room
situation: Ratbert, standing on the Boss's desk, pitches a program that saves money immediately rather than the long-term savings of employee wellness. The Boss mishears or misreads the concept as a "hellness" program and objects to the name, while Alice tells him to try to see the big picture.
punchline: The proposed "hellness" program is the opposite of a wellness program, implying it would save the company money now by making employees miserable, and the Boss is only bothered by the sound of it.
summary: A tiny advisor sells the boss on a short-term cost-cutting scheme that is the evil twin of employee wellness, and the boss objects only to its name.

title: Boss Dithers Longer Out of Spite

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I need a decision, but it involves more than one variable, and I know you can't handle that.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll give you an hour to dither before I badger you into making the correct decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to dither for two hours just to show her who is in charge.

situation: Carol, the boss's assistant, hands him a document needing a decision and bluntly says he can't handle multiple variables. She offers him an hour to dither before she pressures him into the right choice. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, thinks to himself that he'll dither for two hours instead to assert his authority.
punchline: The Boss, knowing he is incompetent and will end up being steered by Carol anyway, wastes extra time out of petty spite to feel in charge.
summary: A sharp assistant gives her indecisive manager a deadline to stall, and he responds by deliberately doubling the delay to prove he's the one in control.

file: 2008/2008-02-23_firing_humorless stain_interview boss_soul of humanity_support thesis_worship satan.gif
title: Reporter Baits Boss Over Comic Firing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Gazette is doing a story on your firing of an employee for posting a comic on the wall.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need some quotes that support my thesis of you being a humorless stain on the soul of humanity.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you say you worship Satan, or do you simply respect his no-nonsense approach to discipline?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a newspaper reporter, interviews the Boss across his desk about firing an employee who posted a comic on the wall. He openly admits he wants quotes proving the Boss is a humorless stain on humanity, then asks a loaded question about whether the Boss worships Satan.
punchline: Dogbert's interview question offers only two options, both damning, so the Boss cannot answer without sounding like a devil-worshipper or a heartless disciplinarian.
summary: A canine journalist grills the boss about a petty firing and fishes for quotes that confirm his own harsh opinion of him.

title: Hiring Someone Who Punched Their Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I want you to interview a job candidate. Let me know what you think.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why did you leave your last job?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I punched my boss.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's exactly what we need.

situation: The Boss asks Alice to interview a job candidate and report back her opinion. During the interview Alice asks why he left his last job, and he admits he punched his boss. Alice then tells the Boss the candidate is exactly what the company needs.
punchline: Alice's enthusiastic endorsement of a man who assaulted his boss implies that she thinks the Pointy-Haired Boss deserves a punch.
summary: A candidate's confession of violence toward his former manager makes him the perfect hire in the eyes of the interviewer who works for a terrible boss.

title: Fired Employee's Sarcastic Server Warning

transcript.speaker: Fired Employee
transcript.text: I don't hold any grudges about being fired for hanging a comic on the wall.

transcript.speaker: Fired Employee
transcript.text: The company will be fine without my secret and exclusive knowledge of the critical systems.

transcript.speaker: Fired Employee
transcript.text: If the framistan starts to gabol, just purge the cache within sixty seconds and the servers won't explode.

situation: An employee carrying a box of his belongings stands before the seated Boss after being fired for hanging a comic on the wall. He sarcastically claims to hold no grudge and says the company will be fine without his unique knowledge. He then casually mentions a made-up procedure that must be followed within sixty seconds to prevent the servers from exploding.
punchline: The fired employee pretends to be gracious while revealing that only he knows how to prevent a catastrophic server failure, leaving the company at his mercy.
summary: A sacked worker leaves behind a breezy, deadly serious warning about the critical systems that only he understands.

title: Leadership By Words, Not Facts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, put together a document showing how our budget aligns with our priorities.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: It doesn't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write it so it seems like it does.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Isn't that lying?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I call it leadership by words.

situation: The Boss asks Tina to produce a document proving the budget matches the company's priorities. Tina points out that it doesn't, so he tells her to write it so that it appears to. When she asks if that is lying, he rebrands it as a leadership technique.
punchline: The Boss relabels deliberate deception as 'leadership by words' to excuse asking an employee to misrepresent the budget.
summary: A manager orders a report that makes a mismatched budget look aligned with goals and dismisses the ethical objection with a flattering euphemism.

title: Time Management Seminar Turns Nihilistic

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's seminar on time management and evolution.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The key to good time management is skipping unimportant tasks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In module two, I will show you that everything you do is unimportant because your genes are a dead end.

setting: Stage of a seminar hall with red curtains
situation: Dogbert stands on a stool on a stage giving a seminar on time management and evolution. He first says the key to time management is skipping unimportant tasks, then tells the audience that the next module will prove everything they do is unimportant because their genes are an evolutionary dead end.
punchline: Dogbert's logic implies that if everything is unimportant, you can skip every task, and he cheerfully insults the audience's genetic legacy while doing so.
summary: A pompous canine lecturer sells a productivity talk that cheerfully slides into the claim that nothing anyone does matters.

title: Smiting the Office Snitch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pronounced Hay-soos

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you find out who ratted you out, Jesus?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FZEEET!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe you have a way of finding out that sort of thing.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug asks Jesus, a cubicle worker unpacking a box, whether he found out who ratted him out. A lightning bolt strikes the coworker, leaving him scorched and smoking. Jesus, still calm, keeps unpacking while the coworker realizes Jesus may have supernatural ways of finding out.
punchline: The office worker named Jesus (pronounced Hay-soos) shares a name with the Son of God, so he apparently answers the question about the snitch by smiting the person who asked.
summary: A man who shares a name with a famous deity gets a lightning bolt to the face for gossiping about who informed on him.

title: Stink Eye Versus Banned Telekinesis

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Beware the power of stink eye, intern. I will make you bow to my will!

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Grrrr!!!

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Must... use... banned telekinetic powers to neutralize threat.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You have a call from the Indian Institute of Technology. It's someone from the Department of Things You Shouldn't Do.

situation: The boss tries to intimidate a young intern with a stare, and the intern, thinking in a thought bubble, decides to fight back with secret banned telekinetic powers. The boss ends up slumped over with storm clouds above his head while the intern holds his head in strain. A coworker then announces a call from a technology institute's department of forbidden actions.
punchline: The intern's use of forbidden mind powers is immediately flagged by an absurd official body, implying that even secret supernatural abuses get reported and policed in the corporate world.
summary: A boss's attempt at intimidation backfires when the intern secretly unleashes forbidden mental powers and gets a call about it.
keywords: department of things you shouldn't do

title: CEO Buys Bonus From Distracted Board

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO presents to the board of directors

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: An underling made these PowerPoint slides and I don't understand them.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: But it doesn't matter because all of you are too preoccupied with your day jobs and mistresses to pay attention.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Who votes to give me a huge bonus just to end this meeting?

transcript.speaker: Board Member
transcript.text: Aye

transcript.speaker: Board Member
transcript.text: Aye

transcript.speaker: Board Member
transcript.text: Aye

situation: A CEO presents a confusing PowerPoint diagram made by an underling to the board of directors. He admits he doesn't understand it, then points out that the board members aren't paying attention anyway. He asks for a vote on a huge bonus for ending the meeting, and the board members unanimously say aye.
punchline: The board is so distracted by their own jobs and affairs that they'll rubber-stamp an enormous executive bonus just to escape a boring meeting, showing how little real oversight exists.
summary: A clueless chief executive exploits his inattentive directors by trading a bonus vote for the mercy of ending the presentation.

file: 2008/2008-10-14_dogcart the ceo_420 times_smarter_system is flawed_contradicting your boss.gif
title: CEO Pay Proves Superior Intelligence

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I earn 420 times what you make. That means I'm 420 times smarter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, it means the system is deeply flawed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you were 420 times smarter, you wouldn't be contradicting your boss right now.

setting: Executive office with a large desk, Dogbert as CEO
situation: Dogbert, acting as CEO, tells Dilbert that earning 420 times his salary proves he is 420 times smarter. Dilbert counters that the pay gap actually shows the compensation system is broken. Dogbert replies that a truly smarter person wouldn't contradict the boss.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses valid criticism of executive pay inequality by arguing that disagreeing with the boss is itself proof of lesser intelligence, a self-serving circular logic.
summary: A canine chief executive justifies his enormous paycheck as proof of genius, then turns the employee's objection into evidence against him.

title: Coworkers Pick Dilbert's Cubicle Outside

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been away from work so long. I wonder if anything has changed.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You weren't here when we moved to new cubicles so your coworkers picked one for you.

setting: Office hallway and the exterior of the office building
situation: Dilbert returns to work after a long absence, wondering aloud whether anything has changed. A horned colleague (the HR-style character in the suit) tells him the office moved to new cubicles and his coworkers chose one for him. The last panel reveals the cubicle is a box hanging off the outside of the building, with Dilbert stuck in it high above the ground.
punchline: His coworkers, resentful of his absence, assigned him a cubicle dangling off the side of the building, a passive-aggressive act of revenge.
summary: A returning employee learns his teammates picked his new workspace and discovers it is a box bolted to the building's exterior.

title: Elbonian Spies Steal Dilbert's Laptop

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Spy
transcript.text: Our spies stole this laptop from an employee named Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Leader
transcript.text: Ha ha! We will find his company's secrets and use them!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Spy
transcript.text: Heh-heh.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six months later

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Do you remember mittens? I loved having mittens.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Shut up!!

setting: Elbonia, a muddy village where people stand waist-deep in mud
situation: Elbonian spies proudly announce they stole a laptop from a man named Dilbert and plan to exploit his company's secrets. Six months later the same Elbonians are stripped of their clothes and sitting in the mud, one wistfully recalling his mittens while the other snaps at him to stop.
punchline: Using the company secrets on the stolen laptop ruined the Elbonians instead of helping them, leaving them even worse off than before, implying the company's business practices are disastrous.
summary: Thieves who swiped a worker's laptop hoping to copy his employer's strategies end up destitute and mittenless after following them.

file: 2008/2008-03-20_smart garbageman_again soul_someone less fortunate_flowers on grave_grave speaks.gif
title: Helping the Less Fortunate: The Dead

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The world's smartest garbage man says I need to help someone less fortunate to regain my soul.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't look at me. I'm happier than a tickled clam.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I brought you some flowers, dead person.

transcript.speaker: Dead Person
transcript.text: I don't need 'em. I'm good.

situation: Dilbert says the world's smartest garbage man told him he must help someone less fortunate to regain his soul. He looks to Ratbert, who insists he is perfectly happy and wants no part of it. Dilbert then visits a cemetery and offers flowers to a dead person, who also declines.
punchline: Dilbert is so determined to find someone less fortunate that he turns to the dead, and even they claim to be doing fine.
summary: Seeking a charity case to restore his soul, Dilbert is turned down by his pet and then by a corpse in a graveyard.

title: Toolbelt Request Has Squirrel Explanation

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: Dilbert, when you come over tonight, wear your toolbelt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because it's sexy?

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: That would be between you and the squirrel that keeps chewing the cable from my satellite dish.

setting: Two homes, connected by a phone call
situation: Liz phones Dilbert and asks him to wear his toolbelt when he comes over that night. Dilbert hopefully assumes she finds it attractive. She deflates the idea by explaining she only wants him to fix her satellite dish, which a squirrel keeps damaging.
punchline: Dilbert mistakes a practical repair request for romantic interest, and Liz bluntly reveals his rival for her attention is a cable-chewing squirrel.
summary: A woman's odd request for her date to bring his tools turns out to be about home repairs, not romance.

title: Critical Updates Excuse for Zero Productivity

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My security software kept insisting that I download critical updates.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't have time to do all that, and I couldn't risk using my computer without critical updates. It was a no-win situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you accomplish anything this week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What part of "no-win" is confusing you?

situation: At a meeting, Wally explains that he got no work done because his security software demanded critical updates. He claims he had no time to install them but couldn't safely use his computer without them. When the Boss asks if he accomplished anything, Dilbert snaps back at him for not grasping the 'no-win' excuse.
punchline: Wally's elaborate 'no-win situation' is a flimsy excuse for doing nothing all week, and Dilbert sarcastically treats the Boss as the dense one for questioning it.
summary: A lazy employee blames nagging security updates for a completely unproductive week, and a colleague mocks the boss for not accepting the excuse.

file: 2008/2008-09-19_eat quieter_asthmatic rhinoceros_rampaging  a cracker festival_prepare sluprer.gif
title: Alice Hates Wally's Loud Eating

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, can you eat quieter?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Crunch crunch mmmph crunch gulp

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You sound like an asthmatic rhinoceros rampaging a cracker festival.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mmmph erm crunch crunch

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Not the beverage!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Prepare slurper! Boop!

situation: Alice asks Wally to eat more quietly while he noisily munches crackers at his desk. She insults his chewing with an elaborate rhinoceros comparison, but he keeps crunching. When he announces he is about to slurp his drink, she recoils in horror.
punchline: Alice's complaint backfires because Wally turns his annoying eating into an even more annoying drinking noise, which he cheerfully announces and seems to enjoy.
summary: A coworker's request for quieter snacking only leads to an even louder, gleefully announced drink slurping.

title: Dilbert's Broken Computer and Coffee Stirrer Fort

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't work on your request this week because my computer is broken and my company is too cheap to replace it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried to borrow one, but the people I work with are a bunch of selfish tools.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I shouldn't take you on sales calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I built a tiny fort out of coffee stirrers.

situation: Dilbert sits at a conference table between a man in a suit and another man, and explains why he didn't complete a request: his computer is broken and the cheap company won't replace it. He complains that coworkers refused to lend him one. When the suited man says he may stop bringing Dilbert on sales calls, Dilbert cheerfully reveals he passed the time building a tiny fort from coffee stirrers.
punchline: Dilbert insults his coworkers and admits to idling away the week building a toy fort, which makes the suited man's reaction (not wanting him on sales calls) entirely justified.
summary: A technician blames a busted computer and stingy employer for missing a deadline, then admits he spent the week playing with craft materials.

title: Chicken Contributes, Pig Committed, Dead Pig

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As I gazed at my bacon and eggs this morning, I realized. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: . . .the chicken contributed, but the pig was committed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I am so clever.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I promise to work like a dead pig, can I go home early?

situation: The Boss presents a slide of bacon and eggs and delivers the classic 'chicken contributes, pig is committed' line about employee commitment, congratulating himself on his cleverness in a thought bubble. Wally, sitting at the table with Dilbert and Alice, responds by offering to work like a dead pig in exchange for leaving early.
punchline: Wally twists the boss's commitment metaphor by pointing out that a dead pig, the ultimate 'committed' one, does no work at all, so he can slack off and leave early.
summary: A manager proudly recycles a breakfast metaphor about dedication, and a lazy employee turns it into a bargain for time off.

file: 2008/2008-04-06_25 questions_before start_bluff_didn't send email_email_excuses_lies to boss_non responsive_slacker_standoff.gif
title: Bluffing About Unsent 25-Question Email

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I planned to be productive this week.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I sent you an e-mail with 25 questions I need answered before I can start on my project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I waited patiently while your non-responsiveness crushed my hopes and dreams.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time to answer 25 questions!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well then, it appears we are at a standoff.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, okay! I'll work all weekend answering your stupid questions!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's great, unless you can't find the e-mail I sent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you really send an e-mail?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's not how I roll.

situation: During a meeting, a bald coworker complains that he cannot start his project because his boss never answered his e-mail of 25 questions. The boss, panicking at the workload, caves and promises to spend the whole weekend answering them. The coworker then hedges that it won't matter if the boss can't find the e-mail, and afterward admits to Dilbert that he never sent it.
punchline: The coworker bluffed the boss into taking the blame and doing extra work for an e-mail that was never actually sent, a claim he can safely make because he also knows the boss won't be able to find it.
summary: A scheming employee guilt-trips his boss into a weekend of work over a message that never existed.

file: 2008/2008-08-17_users want_supply and emnad_idiot_managing_work harder_earn less money_fire me_obvious things.gif
title: The Boss Explains Managing Is Obvious

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Find out what the users want before you build it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you explaining my job to me as if I'm an idiot?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called managing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assume you're dumb because you work harder than I do and earn less money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And my boss would fire me if I just sat in my office and did nothing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I wander around and say obvious things to you idiots until quitting time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I go home and eat until my underpants don't fit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: Dilbert offers the obvious advice to find out what users want before building a product. The Boss takes offense and then candidly describes his job as wandering around saying obvious things so he looks busy, before going home to overeat. He ends by thanking Dilbert for asking, as if Dilbert had inquired about his job.
punchline: The Boss admits that managing consists of stating the obvious to look busy, which is exactly what Dilbert just did, and he concludes with a sarcastic thanks for a question nobody asked.
summary: A manager bristles at obvious advice, then confesses his whole job is to say obvious things to employees until the workday ends.

file: 2008/2008-04-28_planned merger_fast food chain_employees_source of protein_perfect situation_business.gif
title: Merger Partner Plans Employee Burgers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend we cancel our planned merger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They plan to open a chain of fast food restaurants using our employees as a source of protein.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we always waited for the perfect situation, we'd never get anything done.

situation: Dilbert advises the Boss to cancel a planned merger because the other company intends to open fast food restaurants that use the merged company's employees as a protein source. The Boss brushes off the cannibalism warning, saying that waiting for perfect conditions would mean nothing ever gets done.
punchline: The Boss treats the prospect of employees being turned into food as an acceptable imperfection, showing how little he values his staff and how business clichés get used to justify anything.
summary: A manager waves away a warning that the acquiring firm plans to turn the workforce into restaurant meat, citing a cliché about not waiting for ideal conditions.

title: Placebo Juice for Crushed Souls

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I hear your soul was crushed and Catbert slapped off your dried-up head.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Try this juice I've been selling on the side. It's made from actual berries.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Spoit!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Oh, crud. That was the placebo.

situation: Tina approaches Dilbert, who sits slumped and headless at his desk after his soul was crushed and Catbert knocked off his dried-up head. She pours her side-business berry juice into the neck opening of his body. Dilbert's head reappears and spits it out, and she realizes she gave him the placebo version.
punchline: Tina's side-hustle health drink comes in a fake placebo version, and she gives the useless one to a man whose head has literally been knocked off, implying the real product is hardly more effective.
summary: A coworker tries to revive a lifeless, headless colleague by pouring a dubious juice into his collar, only to admit she grabbed the fake version.

file: 2008/2008-11-22_date_perfect_low entertainment value_use our phones_surf the internet_call it a date_perfect woman.gif

punchline: Dilbert is delighted that a woman who ends conversation and lets him stare at his phone in silence is his idea of the perfect woman, which is a sad commentary on his social life and screen addiction.
summary: A bored date proposes that they simply look at their phones together, and Dilbert thinks he has finally found his ideal partner.

title: Dogbert's Squalor-Filled Retirement Plan

transcript.text: Dogbert the Financial Planner

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend a diversified portfolio.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And bacon.

setting: Dogbert's financial planning office, across a desk from a client
situation: Dogbert, working as a financial planner, tells a client that medical advances could let him live to 200. He explains that even with a good plan, most of those years will be spent in poverty. His investment advice is a diversified portfolio plus bacon, while the client looks increasingly grim.
punchline: Dogbert's 'good' financial plan still leaves the client broke for 120 years, and his only extra advice is bacon, a throwaway indulgence that mocks the idea of serious retirement planning.
summary: A canine money manager warns that longer lifespans mean decades of poverty no matter how well you save, then caps his advice with a snack suggestion.

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: I'll give you a banana if you show me your cubicles.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, assumes a young girl is visiting for Take Your Daughter to Work Day, but she says she is a freelancer. She explains she is choosing between being a prison guard or a monkey trainer, so the Boss wonders how visiting his office could help. She then offers him a banana to show her the cubicles.
punchline: The girl treats the office as a zoo or prison, implying the workers in cubicles are like caged monkeys who can be lured with a banana, and the Boss is so clueless he is willing to play along.
summary: A young freelancer researching jobs in animal handling and corrections tours the office, bribing the boss with fruit to see the cages.
keywords: take your daughter to work day

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: See my zipper? I took in a family of squirrels!

setting: Office conference table, likely during lunch
situation: Dilbert shares a strange dream about wearing a goat costume, and his coworker Topper immediately tries to one-up him with increasingly bizarre claims. Topper says he donated all his organs and uses his hollow torso as a backpack, then shows off a zipper where he houses a family of squirrels. Dilbert tries to share a story about a date but Topper keeps topping him.
punchline: Topper's compulsive one-upmanship escalates to absurd, impossible claims, such as keeping a family of squirrels in a zippered hollow torso, making any normal story pointless to share.
summary: A coworker who can't resist outdoing everyone's stories boasts about turning his own emptied body into a squirrel shelter.

title: Is This Conversation Just Venting?

transcript.speaker: Woman in purple dress
transcript.text: And then she acted as if I have no right to my opinion!

transcript.text: Maybe we're bonding.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe not.

situation: A coworker stands in Dilbert's cubicle and vents about another woman who dismissed her opinion. Dilbert interrupts to ask whether she is sharing anything useful or just unloading her feelings on him. She suggests they might be bonding, and he flatly rejects the idea.
punchline: The coworker casually reframes her venting as friendship-building, and Dilbert bluntly shuts down the notion that being a captive audience for her complaints counts as bonding.
summary: A colleague's complaint session is cut short when Dilbert questions its purpose and declines her attempt to call it friendship.

file: 2008/2008-07-09_dead squirrel_insulting_knitting sweater_makeup_meeting_no potential benefit_time management_time management expert_woman as example_hideous outfit_business.gif

transcript.text: For example, why bother putting on makeup if you're going to wear that hideous outfit?

punchline: Dogbert's supposedly helpful efficiency advice is really just a thinly veiled, escalating insult at a colleague's expense, ending in a ridiculous analogy.
summary: A consulting dog uses a coworker's wardrobe as a cruel illustration of wasted effort during a seminar on productivity.

title: Alice Wishes Misfortune on Coworker

transcript.text: Alice, did you make those code changes yet?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No. I find your specifications to be vague and uncompelling. They are a breeding ground for ennui.

transcript.text: Is there any way I can cheer you up?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe if something awful happened to you.

situation: A coworker asks Alice whether she has made the code changes he requested. Alice refuses, saying his specifications are vague, uncompelling and a source of boredom. When he offers to cheer her up, she says it would help if something awful happened to him.
punchline: Alice responds to a sincere offer of help by cheerfully admitting she would be happiest if the requester suffered a misfortune, showing her hostility toward bad specifications and the people who write them.
summary: A developer turns down a request for code changes by blasting the poor specs, then tells the requester his suffering is the only thing that could improve her mood.

file: 2008/2008-02-17_argument_assignment_boss_cubicle_less is more_more is less_not interchangable_wrong pharsing.gif
title: Tough Love and Backwards Sayings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's your assignment. Do it! Do it! Do it, you idiot!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What kind of management is that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's called tough love.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tough love only makes sense if I am doing something wrong and refuse to change.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, sometimes more is less.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The saying is "less is more," not "more is less."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If less equals more, then more must equal less.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Duh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the part where you usually refuse to admit you are wrong.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an assignment while shouting at him and calls it tough love. Dilbert points out that tough love only makes sense if he is doing something wrong and refusing to change. The Boss then tries to defend himself with a muddled argument about the saying "less is more" and gets corrected.
punchline: Dilbert predicts that the Boss will now do what he always does and refuse to admit he is wrong, which exposes the Boss's stubbornness and his shaky logic.
summary: A boss defends his shouted orders as a kind of kindness, then flubs a proverb to avoid conceding the point, and his employee calls out the pattern.

title: Ghost of Popular Predecessor Haunts Alice

transcript.speaker: Ghost

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: Nice try, but you can only kill me with kindness.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa! Gaaa! Gaaa!

situation: A white ghost appears in Alice's cubicle and introduces itself as the spirit of the well-liked employee who held her job before. It says it has stayed behind to remind everyone how unpleasant she is by comparison. Alice, furious, lunges at the ghost and tries to strangle it, screaming.
punchline: Alice's attempt to kill the ghost with violence only proves its point, since the ghost can only be destroyed by kindness, which she is notoriously unable to show.
summary: A friendly predecessor's spirit lingers to highlight Alice's harsh personality, and her violent reaction confirms the comparison.

file: 2008/2008-11-02_fish_microwave_stink_offcie_impossible_microwave things that smell bad_job performance_slippery slope_socioathy_liberating feeling_felt bad_extra fish_animals.gif
title: Wally Microwaves Fish Out of Spite

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: That will stink up the office and make it impossible for anyone else to enjoy life.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Isn't there something else you could eat?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not going to eat it. I just like to microwave things that smell bad.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: After I stopped caring about my job performance, it was a slippery slope to complete sociopathy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a liberating feeling. I can't remember the last time I felt bad.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have an extra fish?

situation: Wally walks past Carol's cubicle carrying a fish and announces he is going to microwave it. Carol objects that the smell will ruin the office for everyone, but Wally explains he has no intention of eating it; he simply enjoys making things smell. He says that giving up on his job led him to complete sociopathy, which feels liberating, and he ends by asking Carol for another fish.
punchline: Wally has become so thoroughly checked out that he deliberately stinks up the office for fun, treats his lack of conscience as freedom, and wants even more fish to do it again.
summary: After giving up on his career, a lazy employee gleefully reheats rotten seafood just to annoy his coworkers and asks for more.

title: Boss Explains Pay Freeze With Sock

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your salary is already above the midpoint for your pay range.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Excuse me while I remove a sock to explain what will happen to your pay going forward.

transcript.text: Let's say the sock is inflation and my hand is your paycheck.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert during a salary discussion that his pay is already above the midpoint of his range. He then takes off a sock to illustrate what will happen to Dilbert's pay, and in the last panel he pulls the sock over his hand, using it as a demonstration of inflation swallowing a paycheck.
punchline: The Boss's sock-puppet demonstration shows that inflation will swallow Dilbert's paycheck, so his real pay will shrink because he won't get meaningful raises.
summary: A manager uses a sock pulled over his hand as a visual aid to tell an employee that his earnings will be eaten away by rising prices.

file: 2008/2008-10-02_cow supervisor_bovine overlord_usurper_food chain_kind of cool_position in food chain.gif

summary: A boss who happens to be a cow relishes ruling over the humans who once ate his kind and demands loyalty unto death.

transcript.text: And never, ever refer to the company as any kind of sandwich you wouldn't want to eat.

He lists increasingly grim phrases to avoid, such as comparisons to Lincoln at Ford's Theatre, circling the drain, and anything involving flies. When he warns against calling the company an unappetizing sandwich, the Boss exclaims that this is his favorite one.
punchline: The Boss's favorite way to describe the company is the exact phrase Dogbert warns against, implying that his own view of the company is already disastrous and that he is hopeless at managing his public image.
summary: A consultant dog drills a clueless executive on which doom-laden metaphors to avoid, only to discover the executive's go-to line is the forbidden one.

situation: The Boss confronts Wally about blaming his poor productivity on seven dead people and three nonexistent ones. Wally explains he switched from blaming living coworkers because it made meetings awkward. When the Boss asks whose fault that is, Wally sips his coffee, implying the Boss is next to be blamed.
punchline: Wally's habit of blaming others for his laziness is so entrenched that when asked to take responsibility, he starts blaming the Boss, creating exactly the awkwardness he claimed to avoid.
summary: A boss calls out an employee's creative excuses for low output, only to become the next target of blame.

situation: A bald executive stands at a podium and announces a write-off of 47 billion dollars in bad loans. He deflects responsibility by blaming poor regulatory oversight. He then asks the audience whether anyone supports a big pay cut for the regulators he has just blamed.
